Śrīḥ.
May there be well-being! Salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas!
May there be freedom from obstacles!
[I offer praise] to the great mountain that is my maternal grandfather, and to his even greater grandfather.
I bow to the cause of the worlds, the elephant [Gajendra] who was above his neck.
The supreme reality of the Lord is devoid of beginning, middle, and end;
it is the support of all worlds, yet itself unsupported and immutable.
I perpetually bow down to the Lord of Ambikā, the Sovereign, who is an ocean of infinite bliss and consciousness, and whose prowess is marvelous.
I bow to the city of Hālāsya; I bow, I bow to Hemābjinī as well.
I bow to her whose eyes are like beautiful fish; I bow to Sundaranāyaka.
Salutation to Śiva, the perfectly complete, the cool one, the self whose nature is consciousness;
salutation to the Lord of the mind, the Protector, the radiant Brahman.
The Daughter of the Mountain King, whose essence is the nectar of the ocean of bliss,
by embracing the pair of her jar-like breasts,
[adorns] his slender body with horripilation...
I worship the Lord, the Master of Madhurāpura, who is known through the Vedas.
I bow to Mahātripurasundarī, who holds a noose and a goad, radiant with a sugarcane bow and flowers, and resembles the rising sun.
Salutations to that Lord Sundara, the dweller of Hālāsya,
by whom the sixty-four kinds of divine play were manifested upon the earth.
I eternally contemplate within my heart the goddess of the illustrious Sundareshvara, whose eyes are like those of a shaphara fish and who dwells in the Kadamba forest.
I take refuge in him whose flow is the intoxication of compassion, who wanders in the forest of liberation,
whose limbs are dark as a monsoon cloud, and whose face is like that of a young elephant.
[He saw] the Child, who nourishes the womb of the daughter of the Himālaya, endowed with the six faces situated upon the immovable throne of the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
Renowned as Śrī-Kailāsa, it is the best among the glorious mountains;
it is served by the gods headed by Śrīpati for the sake of prosperity and liberation.
Even among the givers of fortune, he is the supreme giver of fortune, his abode proclaimed by Śrīkaṇṭha;
for the sake of Śrī herself, he has risen preeminent, having personally conquered the Ocean of Milk.
Merely by hearing it, it removes the cycle of birth and death for people;
it is endowed with all powers and is worshipped by all the worlds.
Even for those who make this earth crowded with gods, it bestows all perfections;
yet for those who behold it as a great forest of asceticism, it grants final liberation.
He was surrounded on all sides by various hosts of spirits, and by the permission of the Lord of the Universe, he was protected even from those gods who are otherwise inaccessible.
Renowned throughout the three worlds and as white as the orb of the moon,
it exists on the earth in the northeastern quarter, even within the minds of learned men.
In the center of that Mount Meru is a most excellent middle peak,
a great summit adorned with a vast mandala.
Above that, the wind becomes exceedingly still, like the surface of a mirror;
it becomes a vast expanse, as pure as the sky.
That place, which cannot be conquered by the obstacles to austerity such as desire and other adversaries, protects it just as the mind of the lords of sages does.
The forest was filled with wish-fulfilling trees laden with fruits and flowers,
with mountains composed of wish-granting gems, and even with manifestations of the cow of plenty.
With excellent rivers consisting of milk, curd, ghee, honey, and nectar, and with most charming paved floors variegated with various jewels; (p. 4)
And with the mansions of the Pramathas, which resembled the peaks of Mount Meru,
featuring many walls, gates, and gate-towers made of gold.
With splendors equal to ten million suns and radiance like ten million moons,
[they...]
May there be well-being.
Salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
May there be auspiciousness!
On the 12th day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in the Krodhi year, on a Friday.
The beginning of the Īpustakavavaravadaka. May there be freedom from obstacles. Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
O Viśvarūpa, obeisance to you, the eternal one who is affectionate toward your devotees;
if my *liṅga* or image is broken, how could there be anything more than destruction?
O Śiva, if an obstacle or other impediment has arisen, how can one perform worship?
O Blessed One, explain this in detail; I wish to hear it now.

The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain in due order the various defects and so forth regarding the self-manifested (svayambhū) Liṅga with Ambā, or the image (bimba), wherever it may be located.
O Goddess, [I shall explain] the defects and the fruits of pacification separately and in detail,
regarding a linga that is broken, cracked, or struck by fire or lightning.
O Goddess, there will be supreme fear for the kingdom for up to three years, without a doubt;
the king will be afflicted by suffering and grief, and there will be a decline in strength.
If it is broken, shattered into pieces, destroyed, or deficient,
there shall be immediate abandonment of the region, and the king shall suffer defeat.
O Goddess, he shall meet his end within three months, without a doubt— whether slain by stones, weapons, and the like, or by the earth, or by enemies.
The king shall meet his death; the fourfold army and the chariots [shall perish]; during the siege, there shall be the flow of blood, along with sweating and trembling, and he shall not survive.
O Goddess, that kingdom, city, or royal capital shall perish;
it will face manifold afflictions from enemies, and there will be drought.
Famine, great fear, pestilence, fever, epilepsy, and the like;
discoloration, smoke, and the appearance of fire and water outside [the city].
O Maheśvarī, if there is a discharge of blood from the female organ due to insects and the like,
there will be suffering for the subjects, suffering for the fetus, and suffering for the king and the twice-born.
O Pārvatī, when there is fear of thunderbolts, serpents, and the like, or affliction by wind, smallpox, and so forth— when such defects have arisen and the nine symptoms are present—
the Rākṣasas enter this body here as if it were empty of self.
In the same way, O Maheśvarī, when the linga is broken or devoid of the deity, it is full of defects; if worshipped, it destroys, and if not worshipped, it utterly destroys.
Therefore, with every effort, one should protect your liṅga;
for when [the time] has arrived, he should perform the rejoining and the pacification.
O Pārvatī, when the *liṅga* is broken, shattered, or marked, the supreme guru [should prepare a substitute] one finger-breadth or half of that, and square in shape.
The supreme guru should bind the *liṅga* with a binding thread and perform the reconnection;
then, having performed the great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) in due order, he should worship that *liṅga* once again.
If [the thread] has become fragmented due to negligence from gold, silver, or other materials,
one should join it very firmly and perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti) rite.
The mantra-practitioner should sprinkle the most excellent guru with water and other substances for the purpose of ritual bathing;
O Goddess, he should also provide protection when danger arises from thieves or enemies.
Having invoked the *kalā* into the jar, one should conceal it with sand;
O Goddess, one should worship that jar at your *liṅga* until the end of fear.

O Goddess, if [the deity] departs from that [liṅga], the mantra-practitioner should perform a rite of pacification according to the rules; having again invoked that digit (kalā) residing in the water-pot into the liṅga.
O Maheśvarī, the Guru should perform [the rite] according to the path as prescribed;
however, O Maheśvarī, if the *liṅga* should be destroyed through negligence, [the following must be done].

Having installed a new liṅga, whether it possesses those specific qualities or not, it should be of that form, composed of that essence, gentle, and of the proper measurement; otherwise, it is not auspicious.
Having understood this, one should diligently extract the worn-out [image] and join it;
one should perform the consecration as prescribed and carry out a great rite of pacification.
O Maheśvarī, if such signs as weeping and the like should arise,
one should wash and purify the *liṅga*, performing the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*) as previously described.
One should perform a great propitiation and worship the new linga;
listen, O Pārvatī, as I shall explain what occurs when the image has been obtained.
If, during the *bali* offering, the image that has been permanently installed— or likewise the primary image (*mūlabera*) and so forth—
should suddenly fall to the ground or become broken;
O Maheśvarī, when the image has been damaged by thieves or enemies, or by fire, or when it is cracked, shattered, or all its limbs have become loose and detached;
When [the kingdom] is broken, there is destruction for kings; when it falls, there is total ruin.
When it is burnt, the kingdom is consumed by fire and the king's enjoyment perishes.
If it breaks, one meets with ruin; if it cracks, there is loss of wealth;
and when all its parts become loose, every purpose is certainly destroyed.
If the foot is broken, there is loss of position; if the thighs or shanks are broken, there is the destruction of one's kin;
if the waist is broken, O Maheśvarī, the king shall become destitute.
If the arms are broken, there will be oppression by enemies and one shall never attain victory;
if the neck is severed, the king will then swiftly meet his death.
If there is a fracture in a limb of the embodied form, there will be the destruction of the kingdom and the loss of wealth;
if a principal limb has met with breakage, one should abandon that image.
Having installed a new image, the most excellent preceptor should perform a rite of pacification;
however, if its subsidiary parts or the like are broken, he should then proceed with the rite of rejoining.
O Dear One, having performed the Great Peace (mahāśānti) rite so that [the image] is indeed immovable by means of gold, bronze, copper, and so forth, one should then worship it after the rejoining.
When the image cracks more than a finger's breadth, one should discard that image in water and perform a rite of pacification according to the rules prescribed for installation.
Having consecrated a new image according to the prescribed methods of ploughing and so forth,
[one should act] when the image has been stolen by thieves or enemies.
If they arise in their proper places, there will be immediate total destruction of wells, ponds, temples, and all other such structures.
When the fire is extinguished, when a boil has burst, when the river has shifted its course, O Śivā;
when the nectar has fallen, or when the vehicle and the retinue have been shattered.
If the banner, the water-pot, or the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) is broken through negligence;
or if the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) or the two gatekeepers (dvārapāla) move or fall;
If the upper garland on the lamp-pillar is broken due to negligence,
as well as on the outer enclosure, the inner enclosures, and the surrounding walls;
Whether in the middle of a street or outside, in a garden, a pavilion, or an open space; during a festival, at the time of an offering, or even for daily or occasional rites.
Or if, O beloved, it occurs at the times for rites performed for specific desires— listen—
and if the image of the deity falls, is cut, or is broken through negligence;
O Goddess, sandals, vessels for offerings, the parasol, chowries and so forth,
banners, a secluded place, a mirror, and a water vessel.
O Girīndrajā, that leaf-cup was her leavings;
O Goddess, if this [universe] has its origin there, they declare it to be established in that very place.
I shall state their names; listen to the portents, O Pārvatī, whether they occur in a self-manifested (*svayambhu*) liṅga or in an image (*bimba*), O Pārvatī.
Obstruction, the arising of blood, perspiration, trembling, and sound; bursting, falling, O Goddess, discoloration, and the appearance of smoke.
If fire appears as red water, milk appears as the sight of insects, and the deity stands with his face turned upward, devoid of hands and feet; [then it is an omen of death].
O Dear One, [the image] may have many defects such as being face-down, or it may have a deformed mouth, be emaciated, or be dwarfed;
or else, O Beloved, the linga or the image may have been destroyed by thieves or enemies.
I shall describe the sanctum and other parts; listen to the portents, O Pārvatī, regarding the inner chamber, the courtyard, or the pavilion known as the Lakṣmī-maṇḍapa.
O Goddess, [one should worship] on the wall, at the gate-tower, on the pinnacle, within the pinnacle, in the pavilion, on the vehicle, O Goddess, and in the abodes of the retinue and so forth.

At the doorway, in the assembly hall, one should cause an eight-cornered [pit] to be made in the northeast; however, between the directions of Indra and Śaṅkara (the north), one should have a circular pit constructed.
To whatever extent its width may be, to that same extent should its measurement be;
it should be provided with three girdles and endowed with all the auspicious characteristics.
The pit should be two cubits in measure, together with an upper girdle;
in this manner one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), provided with thirty-two water-channels.
Adorned with mango sprouts and beautified by banners and flags,
it is yellow in color at the eastern gate and black in color at the southern one.
The western [gate] is red in color, and the northern is white;
the gateway regions starting from the east are likewise adorned with arches.
Having established the plantain tree, the wise one should wrap it with a new cloth.
Having thus adorned the beautiful pavilion with fruits, sprouts, and flowers, the wise practitioner should perform the rite of peace (śānti).
O Goddess, for nine days or seven nights, or five [days],
the kingdom, the fort, and the army shall be seized by an enemy king.
Indeed, the three varṇas beginning with the twice-born fall into the state of a śūdra;
they become devoid of strength, devoid of people, and all their ritual actions come to naught.
"Thus, O Goddess, the best of kings should show that which removes faults,
when the moon and stars are favorable and it is endowed with an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and karaṇa."
O Queen, on a day auspicious for the king and favorable to the kingdom,
the preceptor should have pavilions constructed at the site of your linga and other sacred objects.
To the east, the north, or the northeast, the preceptor should construct a pavilion measuring twenty cubits in size, square in shape, and provided with an altar.
And around the nine sacrificial pits, starting from the east and proceeding in order:
that in the east shall be square, while that in the southeast is shaped like a vulva (bhaga).
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the south is half-moon shaped, while in the southwest it is triangular;
in the west it is circular, and in the northwest it is hexagonal.
To the north, however, is the lotus pond (*padmakuṇḍa*),
which immediately removes all defects and wards off untimely death;
one obtains all enjoyments— this is the truth, the truth I have declared.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Location of Arisen Portents," in the Prāyaścitta-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-vātulottara.

The Goddess said: "O Śambhu, you have spoken correctly regarding the portents that arise; all of that has been heard by me, O Lord. But how [should] the fault and its pacification be treated separately?"
"Speak, O Lord, out of compassion for the welfare of all the worlds.
Śiva said: "Now, therefore, I shall explain the defects and the pacification for each one separately."
And hear from me in detail, O Pārvatī, the results of these in their proper order:
if an earthquake occurs or if the burning of the quarters takes place, there will be great fear.
That kingdom meets with destruction within three months; of this there is no doubt—whether it be in a city, the capital, or any other location, if an earthquake occurs.
O beloved goddess, the death of the king would result in immediate total destruction;
O goddess, the one who bestows royal gifts perishes.
There will be various afflictions from enemies and, without a doubt, drought;
if a river enters one's house, one shall meet death within three months.
Affliction of the subjects, affliction of the fetus, and affliction of the king toward the twice-born and others;
as well as vetālas, kṣetrapālas, fevers, epilepsy, and so forth.
Other such portents as these may arise in that region;
for the sake of pacifying those evils, the best of kings should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*).
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, when a portentous calamity has arisen that produces great upheaval, if peace is established, tell me how its destruction can be prevented."
Śiva said:
"O Goddess of gods, O beloved, just as one bitten by a serpent becomes healthy through the Gāruḍa herb, so too does peace come to those who possess it."
Therefore, with every effort, the physician should always administer medicine whenever such a conflict arises.
O Goddess, [the practice] occurs in houses such as market-towns, in forests, in groves, on level ground, and on mountains;
O Goddess, listen to the sequence of their emergence.

O Maheśvarī, [one must perform penance] for the killing of a cow, the killing of a woman, the destruction of twice-born men and others, or from wicked beings such as Vyālis using weapons and the like.
O Goddess, when a frog dies in a well, O you who are born from a water-jar;
and when a bull, buffalo, tiger, donkey, camel, or similar creature enters [the well].
O Maheśvarī, when there is a deep collapse of the ground in villages and other places,
or when the Liṅga is destroyed by the deep currents of rivers and so forth;
If a sacred tree or the like falls, or if all the trees in a forest fall,
or if a mountain is cast down to the earth, shattered into fragments;
O Maheśvarī, such names as these are portents;
O Goddess of lovely countenance, listen as I explain the fault therein.
O Maheśvarī, there shall be the immediate death of the king, the destruction of his fourfold army, and [the ruin] of that kingdom, city, and weapons.

O Goddess, the cane, the offering lamp, and the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and so forth— whether the image be made of clay, stone, or wood— should be placed under the guidance of a preceptor who protects others.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, when the musical instruments or the attendants have fallen,
or when the palanquin or the chariot breaks, or likewise when the vehicle falls;
For the purpose of transport, O beloved, there were elephants, horses, and the like, as well as decorated bulls,
and men carrying the garments of the army commanders.
When blood has been shed through mutual conflict,
in a fistfight or a staff-fight, or when wounds have been inflicted by nails and teeth;
When these beings have been struck by weapons or killed,
O Goddess, listen to what occurs when death ensues upon their entry [into the womb].
And when it is defiled by wild animals, wicked quadrupeds,
bipeds, small creatures, snakes, or by swans and vultures;
It may arise from anthills produced by honey-bees,
or it may be formed by large ants entering through a small opening.
O Dear One, the Guru should perform the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) and administer initiation;
he himself, being pure, should wear white garments and observe shaving, bathing, and silence.
O beloved, one should always eat milk-rice, avoid bad company and the like,
and observe the vow of celibacy toward the preceptor and other twice-born ones.
The rite of initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed according to the rules during the nine nights;
one should not perform the rite of initiation for only three nights or a single night.
Having procured the materials for the sacrifice, together with the officiating priests, chanters, and others,
one should rise in the morning and perform the ritual cleansing of the teeth according to the prescribed rules.
The preceptor and the patron should perform their morning ablutions and carry out the twilight rituals according to the rules for daily duties.
(14) Preceded by a bath with clay, and [anointed] with *kuśa* grass, cow dung, and ashes,
accompanied by all sounds of chanting, and attended by auspicious women.
With various auspicious musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas and hymns,
perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules and bring about peace, O Maheśvarī.
Then, having gone to the temple and offered fruits and flowers,
one should pray with devotion through prostrations and the recitation of the Yajamāna mantra.
The preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should enter the sacrificial pavilion;
first, he should perform the salutation to the preceptor in the northeast corner.
Having sat upon a seat of darbha grass, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O Dear One, one should sprinkle the auspicious day (puṇyāha) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with water from the vessel.
Having performed the binding of the ten directions preceded by the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters,
one should make a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) according to the prescribed rule, specifying the number of days.
Having propitiated Gaṇeśa, one should perform the Nāndī-karma;
O Dear One, one should then consecrate the Puṇyāha and the Pañcagavya, and [perform] the ritual consumption.
O Goddess, I choose the best of the twice-born, such as the preceptors and others,
who are devoted to their own Vedic branches, and who serve as the Brahmā, the preceptor, and the Hotṛ priests.
O Goddess, O Beloved, the mantra-practitioner should invite the reciters and chanters, each accompanied by their own Vedic branch,
after giving them separate fruits.
The preceptor should cause ornaments, fine garments, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) to be offered;
and preceded by the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), he should purify the pavilion.
O Dear One, one should install and worship the door-arches and the water-pots;
one should perform the Vāstu-homa which destroys Rākṣasas, as well as the worship and the offering of oblations.
The Gaṇeśa-hymn, the Kṣetrapāla-hymn, the Bhūsūkta, the one known as Vāstu,
the Rākṣoghna, the Caturasra, the Mṛtyuñjaya, and the Navagraha.
O Maheśvarī, one should recite the Mahāsaura, the Saptashatī, the Prāsāda mantra,
the five-syllabled Śakti mantra, and the complete recitation of the Vedas separately.
O beloved, one should perform the rite of waking again at sunrise;
then one should perform the daily rites, such as the declaration of an auspicious day and the ritual sprinkling.
In the eastern part of the pavilion, the wise practitioner should delineate the mandala of the planets, having made it square and level, in the form of the planets.
O Maheśvarī, one should construct squares there equal in number to the planets;
one should write that [diagram] in five colors, distinguished by the respective letters.
One should fill the respective locations with grains such as wheat,
using gold weighing one *karṣa*, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should fashion the images according to the specific distinctions of each planet;
having installed a water-pot there, O Pārvatī, [one should place] as many [vessels] as there are planets.
One should worship [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with the various planets, beginning with the Sun;
having drawn a lotus in front of that [deity], one should fill it with rice grains.
The practitioner of mantra should draw the yantra of the solar seed-syllable, which has the form of the twelve Ādityas; having worshipped it according to the rite upon seeing a reflected sun.

O beloved, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus in the northeast corner and filling it with a *droṇa* measure of grain, one should arrange the supporting vessels (*ādhāra*) and so forth in their proper order.
One should fashion a golden image with its characteristics in due order,
including the bulb, the stalk, and the lotus, together with the eight elephants of the quarters.
Having filled the tortoise and the earth [with substances], the Guru should establish and worship them;
having worshipped the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) according to the ritual rules starting from the east and so forth, he should surround [the site].
O Dear One, if there is suffering due to an earthquake, one should worship [the deity] with their respective names and so forth;
having established [the image] in the center of the altar, one should perform a thousand or half of that number [of offerings].
The practitioner of mantras should worship the jars according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O Goddess, having seated Brahmā and the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in their proper order,
O Beloved, one should generate the fire after first performing the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The mantra-practitioner should carry the fire in the directions starting from the east in due order;
the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should perform the fire-ritual as prescribed in each respective pit (kuṇḍa).
O Maheśvarī, one should offer oblations into the primary sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the root mantra ten thousand times,
or half of that, or a thousand times, O Maheśvarī.
O Maheśvarī, one should place the seed-syllable of the Earth (laṃ) and Bhuvaneśī in the east, beginning with the Ādhāra;
and Aghora in the southeast, and half of that again [in the south].
One should install Mṛtyuñjaya in the south and Varāhaka in the southwest;
Prāsāda in the western pool and Śāntidaurgaka in the northwest.
O Goddess, one should offer a thousand oblations for each respective mantra of the Pañcabrahma, Soma, and Īśāna Tattvas, offering them individually.

One should offer oblations with sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), mustard seeds, sesame seeds, along with rice grains, parched grain flour (saktu), wheat, and flattened rice (pṛthuka).

O Pārvatī, having divided the number of oblations around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) among the officiating priests (hotṛka) in the various directions according to the number of days, the mantra-knower [should proceed].
Having offered oblations according to the previously stated number on that day for the sake of the intended recipient,
the preceptor, the spiritual guide, should then perform the subsidiary oblation (upahoma) together with the officiating priests.

Having offered oblations with the mantras of Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Tryambaka, and the nine planets, as well as those of the guardians of the quarters, one should thereafter perform the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.

At the end, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation; O Dear One, if there is an earthquake, the practitioner of mantra should likewise offer oblations upon seeing a mock sun (*pratisūrya*), following the proper sequence.
One should offer oblations to Āditya in the eastern pit, to Aghora in the south-eastern direction,
to Mṛtyuñjaya in the north, and to the nine planets in the south-west.
One should offer oblations with the mantras of the guardians of the directions in the west; with those of Vāyu, Īśāna, and Durgā in the northwest;
with those of the twelve Ādityas in the north; and with the five-syllable mantra in the northeast.
O Dear One, one should offer the mantra separately for each of the previously mentioned substances;
at the conclusion of the oblation, the practitioner of mantras should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and then the final *pūrṇāhuti*.
The mantra-practitioner should sprinkle the consecrated jars upon that *liṅga*,
O beloved, according to the rules, with the Mahārudra mantras and the great five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
After the final sprinkling and having performed anointing with fragrant unguents, one should perform a great worship (mahāpūjā),
O Dear One, with various flowers, perfumes, and manifold food offerings.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and moved it around, one should offer the ritual services (upacāras).
Then, having given the ten gifts, one should offer a sun-god fashioned from gold.
Having fashioned twelve images, one should cause them to be given to the Brahmins;
O Goddess, one should have a mandala of the earth made, measuring ten niṣkas.
It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
then, having honored the teacher with cows, land, garments, and gold.
There, O Maheśvarī, one should present these along with ritual implements,
and one should devoutly cause the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the image-keepers in due order.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins according to the extent of one's wealth;
then, the preceptor should bestow a gift of land and hold a lamp festival at night.
Having offered the *bali* to the spirits, one should cause the gift for the alleviation of distress to be bestowed;
in this manner, O Maheśvarī, one should perform the rite with devotion during an earthquake.
O beloved, one should perform this rite of pacification when seeing a solar halo or a double sun;
it bestows longevity, health, sovereignty, and all prosperity upon men.
There shall be abundance on earth, increasing the lifespan of men,
for the sake of the further growth of the respective duties of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
O Goddess, for the sake of your pleasure, I have declared this expiation, which is merit beneficial to all living beings and a warder-off of the flood of all sins.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Pacification of Earthquakes and the Sight of a Counter-Sun," in the section on Expiatory Rites (*prāyaścitta*) within the glorious *Vātulottara*.
Henceforth, O Śivā, I shall declare the day of the waning of the moon,
as well as when the stars vanish at night and when Indra’s bow (the rainbow) appears in the sky.
O Maheśvarī, if both [the new moon] during the day and the appearance of the stars [at night] occur while the flesh is still increasing,
and both have arrived within the same year;
And when there is a conjunction with cruel planets in the fifth or the seventh house,
or when Ketu has arisen in the thirty-second [navāṃśa], there occurs the shedding of a flow of blood.
O Maheśvarī, if fire or rain should fall upon the earth during the purification of the lunar day (*masauca*),
O Goddess, one obtains peace from that fault; listen now, Pārvatī, to the sequence [of the rite].
When the moon has set, when the stars have vanished, when a rainbow appears at night,
or if a star is visible by day— at any such auspicious place whatsoever—

If [the planet] is in the second house, there will be a ruler of the country, as well as a minister and the destruction of the commander-in-chief; if it is in the fourth house, both [the minister and the commander] perish within two months; and when both [the second and fourth houses] are reached, this occurs within a year.
O Maheśvarī, O beloved, when there is a conjunction of cruel enemy planets in the zodiac sign of men, there will be famine for the army, the people, and the cattle.
If Ketu is seen in various auspicious positions, there will undoubtedly be the affliction of death within six months; of this there is no doubt.
There will be emaciation and exhaustion in the kingdom; kings will meet their death, and there will be fire, rain, and the falling of blood upon the earth.
Likewise, O Goddess, there will be drought and the destruction of fruits everywhere;
there is no doubt that the destruction of crops will occur in the world for several years.
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying those faults, one should perform rites of propitiation in the capital city, in your residence,
and in every region and individual village.
First, the Guru should have a pavilion constructed measuring ten cubits;
it should consist of either one or five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), each provided with three cubits [of space].
O Goddess, the wise preceptor should construct the pavilion according to the measurements and characteristics as previously described, including the doors, ornaments, and other features.
When the lunar day and the asterism are auspicious and favorable to the king and the village,
he should then rise at dawn and perform his bath, twilight prayers, and libations.
Having completed the rite according to the rules together with the Brahmins and with devotion,
the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should then enter the temple, preceded by the worship of Vighneśa.
One should perform the Puṇyāha, the Pañcagavya, and the Nāndī-karma;
the mantra-practitioner should select the Brahmins, the Ācārya, and others as prescribed.
Having given ornaments such as jewelry, garments, gold, and rings, as well as betel-leaf, fruit, and the madhuparka offering according to the prescribed rule.
O Maheśvarī, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (aṅkura) either immediately or [at the proper time];
one should purify the pavilion at night, and having installed the ritual jars (kumbha), one should perform the fire oblation (homa).

One should perform the oblation for the destruction of the *vāstu-rākṣasa*, as well as the offering of bali and worship; O Śivā, one should recite the Vedas in the cardinal directions and the weapon-mantra (*astramanu*) in the intermediate directions.
The Kṣetrapāla mantra, the Vāstu mantra, the Mṛtyuñjaya and Navagraha mantras, the root mantra, the Diśā mantra, the Bhūsūkta, and the Viṣṇusūkta. (p. 23)
The *Abhayankara*, the *Śāntidurgā-prāsāda*, the *Bhuvaneśvarī*,
the seven hundred *ketu-mantras*, the eight *vākyas*, and those [mantras] that are their progenitors.
One should recite [the mantra] until the conclusion of the fire offering (homa) and perform the binding of the protective thread;
then, having risen at dawn and performed the daily rites, one should proceed.
O Goddess, having joined with the Brahmins and made the formal resolve according to the rules,
the preceptor should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited in his own sacrificial pit according to the prescribed ritual.
One should establish the fire for the birth-rite (jananāgni) together with a Brahmin priest and the Hotṛs;
and one should place that fire into other sacrificial pits in the proper sequence.
One should perform [the rite] as prescribed for the fire-ritual, separately around the sacrificial pit;
having sat down according to the rule, one should recite the root mantra one million times.
One should offer oblations with the Aghora mantra into the principal fire-pit, with the planetary mantra into the eastern pit,
and with the Abhayaṅkara mantra into the southern and western pits.
And in the north, one should offer oblations separately with the *triyambaka* mantra and that same mantra [for each of the following]:
*khadira*, *palāśa*, *arka*, and likewise *audumbara*.
Having offered *dūrvā* grass and sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), one should perform the primary oblations and so forth in due order—
namely, clarified butter, cooked rice (*caru*), sesame, mustard seeds, and flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), O Dear One.
Having offered groats, rice, wheat, honey, and milk in the sequence mentioned,
according to the previously stated number, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, [performs the rite].
Then, having performed the *upahoma* (subsidiary oblations), one should perform the principal oblations and so forth in due order:
the *śānti-durgā-mantra* homa, the deities of the respective month and lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the *pañcabrahma*, and the *prāsāda* mantra; one should offer these a thousand times, O Dear One.
O Śivā, one should place a thousand [offerings] in the center of the altar; this is the most excellent method.
Having worshipped half of that [number] of jars according to the rules,
the Guru should perform the recitation of the Pārāyaṇa, concluding at the end of the day.
At the end, the Guru should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation and sprinkle those jars with water,
reciting the *Śatarudriya* and the *Atirudriya* according to the procedure prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
One should sprinkle the *liṅga* separately with the great five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*),
and having consecrated it with various *sūktas*, one should then smear it with fragrant unguents.
One should worship the Liṅga with various leaves and flowers,
as well as with incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of edibles of the six flavors.
Then one should offer ripe betel nut and blue collyrium;
thereafter, one should present the bali offering and feed many Brahmins.
O Goddess, at night during the festival of lights, one should perform the worship of the stage;
one should offer the bali-oblation to the great elements and cause the ten gifts to be bestowed.
And in the event of the destruction of the moon, the stars, and so forth, O beloved, one should have an image of that form made of gold and especially give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thereafter, one should give abundant gifts, and after that, gifts for the sake of relieving distress;
one should worship the preceptor with devotion by means of vehicles, ornaments, and other such items.
Having given cows, land, and so forth, as well as a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity,
[one should honor] the Brāhmaṇa, the Sadasya, the Hotṛ, and the others in their proper order.
One should cause each respective portion and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given separately;
in this manner, one should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti), which brings all auspiciousness to men.

"O Auspicious One, this brings prosperity to the king, the ministers, and all the subjects. Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Pacification of the Eclipse of the Moon, the Stars, and Rāhu," in the section on Expiatory Rites (*prāyaścitta*) within the *Śrī-Vātulottara*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
The Goddess said:
"O God, O Sadāśiva, I have heard everything you have told me— the rules for expiation in their entirety, including those that are constant, occasional, and additional."
Now I wish to hear about the many portents on earth;
O Lord, tell me the cause of this weakness at present.
O Lord, what are their names, and how are those defects distinguished individually?
And how is their pacification achieved, O Śambhu? Tell me, O Śiva, out of compassion.
Īśvara said: "Excellent, O Goddess! You have asked well concerning the many portents that arise.
O Goddess, as to how they arise, hear the cause from me according to the truth."
O Śivā, for some there is the destruction of their dwellings, for others the fear of death, and for others the fear of enemies; furthermore, famine arises upon the earth for men.
In some cases, I produce on earth portents such as the seizure of wealth by men, or the destruction of villages, districts, and cities, during such times as these.
Therefore, having understood this, the best among men should perform the propitiatory rite according to the rules for the pacification of those defects and for the welfare of all living beings.
(p. 27) I shall state their names; listen in due order, O Pārvatī:
an earthquake, the burning of the quarters, and the appearance of a mock sun.
A star appearing by day, a rainbow appearing at night,
the disappearance of stars at night, and on the day of the waning of the moon, O Auspicious One—
If [the period] is exceeded by two months, both [periods] are deficient when the year has arrived;
likewise when there is a conjunction with malefic or inimical planets in the fifth or seventh house.
When the thirty-two omens appeared, as well as many other auspicious signs,
there was a rain of fire upon the earth and the falling of streams of blood.
O Maheśvarī, it is born in the divine realm, the intermediate space, and on the earth;
whether in a temple, a house, a village, a city, or any place.
In a city or the capital, in a forest or even a grove,
on a riverbank or by a pond, in a woodland, on a mountain, or on dry land.

And on the bank of the Sindhu, in the region of Diksthāna, upon the earth... [omitted] ...O beloved, when that image is recovered again with effort, the Guru, having performed worship, should perform a rite of peace and commence a festival.

If the image [of the deity] has been destroyed or damaged, one should fashion a new image according to the characteristics previously described, and then perform the consecration and rites of pacification.
It stands upon an upward-facing image that is devoid of hands and feet;
there are many others with downward-facing faces, as well as those with deficient mouths, emaciated, and dwarfish.
If this image is seen, it causes amazement at that very moment;
yet the Vetālas, Kṣetrapālas, and the afflictions of spirits increase.
In that country, fear of snakes and disease arises for the king;
to pacify those evils, one should perform an expiation.
O Goddess, I have duly explained in sequence the defects of the image and so forth regarding your linga and other icons; now hear in detail the pacification [of those defects],
as they occur in their proper order when such flaws as breaking arise.
One should first feed the preceptor with milk-rice and ghee.
Gold, jewels, and so forth, as well as vehicles and the like, should be given to him.
To the right of the deity, one should worship the pavilion and the pitcher as previously described.
Having performed the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rite as described for the ritual of withdrawal, the preceptor,
having worshipped the liṅga and offered libations, should dismiss the three principles (tritatva).
Having covered the door with a cloth, one should offer the ripened fruit;
then, having joined [the ritual], one should install the previously mentioned *liṅga* or the image itself.
O Maheśvarī, the preceptor should perform the expiation;
he should construct an excellent, most excellent pavilion in front of you and in the northeast (Īśa) direction.
Then, having prepared nine sacrificial pits according to the path previously described,
O Goddess, one should construct a pavilion adorned with doorways and arches.

O Great Goddess, one should perform the expiation on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and endowed with a suitable yoga and karaṇa; or else, O Maheśvarī, it may be performed immediately.
Then, having risen at dawn, the preceptor, together with the brahmins, performed his daily rites,
beginning with a bath of clay.
Clad in washed garments and adorned with ornaments such as sacred ash,
one should then go to the temple and offer prayers, O Maheśvarī.
Having sat upon the seat in the east or in the northeast,
the practitioner of mantra should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the recitation of the Mātṛkās in their proper sequence.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the mantra-practitioner, preceded by saluting the guru, should designate the day and make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for five, seven, or nine days. Then,
having worshipped his own self as the deity, he should perform the *nāndī* and *puṇyāha* rites.
O Goddess, one should choose Brahmins endowed with the characteristics previously described.

O Goddess, one should worship the Guru, the Ritual Procedure (Vidhi), Dhanada, the Sadasyas, and the guardians of the eight forms (Aṣṭamūrtipās), along with the Hotṛ priests, in numbers equal to the count of the oblations, according to the prescribed rule.
Half of that [number] should be for the purpose of recitation, sixteen for the purpose of Vedic study,
ten Brahmins for the sake of others, and those numbering eleven as sprinklers.
For the sake of worship, the practitioner of mantras should choose ten Brahmins for prostration and circumambulation,
and six persons for other rites, and he should cause them to be offered madhuparka.
The preceptor should present garments and ornaments, or even fruit and betel leaf;
and preceded by the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), he should perform the fetching of the earth.
O Maheśvarī, thereafter, during the nine nights [of Navarātra],
the Guru should worship the banner for one, three, or five nights.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions and entered the sacrificial hall,
one should perform the rite for an auspicious day, prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and purify the sacrificial pit and the pavilion.
Having installed the jars for the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) and others, as well as the door-arches and the central pitcher,
one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, which destroys demons, using vessels filled with rice and water.
One should scatter the *bali* offering and perform the rite for binding the protection of the site (*vāstura*).
Having established the purification of the location and the ritual jars (*ghaṭa*), one should likewise perform the purification of the image (*bimba*).
Having established the ritual vessels for the purification of the *liṅga*, the Guru should worship them according to the prescribed rite;
meanwhile, the recitation of the Vedas should take place in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and one should mutter that mantra.
O Goddess, the preceptor should recite all the mantras and their respective hymns (sūktas) according to the ritual formulas,
and he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) just as previously described.
Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the *liṅga* using the previously mentioned substances and mantras;
having then rendered them sleepless, one who is intent upon that [practice] should rise in the morning.
Having performed the rites of bathing and the twilight prayers (sandhyā), one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
O Dear One, having brought the fire of the Preceptor, one should place it within the primary altar.
The practitioner of mantras should generate the fire with the reciters of the *hotṛ* formulas and others;
he should perform the study of the Vedas (*vedapārāyaṇa*) together with the rite of the fire-oblation (*homakarman*).

The root mantra should be the primary one; one should offer oblations in the fire-pits starting from the east, numbering either one hundred thousand or half of that, increasing by a digit (kalā) for each pit according to the principles (tattva).

One should offer oblations into the square sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) located in the intermediate directions, one by one, in due order, for Śāntidurgā, Mṛtyujit, and half of that [number] respectively.

The practitioner of mantras should perform the fire-oblation with the ten substances, beginning with fuel-sticks and clarified butter; thereafter, he should perform the subsidiary oblations and the primary oblations in their proper sequence.
O Dear One, the knower of mantras [should perform] the purification of the *liṅga*, the purification of the image, the purification of the site,
the mantra, the temple, the directional mantra, and the fire-oblation for the planets.
O Śivā, one should separately offer oblations of ghee into the fire for the Mūrti-homa, for Gaṇeśa, and for the mantra of Kṣetrapāla, either a thousand times or half of that.
O Dear One, the practitioner of mantra should perform the recitation and study of many respective mantras;
he should also establish one thousand water-pots (kalaśas) according to the prescribed rule.
Thereafter, O Dear One, one should worship and touch the root mantra,
while the officiating priests perform the fire-oblations individually throughout the day.
Having offered oblations according to the previously stated number, he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
At the conclusion of the homa, the preceptor should join the kalā into your liṅga.
The one most skilled in mantras should sprinkle the consecrated jar of life;
he should perform the rite of inspection and remove the cloth from his face.
Then, O Pārvatī, one should sprinkle the liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) while reciting the Rudra-mantra,
various Sūktas, the Pāvamāna hymns, and their respective mantras.
The mantra-practitioner should bathe [the image] with thousands of jars in the proper sequence;
at the conclusion of the sprinkling, having lifted it up, one should smear it with the eight fragrances.
And one should perform the great worship with various flowers and by name,
O Maheśvarī, using bilva leaves, drāṇa flowers, and lotuses.
One should fashion those lingas out of gold and worship them;
one should offer various kinds of cooked rice as food offerings, along with solid foods, soft foods, and milk-rice preparations.
Then, O Pārvatī, the mantra-practitioner should offer [the oblation] with the root mantra;
having presented betel-leaf, he should thereafter perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then one should perform the offering of oblations (balidāna) and especially the festival;
this should be carried out day by day until the end of the designated period.
Then, O beloved, one should give the ten-fold gift; one should fashion a linga made of gold, or else an image, and provide a sacrificial fee according to one's own capacity.
And one should give to the guru with devotion; one should cause the gift for the Kṛcchra penance to be bestowed.
O Goddess, one should feed Brāhmaṇas according to the number of oblations.
At the conclusion, one should cause the preceptor and others to receive the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as previously described;
thereafter, one should give a gift of land and perform worship of the guru.
"O Dear One, having given cows, land, and so forth, along with the ritual implements,
one should thus perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) in cases such as the destruction of the *liṅga*."
O Maheśvarī, if the image is broken, cracked, burnt, or shattered in any way whatsoever, one should fashion another that is half of that size, or even half of that again.
Regarding defects such as weeping and so forth, there is the illustration of insects and the like;
likewise, when one sees someone devoid of hands or feet, or someone who is emaciated or dwarfed.

In the event of defects such as falling [of the vessel] and so forth, one should perform the previously mentioned propitiatory rite (śānti), which wards off all faults, for half that amount and then for half of that again.
It brings all peace to the world and bestows all prosperity upon men;
there shall be an increase in the four constituent elements of the state, and the king's kingdom shall flourish.
There shall be an increase of sons, grandsons, and so forth, and victory everywhere;
O beloved, it quickly removes all death and increases one's lifespan.
The presence of Śiva in the liṅga bestows all desired objects;
I shall now describe the sanctum and other matters, as well as the defects and their pacification—listen in due order.
When a fire breaks out or a structure cracks in the inner sanctum, the pavilion, the enclosure wall, the gate-tower, or anywhere else within the temple complex, such as the main shrine and so forth;
If, upon the entry [of the deity], there occurs breaking, splitting, or fragmentation, or if death should occur,
or if such happens to the vehicle, the attendants, the banner, or the flask;
O Maheśvarī, on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) are the Kṣetrapāla and the Dvārapāla;
and on the lamp-pillar, as well as upon the upper garlands, the umbrella, the chowries, and so forth.
When a palanquin, vehicles, and the like, or sandals, musical instruments,
and so forth, have fallen, been broken, burnt, or carried off by thieves;
When such [omens] arise, there will be danger for the king and the kingdom;
and when they occur within the inner sanctum, there will be the destruction of the realm and the loss of people.
O Goddess, if [the omen] occurs in the pavilion or the gateway, there is the destruction of ministers for three months;
if it occurs in the temple and other such structures, it brings about the destruction of the army commander.
O Maheśvarī, if these [omens] appear among the attendants during the narration, there will be fear of thieves and pestilence, and the affliction of the wicked will increase.

If the ritual objects or the vehicle are destroyed due to negligence—whether the banner, the pitcher, or the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) breaks—the [deities] perish within three years; of this there is no doubt.
O beloved, if [this occurs] regarding the field-protector, the gate-keeper, the lamp-pillar, and so forth,
there will immediately be affliction from enemies, and affliction by spirits will increase.
If proximity [to the deity] does not exist in the *liṅga*, that place shall go to ruin;
[the same applies to the loss of status] for those who serve with the parasol, the chowrie, and so forth, or who possess the palanquin, the sandals, and the like.
If musical instruments and the like in Bali-dīpa fall or become broken,
there will be the destruction of the enjoyments of kings, as well as the loss of elephants, horses, and cattle.
Total ruin would occur immediately, and the prosperity of the village would depart;
when such faults and other defects have arisen, one should perform the pacification rite as previously described.
O Pārvatī, having offered one hundred thousand oblations with the Aghora mantra and the root mantra,
the Guru should perform the directional fire-offering (diśāhoma) along with the mantras of Śānti, Durgā, and Mṛtyuñjaya.
Then, having offered half of that again, and according to the strength or weakness of the specific defect,
the mantra-practitioner should sprinkle five hundred jars, or half of that, or even a quarter of that.
One should bestow various kinds of gifts and perform everything previously described;
this is declared regarding rites of pacification (śāntika) in the event of the destruction of a linga, an image, or similar objects.
Bestowing all prosperity upon men and always granting auspiciousness,
may there be an increase in my kingdom and treasury, and may I dwell long in this world.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Repairing and Pacifying Defects of the Liṅga, Image, and so forth," in the section on Expiation within the *Śrīvātulottara*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
Hail!
I shall now describe the breaking of the chariot (rathabhaṅga) when it occurs during rites performed for specific desires or on special occasions,
as well as at the beginning, middle, or end of festivals held at the start of the year and so forth.
O Maheśvarī, when a cart or similar vehicle is broken, overturned, loosened, burnt, lost, or its parts are shattered;
O Pārvatī, listen now to the fault, the pacification, the restoration, and the resulting fruit if, through negligence, [this occurs] when your wonderful festival has arrived.
If the wheel is deficient, misfortune shall arise and that village will meet with destruction;
O Pārvatī, when it is punished by the king, it destroys strength and causes the loss of wealth.
If there is a crack slanting across the side, it portends the destruction of ministers; if it occurs on a slab, it is a banner of ruin.
If it appears on a pillar joined with a statue, it indicates the loss of one's own kingdom and the destruction of the city.
O Pārvatī, if [the planet] is in the middle of the path, or in the interior, or if it is in a depression,
the king will suffer affliction from disease and shall incur the loss of his own wife.
If the doors and other parts of the chariot are destroyed, the royal fortune has departed;
likewise, if the walls of the chariot are missing or the canopy is absent.
O Pārvatī, everyone shall encounter famine and the affliction of death;
and there shall be [conflict] with wooden stakes and the binding of ropes for the army commanders and ministers.
O Śivā, death occurs as destruction at the site of the *baliberas*;
or if [the image] is broken on a Tuesday or in the middle of the interval, one may even die.
Or if it falls while being contracted, the king shall meet his death;
likewise if it falls upon the image of Bali while the preceptor and other attendants are present.
The teaching would immediately perish, the fourfold army would be destroyed,
the king’s treasury would be ruined, and men would face the affliction of enemies.
If the parasol or the banner is devoid of ornaments,
it destroys fame, renown, and the like, and royal enjoyment perishes.
When the frontal pitcher of the chariot is broken and the front of the chariot is cast down,
there will undoubtedly be total defeat for that king and his state of poverty.
If the royal fortune has departed, one meets death within three months;
likewise if the rope is severed or the banner breaks, having been struck down by that person's own people.
O Pārvatī, there is no victory in approaching [the enemy], and there is the destruction of kinsmen;
when all one's limbs have become weak, every purpose is certainly lost.
O Goddess, if the chariot falls or is shattered upon the ground,
there will be the immediate death of the king and the destruction of the fourfold army.
That kingdom meets with destruction within three years; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśvarī, I shall now describe the guardians of the directions in relation to what occurs when [the king] has fallen.
The king shall attain the abode of the universal monarch (Sārvabhauma) in the south-east of his house;
likewise, the Cakravartin and the Maṇḍalika shall attain the abode of Yama in the south.

In the northwest (Vāruṇī) there is the destruction of the master; in the north (Vāyavyā), the destruction of the master’s charioteer; in the north-east (Soma), death; and in the northeast (Īśa), the destruction of the king and his queen.
Therefore, peace should be established for the welfare of the entire world;
the best of kings should perform the rite of peace, which removes all the faults of men.
At that time, the preceptor, along with the artisans, his disciples, the attendants, and others, must never show the breaking of the king's chariot.
Having observed the breaking of the chariot at that time, one should join it back together right there;
one should have the craftsmen make it very firm.
There, preceded by the worship of Vighneśa, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra of Cakra and the others.
O Pārvatī, the Guru should offer oblations with the Ghoramantra, its half-mantra, the Mūlamantra, as well as the Prāyaścitta, Śānti, and Diśā mantras.
The Guru should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, along with *tuṭika* and mustard seeds,
using their respective mantras, when the body of the disciple is weak.
The Guru should bathe [the image] with water from a jar one hundred and eight times;
O Maheśvarī, he should also bathe that image if it has been moved to another location.
Thereafter, the mantra-practitioner should bathe that chariot and its half separately,
and then worship it with the recitation of the Vedas and other rites.
O Maheśvarī, one should cause the gift of distress to be given in ten ways;
heaps of excellent food should be placed in all directions around the chariot.
Then, one should offer the *bhūtabali* together with pieces of *kūśmāṇḍa* fruit;
having struck [the ground] with the fruits of the *lāṅgulī* and other trees, one should perform the remainder of the festival.
Then the most excellent preceptor should perform the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) according to the ritual procedure;
O Śivā, if that chariot has not been repaired, then [this must be done].
Having installed your image with the Svasti-sūkta, the preceptor should place it upon a palanquin or similar vehicle and conduct the festival.
Then, having completed the remaining rites and having made a new, sturdy chariot,
one should act as previously described during the seventh auspicious three-month period.
In the year, month, lunar mansion, and lunar day following that,
one should again perform the festival, beginning with the rites for the seed-syllables and ending with the consecration at the sacred ford.
On the preceding day, the preceptor should perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti) according to the prescribed rules;
thereafter, he should conduct the chariot festival, beginning with the hoisting of the banner.
I shall proclaim the Great Peace; listen in detail, O Pārvatī.
The preceptor should construct a pavilion in front of you, or else in the northeast.
It should be square on all sides, measuring thirty-two cubits in extent,
with a central altar (vedi) possessing the proper characteristics, elevated by one cubit.
One should construct [the pavilion] provided with thirty-two pillars and four doors;
having erected the staff and adorned it with arches and *kudalī* [festoons].
One should construct a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring two cubits on each side in the four cardinal directions;
in the intermediate directions, there should be circular pits, all of which should be arranged upon a raised altar (vedī).
Between the directions of Indra and Īśāna, the primary circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) is situated;
it is provided with a navel and adorned above its girdle (mekhalā).
O Maheśvarī, having thus determined these days, one who is truthful and has conquered the senses should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) for the beautiful pavilion.
The preceptor, initiated, devoted to ritual action, and possessed of knowledge, having invited the Brahmins,
should perform his morning bath after completing his daily obligatory rites.
Then, having gone to the temple and offered fruits and flowers, the practitioner should pray: "By your command, may you grant peace."
Thereafter, one should perform the rites together with the twice-born, beginning with the preceptor;
one should undertake the commencement of the ritual in the evening at night and in the morning during the day.
Then, having entered the pavilion and sat upon the seat,
one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), preceded by the salutation to the guru and other preliminary rites.
Having designated the day and made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the extent of one's means,
[one should perform] the worship of Vighneśa, the Ānanda-rite, the Puṇyāha-rite, and the offering of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

O Goddess, one should choose the preceptor (ācārya), the patron (yajamāna), the Brahman priest, and the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) for the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), according to the number of oblations (āhuti).
Having determined the number of days required,
O Śivā, one should select sixteen Brāhmaṇas in due order for the purpose of reciting the Vedas in their entirety.
O Pārvatī, there should be fifty for the purpose of recitation and fifty for the purpose of service;
for the purpose of worship, there should be ten Brāhmaṇas, equal in number to the Rudras, each separately.

O Maheśvarī, the Guru should select six *ghana* priests for the performance of circumambulations and prostrations, as well as ten Brahmins for the purpose of recitation, choosing each one individually.
Having given clothing and ornaments, or even fruit and betel leaf,
one should honor the preceptor with crowns and other regalia, as well as golden sacred threads.
And with fine linen shoes and the like, with umbrellas, fans, and vessels,
as well as golden earrings and a ring, O Maheśvarī.
Having given according to the extent of his wealth, he should worship the Preceptor;
afterwards, he should purify the pavilion by sweeping it and smearing it with cow dung and [cow] urine.
The temple should be adorned with canopies and other ornaments as well as arches;
it should be encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass, and the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of eighteen [vessels] should be performed.
The Guru should install and worship the pitchers situated within the pavilion;
or else, O Maheśvarī, he should perform the rite of sprouting (aṅkurārpaṇa) immediately.
One should commence the oblation for slaying the *vāstu-rākṣasa* and the worship with offerings;
having bound the protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*) upon the preceptor and the other twice-born ones individually.
O Dear One, one should perform the complete recitation of the Vedas and mutter the respective mantras;
having kept a vigil at night, remaining without food and with senses subdued.
Then, having risen at dawn and completed the daily rites,
one should perform the *puṇyāha* ceremony and prepare the water-pots (*kalaśas*), O beloved.
O Goddess, one should worship a thousand supreme [offerings] according to the prescribed rite,
having established the *jananāgni* fire within the preceptor’s sacrificial pit.
One should dwell in other sacrificial pits and perform the fire-ritual as prescribed;
O Pārvatī, having invoked the fire into the center with your root mantra.
Aghora should be in the eastern pit, Sudarśana in the southeast;
Mṛtyuñjaya should be in the south, and the five Durgās in the southwest.
O Goddess, having invoked the weapon of the Goddess, the Vāruṇa [weapon], and my own temple (Prāsāda) into the Vāyavya pit, one should offer oblations of the Tattva and Kalā into the Soma pit.
O Pārvatī, having invoked Śāntidurgā in the northeast with her respective mantra,
and having likewise invoked the eight forms (mūrtis), one should then offer oblations to the guardians of those forms.
O Pārvatī, one should recite the Ghoramantra ten thousand times, and likewise the Mūlamantra;
one should offer oblations half of that, or half of that again, into each respective fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
The Guru should offer oblations separately to Gaṇeśa, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Lokapālas;
he should also offer oblations to the nine planets, the personified mantras, and the deities of the chariot.
O Pārvatī, [one should offer] sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and caru-oblations, along with truṭikas,
mustard seeds, wheat separately, parched grain, flour, and rice.
The Guru should offer oblations with the respective mantra, preceded by the formal dedication (*uddeśa*) and renunciation (*tyāga*);
at the end, he should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), dedicating it to the day.
One should bathe [the deity] with thousands of jars using Rudra-mantras and Sūktas;
one should perform a great worship and offer many kinds of oblations.
Then one should perform the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) and cause the ten gifts (daśadāna) to be bestowed;
afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins according to the number of oblations (āhuti).
Or else, O Goddess, according to the number of jars, one should [offer] desired foods and edibles;
and that [destruction] of the limbs in different locations follows the path described for reabsorption (saṃhāra).
O beloved, one should perform the worship of the chariot, offer oblations, and have the ritual bathing conducted;
then, having dismissed those deities, one should present the bali-offering to the great elements.
Having fashioned a chariot either of gold or silver, one should cause it to be given;
having bestowed various gifts, one should likewise cause abundant charity to be performed.
Then, O Dear One, one should perform a great festival and worship the preceptor,
having given cows, land, and other gifts, as well as wealth according to one's desire.
In that regard, O Goddess, one should provide the necessary implements along with a cloth-covered image;
O Goddess, one should cause the jars, the pavilion, and first of all, the chariot to be given.
O Goddess, one should satisfy the preceptor, who wards off all defects;
one should cause sacrificial fees to be given with devotion and perform rites for the Brahmins.
O Pārvatī, having completed the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) at your liṅga, the supreme guru should perform this [rite] with devotion even when the chariot breaks down.
It removes all defects of men, wards off all calamities,
bestows long life and joy, and is accompanied by sons and grandsons, O King.
Endowed with a fourfold army, he attains stable prosperity;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, he shall become renowned and wealthy.
"But in the event of the breaking of the chariot, O Goddess, this auspicious expiation [is prescribed].
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Determining the Expiation for the Breaking of the Chariot," in the section on Expiations within the venerable *Vātulottara*.
(47) Hereafter I shall explain, O Goddess, listen according to the sequence:
for the purpose of vehicles, by means of elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as adorned bulls.
In the event of a bloodshed occurring through injury to a living being,
or when death results from a wound inflicted by nails, teeth, or horns;
O Goddess, when an obstacle has arisen, or during a daily offering, a festival, a fortnightly festival, a monthly festival, a solstice, or annual festivals;
O Maheśvarī, if [the conjunction] occurs at the beginning, middle, or end,
there will be manifold affliction from enemies and a drought shall come to pass.
Famine shall arise in the world, along with the fear of great pestilence for men;
the king shall meet his death, and royal fortune shall depart abroad.
O Pārvatī, if the presence [of the deity] does not remain in the liṅga once it has been destroyed,
then, for the sake of pacifying that fault, one should perform the Mahāśānti rite.
When there is an abundance of ritual acts, one should not perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) at that time;
rather, one should perform the remaining festival rites from the commencement of the work until its conclusion.
When that [lunar] month has arrived, under that same asterism and on that same lunar day—
whether in the third, fifth, seventh, or ninth month, O Auspicious One.
(48) And one should perform the great rite of pacification; listen to the procedure, O Pārvatī.
The Guru should construct an excellent, most excellent pavilion in front of the deity.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be provided with an altar (vedikā), adorned with all ornaments,
measuring two cubits in size, and endowed with both the womb (yoni) and the navel (nābhi).
The arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is prescribed all around the center of the altar (vedikā);
it is proclaimed that the principal pit should be either square or circular.
One should construct a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the four directions,
provided with three girdles, according to the characteristics described by the Guru.

At night, preceded by the worship of Vighneśa, he should cause the twice-born to be invited for the Nāndīmukha rite and the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), accompanied by the madhuparka offering.
He should invite all the Brahmins, including the preceptor and others, individually;
immediately, the sprouting of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed, as well as the purification of the sacrificial pit and the pavilion.
One should perform the oblation for the destruction of the Vāstu-rākṣasa and the offering (bali) to Vāstu;
having worshipped the eight pitchers beginning with Vidyeśa, as well as the arches, the water-jars, and so forth.
Then one should perform the installation and carry out the binding of protection;
thereafter, O Maheśvarī, one should perform the purification of the site in that very place.
Excavation, removal, burning, filling, and the settling of cattle;
likewise, the remains of a Brahmin's meal and products of the cow—this, O beloved, is the purification of a site.
One should sweep and smear [the ground], scatter all kinds of parched grain,
perform the binding of protection, and then encircle it with a garland of *darbha* grass.
With the two mantras beginning with "vāstoṣpate," the Guru should recite the Pāvamāna hymn;
then, with the Bhūsūkta and the Brahma-sūkta, he should sprinkle that place.
One should perform the complete study of the Vedas and recite the mantra as prescribed;
then, having risen in the morning and completed the daily rites.
Having worshipped Vighneśa and performed the ritual of the declaration of auspiciousness (puṇyāha-saṅkalpa),
one should designate the day and, having made the formal resolve, commence the rite of the fire-oblation (homa).
O beloved Maheśvarī, [appoint] Brahmā and the Sadasya, fifty Hotṛs,
and fifteen who are knowers of the mantras of various Sūktas and so forth.
O Goddess, for the purpose of studying the four Vedas, one should appoint six sprinklers in each of the four directions in due order for the sake of others, and eleven sprinklers [in the center].

For the sake of worship, the practitioner, accompanied by the Brahmins, should perform prostrations and circumambulations individually with each of the ten Brahmins, reciting the respective mantras for each.
Having sat down in the sacrificial hall upon the seats in their proper order,
together with ten officiating priests (hotṛs), at the principal and middle fire-pits (kuṇḍa).
O Śivā, together with the member Dhanada and Brahmā, the Preceptor shall generate the fire after first performing the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should perform ten thousand *homa* offerings with the *aghora* mantra, preceded by the formal dedication (*uddeśa*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*),
separately in each of the four directions with ten Brahmins for each.
O Goddess, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should perform the fire-oblation with the mantra using wood from the Udumbara, Śamī, Dūrvā, Khadira, and Palāśa trees.
One should offer oblations into each of those sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in due order, beginning with the principal deity:
clarified butter, cooked rice (caru), sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and likewise tuṭika.
One should offer marīca, jīraka, parched rice (lāja), and flattened rice (pṛthuka) separately;
having offered them with the previously mentioned number of oblations, one should then offer other mantras in due order.
One should place the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra in the east, the Pāśupata mantra in the south,
Śāntidurgā in the west, and the Mūlamantra in the north.
O Goddess, one should perform the fire-oblation ten thousand times for each pit in due order with the mantra; meanwhile, the most excellent Brahmins should recite it.
The propitiation of the nine planets, the pacification of the site, the Rakshoghna, Bhuvanesvari,
the quadrangular Kshetrapala, Ganesh, and Sarasvati.
One should recite the Mṛtyuñjaya, the Prāsāda, the Saptaśatī, and so forth; or, O Maheśvarī, one should bathe [the deity] with a thousand jars or half that number.
Having worshipped with the previously mentioned rites, including garments, images, and so forth,
and having placed the medicinal herbs therein, one should mutter the root mantra, O Dear One.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should sprinkle the Goddess with Rudra-mantras and Vedic hymns (*sūkta*);
having bathed the *liṅga* with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the preceptor should smear it with fragrant pastes.
The mantra-practitioner should worship in many ways and offer various kinds of food-oblations to Śivā;
thereafter, he should perform the bali-festival and cause gifts of cows, land, and other such things to be bestowed.
Having mounted an elephant, a horse, or a bull, one should perform the reconsecration;
then one should give a sacrificial fee according to the extent of one's wealth.
O Maheśvarī, one should subsequently feed a thousand Brahmins,
and at the conclusion, one should satisfy the preceptor with ritual implements and other offerings.
It is said that this rite of pacification wards off all defects;
O Goddess, it removes all sins, and there shall be an abundance of food at that very moment.
There shall be an increase in kingdom, fortresses, and so forth, as well as the stationing of the fourfold army;
it immediately destroys all enemies, and one shall attain stable prosperity.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Pacification of Elephants, Horses, Bulls, and Other [Animals]," in the section on Expiation within the *Śrīvātulottara*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
Now, therefore, O beloved, I shall fully explain the [rites] for men who carry weapons—
namely, army commanders, servants, and others who are assembled together.
O Maheśvarī, when a battle broke out between them due to mutual hostility—
consisting of fist-fights, staff-duels, and wounds inflicted by nails and teeth—
O Maheśvarī, when a wound has been inflicted by stones, weapons, or the like,
and blood has flowed, if a person should die;
O beloved, listen to the fault and the pacification regarding an obstacle that arises at that time, whether during a daily or occasional rite, a festival, or at the time of an offering.
In fist-fighting, there is a great disease; in staff-fighting, the destruction of a lineage;
and when nails and teeth are used for injury, O Goddess, famine arises upon the earth.
(53) In a battle where stones are produced, the subjects shall meet with destruction;
furthermore, if blood falls, there will be drought or other calamities.
When a wound has been inflicted upon men, those who are proud shall suffer defeat;
and if death should occur, the king shall meet his own death.
Through your linga, there shall be the presence [of misfortune], the destruction of the fourfold army, and the swift loss of fortune and longevity; the village will meet its end in ruin.
To pacify those defects, I shall prescribe an expiation:
one should construct the previously described pavilion with either nine or five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
One should construct it with its characteristic features and adorned with gates and arches;
having decorated your abode, one should wash it with water mixed with cow dung.
Then, having risen at dawn and completed his daily obligatory rites,
he should first worship Gaṇapati and thereafter perform the Nāndī-rite.
The Guru should sprinkle the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the mantra;
O Goddess, he should then invite Brahmins according to the number previously mentioned for the twice-born.
Then, having offered the madhuparka, the preceptor should purify the pavilion;
he should worship the door-arches and the ritual jars with their respective names.
O Dear One, one should perform the complete recitation of the Vedas and chant the Caturasra mantra;
one should carry out the fire-sacrifice for destroying the Vastu-demons and perform the offering of oblations and worship.
Then the Guru should perform the purification of the body and purify that location by means of digging and other methods,
as well as by sweeping and sprinkling with water.
O Pārvatī, one should scatter mustard seeds with the Bhūsūkta, the Pāvamāna, the Viṣṇusūkta,
and the Vāstusūkta, while reciting the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Then one should perform the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) and commence the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana);
according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should offer oblations into the various sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Then, O beloved, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *bhū* seed-syllable,
the Guru should present an offering (*bali*) to the spirits all around the house.
Accompanied by dance and song until the time of sunrise,
and having risen again at dawn and completed the daily rites;
