Afterwards, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and perform the purification of the *liṅga*,
as well as the purification of the image and the temple, with their respective mantras and ritual substances.
Then the mantra-practitioner, having entered the sacrificial hall, should purify it according to the prescribed rules by means of Brahmā, Dhanada, and the Hotṛ priests.
Having sat down according to the rule in each individual *kuṇḍa*, O Maheśvarī,
one should establish the *jananāgni* and perform the ritual movement in another *kuṇḍa*.
O Maheśvarī, one should perform ten thousand oblations with the root mantra;
the Ādhāra [vessel] is in the eastern pit, while your Astra [weapon] is in the southeast.
O Goddess, one should perform the Mṛtyuñjaya rite in the Yāmya direction, the Diśāhoma in the Rākṣasa, the Prāsāda in the Vāruṇa, and the Śānti and Daurgaka rites in the Vāyavya.

The practitioner of mantras should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for the increase of prosperity in a gentle land, offering to Pañcabrahma and Īśa separately, according to the previously stated number.

Having performed the previously mentioned oblations of substances and the secondary oblations (upahoma) as before, one should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the end; O Dear One, one should then perform the ceremonial bath with the ritual jars (kalaśas).

O Śivā, the mantra-practitioner should [offer] five thousand [oblations] according to the rule, or half of that, or a quarter of that; the five substances, beginning with milk, constitute the *pañcāmṛta* measured in one *droṇa*.
O Goddess, having bathed [the deity] with the five fruits and the five nectars according to the rules, and with other hymns, O Śivā, one should rub [the image] with *āmalaka* fruits.
Having anointed [the image] with the eight fragrances, one should worship it with various flowers;
and one should offer as an oblation rice cooked with ghee along with the five types of edible foods and other offerings.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), and conduct the propitiatory worship (*prasannayajana*).
O Dear One, having given the ten kinds of gifts according to one's capacity, [one should do so] abundantly.
O Maheśvarī, having fashioned a figure of sesame or gold,
one should devoutly cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given according to the extent of one's wealth.
One should perform the offering of the sacrificial victim and the festival, feed many Brahmins,
hold a lamp festival at night, and present an offering to the spirits.
O Goddess, one should cause the dedication of the ritual action and the offering for the difficult penance (kṛcchra) to be made;
one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given with devotion to the preceptor and others in their proper order.
O Goddess, one should cause this to be performed; it removes all defects for men.
There shall be abundance of sons, grandsons, and so forth, and victory everywhere.
May there be the swift removal of all death, the constant increase of lifespan,
and the presence of Your Linga, which brings happiness to all living beings.
O Goddess, when a wound has occurred among men, this great remedy is the destroyer [of pain];
it is likewise for quadrupeds, bipeds, wild animals, and those of wicked life.
When entering [the womb] or death has occurred, provided it is associated with faults as previously described,
the penance shall be half of that, or according to the strength or weakness of the fault.

The knower of mantras should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) according to the path previously described. Thus ends [the chapter] titled "The Procedure for Pacifying the Entry of Two-Legged or Four-Legged Creatures, Death, Fist-Fights, and Hostilities" in the Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa of the Śrī-Vātulottara.
The forty-sixth chapter.
Hereafter, O Goddess, I shall declare the expiation for cities, houses, and so forth, when portents arise; listen, O beloved.
O Maheśvarī, [I am present] in the city, in the capital, in your field, and in the fortress; in the palace of kings, in other houses, and in the dwellings of the twice-born and others.
O Maheśvarī, if an ox, buffalo, tiger, donkey, camel, or similar animal should enter the house, or if one should suddenly climb upon it;
That place shall meet with destruction, and the queen shall die;
O Śivā, wherever death occurs at the time of entry, that very spot shall perish.
One meets death within three months, and there shall always be oppression by the king,
if an ant nest is formed inside a honeycomb or beneath a mushroom.
O Pārvatī, wherever anthills are seen, that house is constantly afflicted;
there will soon be the torment of death for the patron.
In the event of death resulting from the killing of a cow, the killing of a woman, entering a lizard or a boat, or entering among beasts of prey, pythons, vultures, and the like;
In that case, there is no doubt that the village will perish along with the sacrificer,
or his son, or his brother, will be severely afflicted by disease.
O Goddess born from the pitcher, if a frog dies in the fire-pit or a house,
or if pigeons, crows, bears, and the like enter the home;
O Pārvatī, the loss of cattle, the loss of progeny, and the loss of wealth occur;
furthermore, oppression by the king, fear of enemies, and the affliction of death increase.
Or, O Maheśvarī, if it is defiled by other wicked living beings,
then upon entering or dying therein, all one's purposes will certainly perish.
I shall now declare the results of the directions, beginning with entry, in their proper order:
in the east there will be the destruction of sons, and in the southeast the destruction of women.
In the south there will be an increase of enemies; in the southwest, the destruction of wealth;
in the west, the affliction of death; and in the northwest, the torment of disease.
O Goddess, if [the shadow] goes from the entrance door toward the northeast (īśa), there is fear of the king and the destruction of all wealth; one should abandon the house for one month.
O Goddess, if one avoids another door for six months,
there is no doubt that upon entering the middle of the house, [the result will follow] within a year.
O Goddess, one should avoid that house, as well as its beds, seats, and food;
O Goddess, one should especially avoid going there.
One should fill the doorway with thorns, stones, clods of earth, and other such materials;
one must never do this at a temple or in a royal palace.
Immediate pacification should be performed according to the path previously described;
O Goddess, one should avoid [the area] for seven nights, whether in a city or a house.
Then, one should perform a propitiatory rite for the cessation of all defects;
I shall now describe that propitiation to be performed in the king’s house and among the twice-born and others.
One should perform [the rite] in a well-decorated pavilion or water-shed, either at the entrance, in the eastern part, or in the northern part of the house.

O Śivā, having first purified that site— whether it be an altar (kuṇḍa) or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila)— along with its gateways, pillars, and so forth, one should perform the excavation and discard the earth.
Having filled it with salt or earth, one should wash it with cow-dung water on a day when the moon and stars are favorable, and on an auspicious lunar day (*tithi*) sacred to Rudra.
On that day, one should perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) according to the prescribed rules;
then, having risen in the morning, the preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the Brahmins, [should proceed].

Having first performed the bath with clay, and having then performed the ritual bath according to the rules using *kuśa* grass, cow dung, and ashes, one should perform the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), recitations (*japa*), and libations (*tarpaṇa*).
Then, having performed his daily rites and returned home, the preceptor should perform salutations to the Guru and others, and carry out the worship of Vighneśa.
O Dear One, [one should perform] the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and the consumption (prāśana);
having announced the Nāndī, one should offer the previously mentioned madhuparka according to the prescribed rule.
O Śivā, one should subsequently choose a Brāhmaṇa preceptor who bestows wealth;
a wise person should choose three or five officiating priests (ṛtvij), according to the number of sages.
For the purpose of recitation and for the purpose of Vedic study, one should choose [the preceptor] separately for each;
thereafter, one should perform the purification of the house with sprinklings using the Pāvamāna hymns.
Having scattered barley, mustard seeds, black gram, and mung beans,
and having swept the area, one should smear it with fragrant substances, performing the rites with the Vāyu-mantra and the Astra-mantra.
The Guru should sprinkle water everywhere with the *Bhūsūkta* and the *Pāvamāna*;
having worshipped the two doorposts, he should then perform the *rākṣoghna* oblation.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, the preceptor should scatter the bali offering;
thereafter, on the following day, the preceptor should perform the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha).
Then the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should perform the purification of the house;
for the purpose of installing the water-jars, he should prepare a heap of rice.
One should not have it made less than two *khāris*, or half of that;
one should place there a jar (*droṇakumbha*) that is very smooth and free from cracks.
The Guru should worship nine, five, or one water-pot according to the prescribed rite,
provided with five types of sprouts and accompanied by the five products of the cow.
One should fill [the vessel] with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) combined with the five jewels,
using half a pala of gold, or one karṣa, or according to one's own capacity.
With devotion, one should have images fashioned of Tryambaka,
the Lord of Śacī, Aghora, the world-protectors, Gaṇeśa, and the nine planets.
Having placed Durgā and the Kṣetrapālas, each in their respective forms,
individually within the jars, one should envelop them with a pair of cloths.
Having performed worship, the mantra-practitioner should then recite each respective mantra individually,
using either the sixteen types of offerings or the five types of offerings.

Then, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit or to a consecrated spot (sthaṇḍila), the most excellent preceptor should perform the rite up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) according to the procedure prescribed in his own Gṛhya-sūtra.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten thousand or one thousand times with the Mṛtyuñjaya, Aghora,
Navagraha, Vāstu, and Śāntidurgā mantras.
O Dear One, one should offer oblations to the world-protectors who grant fearlessness and to the guardian of the field;
[using] palāśa wood-sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and caru made of rice and sesame seeds, each separately.
Having offered oblations, O Śivā, the mantra-practitioner performed the recitation of the mantra as previously described;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he proceeded with the ritual jars in their proper order.
One should sprinkle the patron and others, bathing them with the waters from the ritual jars;
then, having performed the tenfold gift, one should cause abundant gifts to be given.
O Goddess, one should then feed many Brahmins according to one's capacity;
at the conclusion, one should cause sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the preceptor and others in due order.
In this manner, one should perform the rite of pacification, which destroys all misfortunes,
quells all deaths, and increases the lifespan of men.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Pacifying Death Caused by the Entry of Malevolent Beings into Temples, Royal Palaces, Dwellings of Twice-borns, and Other Such Places," in the section on Expiatory Rites (*prāyaścitta*) within the *Śrīvātulottara*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, salutations to you, for the happiness of the lord of the earth,
for the welfare of the great people, and for the increase of the royal treasury."
The officiants and others have been fully described regarding the rite of bathing your liṅga;
the bathing ritual, ending with the worship of the jar, has been declared by you to consist of five hundred [verses].
O illustrious one, tell me in detail how the ritual of the ceremonial bath with one thousand and nine jars is performed.
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain for the sake of sovereignty and prosperity the rite of a thousand ablutions, O beloved, which involves nine additional jars.
The number of sūtras, the streets, their junctions, the number of arrays (vyūha),
the names of the arrays, the medicinal herbs, and in detail, the deities of the jars.
O Śaṅkarī, one should perform all their worship, offerings,
and fire-rituals in front of your liṅga, having constructed an excellent and most magnificent pavilion.
The most excellent of men [constructed] a square, well-proportioned structure endowed with eight doors,
adorned with arches and the like upon a foundation of pillars.
A wise person who knows the procedure for the ritual of bathing should prepare everything, such as the sacrificial pit and the excavation, exactly as prescribed for my linga.
In rites that are regular or occasional, in those performed for specific desires, in consecrations, in great festivals,
in expiatory rites, as well as in portents, in battle and the like, and in achieving victory therein;
O beloved, in all matters of doubt, during the rite of binding, and in times such as famine, one should cause the ritual bathing to be performed according to the Śāmbhava tradition.
For the purpose of establishing the water-pot (kumbha), one should perform the laying of the lines;
there are forty-four lines and six additional lines.

The wise man, following the injunctions of Manu, should draw lines that are perfectly even, with their tips pointing eastward and northward; and upon those lines, he should mark distinct points at regular intervals.
Having abandoned the four lines, one should cleanse it from a single square;
then twenty-one [squares] are seen as the arrayed path.
Each individual array is composed of nine compartments;
there are twelve paths, with some oriented toward the east and others likewise toward the north.
O sinless one, I have thus described to you the number of joints for the paths: four hundred and forty joints in total.
By exceeding the height of the central altar of the four-pillared high platform, all the arrays (vyūhas) should be made equal; the central array, however, should consist of eight [parts].
In the center of that are the nine arrays, and outside of that is the enclosure of Kālikā.
In the center of that are the sixteen arrays (vyūhas), and outside of them is the enclosure of Ramā;
within that [enclosure], twenty-four arrays are proclaimed.
Outside of that, O Maheśvarī, are the thirty-two arrays of Śāradā on the elephant;
they are surrounded by a forest-fortress, and outside of those are further arrays.
O Dear One, it is known as forty when excluding the central array;
here, there are five arrays in the enclosure and nine arrays in the middle.
Then, having swept the pathway,
one should subsequently prepare the squares within the enclosure using the five colors, beginning with white and yellow.
One should color all the compartments with lotuses of eight petals and so forth;
then, one should fill the pathway with a dark-colored powder.
In the arrangement for placing [the deity] in the center of that, one should place the nine-syllable mantra in the middle;
likewise, in the eightfold arrangement situated within the circle of Kālikā, one should place it in the center of the arrays.
Having written down the sixteen vowels in order starting from the east and so forth,
one should write the consonant of the arrays of the enclosures of Ramā in the center.

In the midst of the Śāradāvyūha, the preceptor should write the letters beginning with 'ma' and ending with 'sa' in the cardinal and intermediate directions, followed by the three supreme seed-syllables of Bālā.
The wise one should cause [the diagram] to be drawn in the remaining central square,
in the middle position of the arrays belonging to the ninefold enclosure of Durgā.

The best of men should first perform the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa) according to the sequence beginning with the sounds such as *nāda* and starting from the east; then, he should fill [the vessel] with husked rice.
First, within the new arrangement (navavyūha) of your own lineage, there is grain produced from the mountain;
specifically, three *prasthas* each of rice, half a *prastha* of rice, and sesame.
Having filled it with half a measure of rice, one should worship that supreme mantra from the root within the central cell of the array of Kālikā’s enclosures.
O Goddess, having filled two *prasthas* of grain, one and a half *prasthas* of rice,
and one *prastha* of sesame seeds, one should worship with the *Kālikā-mantra*.
O Śaṅkarī, within the central compartments of the array of the inner enclosure, there should be grain measuring one and a half *prasthas*; rice is said to be one *prastha*.
Having combined half a portion of rice with sesame seeds,
the Guru should worship it with the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrī) in the midst of the array of Śāradā’s enclosure, together with grain.
The expert [should provide] one *prastha* of rice and half a *dhānya* of grain;
sesame is said to be half of that, as are the primary autumnal seeds.
Having worshipped the Earth with great devotion for the sake of the purpose, one should then show the supreme six mudrās;
thereafter, the enclosure of the nine Durgās should be arranged in the central cell of the array.
A quarter-measure of grain is called a *prastha*; half that amount of grain is called half a *prastha*.
A wise person, having filled [the vessel] with rice and half-rice, or with sesame seeds, [should perform the offering].
O Maheśvarī, having worshipped with those nine seeds and the yonimudrā,
one should place a prastha of grain separately in each of all the grid squares.
O beloved, having filled half the vessel with rice and half the rice with sesame seeds,
the Guru should worship those compartments with your root mantra.
One should place a *darbha* grass stalk, one *tāla* in length, upon each individual square;
[these squares] may be made of gold, silver, copper, and so forth, or from clay, pearls, or mother-of-pearl shells.
The jars should be made from cups and filled with water in quantities of half and half a *droṇa* respectively;
one should wash them all with water and wrap them with threads of *guṇa*.

O Dear One, the Guru should fashion a *kūrca* (bundle of grass) using *darbha* grasses fixed in the directions of the planets, numbering five and so forth, with either the root mantra or your seed-syllable, O Beloved.
One should place a water-pot inside, and above and below it, separately, one should set down three bundles of *kūrca* grass;
in the nine central arrays, one should place water-pots with a capacity of one *droṇa*.
O beloved, in all the central compartments, place jars measuring half a *droṇa* each, and in the surrounding side compartments, jars measuring three *prasthas* each.
One should worship separately in a separate compartment the [deities] residing in the pot, starting from the east.
First, all [the vessels] should be placed face-down; then, having fumigated them with incense, they should be turned face-up.
In all the central arrays and so forth, beginning from the central cell, the Guru,
having placed the multitudes of jars in due order, should worship them sequentially.
O Goddess, having stirred the eightfold nine-fragrance in auspicious water,
the Guru should fill all the jars with that water while reciting the mantra.
Sandalwood, camphor, agallochum, saffron, *kapī*, *māṃsī*, and yellow orpiment— these are your eight fragrant substances (*coragandhāṣṭaka*).
O Caṇḍikā, one should not perform a separate consecration for the nine central jars; however, within the remaining jars of the array, one should place five jewels.
Having separately prepared nine golden images, each measuring one and a half niṣkas, the mantra-practitioner should then inscribe that seed-syllable upon them.

Having separately placed [the substances] in nine central jars in due order, [one should perform the rite] with the measure of a niṣka for each image, accompanied by the seed-syllable (bīja) of Durgā.
The wise one should place [the image] inside a jar situated in the center of the array beginning with Kālyā;
he should then place a half-niṣka image in the jars located in the side-chambers.
Hereafter, I shall declare the medicinal herbs beginning with the central jar:
cardamom leaf, cloves, usīra, ginger, and jaṭha.
Having placed one pala each of jasmine, maruga, and davanānta— nine in sequence— along with sprouts and fruits into the nine jars.
A new cloth made of fine silk (dukūla), measuring seven, six, or five cubits in length,
and distinguished by colors such as white and others, should be folded separately.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a new water-pot and having worshipped it with devotion using the root mantra,
O Dear One, [one should then worship] the array of Kālikā’s enclosures within the central pots.
I shall describe the distinct substances: milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise the water of the five trees (pañcavṛkṣodaka).
Sesame seeds, darbha grass, barley, mustard, pomegranate, vacā, mātuluṅga, that which is called niśā (turmeric), and likewise parched grain flour.
One should place these sixteen substances within the central squares:
saffron, yellow orpiment, costus, long pepper, and black pepper.
O Maheśvarī, sandalwood, cumin, and rāsnā—these are the eight substances;
one should place them around those [liṅgas] within the eight clusters of jars.
Now, the arrangement for the enclosures of Ramā in the central jars is described:
dūrvā grass, ramā, bhadra, viṣṇukrāntā, and śatāvarī.
Śakravallī, as well as kāśa, vārāhī, bhṛṅgapatraka,
śamī leaves, the two types of apāmārga, and likewise the two types of karṇi.
The gateway (gopura), ash, chickpeas, mung bean flour,
as well as pigeon pea, ground black gram, jackfruit, wood-apple, and coconut;
O Śaṅkarī, these substances, numbering twenty-four,
should be placed individually with their respective root-mantras into the central pitchers previously mentioned.
Tulasī, Bilva leaves, Pārijāta, Tamālaka, Hibiscus, Bhadramustā, lotus, and likewise blue water-lily.
The wise practitioner should devoutly place the eight substances, one by one in order, around all the eight jars of the Ramā-vyūha and within the vyūha of the Lord.
I shall now describe, in order, starting from the east, the thirty-two waters located within the central compartments of the Śāradāvaraṇavyūha.
Combined with Tulasī, Maru-gā, and Bilva leaves, it is known as "patrodaka"; thereafter come the lotus and the blue water-lily.
The flower-water for you is known as the red lotus;
the fruit-water consists of the fruits of the orange, the *vikaca*, and the *āmra*.
This water, joined with the essence of the *kapittha* and the bark of the *bodhi* and *palāśa* trees, is called *pippala*; it is pure and constitutes your very self.
One should place water infused with the sprouts of *palāśa*, *aśvattha*,
and *cūta* into the five pitchers located in the cardinal directions starting from the east and in the central pitcher.
(72) Together with *hrīvera*, *bhadramustā*, and that which is called *kuśa*,
it is known as "root-water" (*mūlodaka*), which bestows your presence.
The seed-water is known to be prepared with priyaṅgu, śāli, and nīvāra rice,
combined with the three tubers of vidārī, utpala, and padma.
That which is known as *kandodaka*, as well as *śrīgandha* and *agaru*, together with that called *nimba*— water mixed with these is celebrated as *gandhāmbhas*.
I have described the water consecrated with sesame, barley, and white mustard seeds;
it should be poured into the five southern arrays beginning with fire, as well as into the central ones.
The supreme mantra-practitioner, reciting the root mantra with devotion, should pour it out;
this is known as "jewel-water," combined with rubies, pearls, and lapis lazuli.

Water containing gold, durvarṇa, and copper is considered iron-water (lohodaka). It is also [considered such] when it contains sun-crystal (sūryakānta), magnet (ayaskānta), and moon-crystal (candrakānta).
O Goddess, *kāntāmbhas* is said to be combined with three parts of honey;
whereas *mākṣikāmbhas* has honey in the middle and is combined with three parts of mica (*abhra*).
O Mistress, while reciting your root mantra, [the practitioner] should place the water of mica (abhrakodaka) within the fivefold array of the Lord of the Daityas situated in the central compartment.
At that time, reciting the Prāṇamantra along with the Nyāsasūktādi mantras,
he [bestowed] the water of knowledge combined with Kālīyañjana and Saurāṣṭra.
Together with sindhūra, gairika, and the mineral [cinnabar], these three are known as *dhātūdaka*; likewise, *haritāla* and *manaḥśilā*.
When combined with *kucandana*, it is known as "red water" (*raktodaka*);
and when combined with the earth from the banks of rivers, it is "mud-water" (*mṛjjala*), consisting of the lord of rivers and the earth from riverine fields.
Water combined with the three myrobalans (triphalā) is declared to be a decoction;
thus, there are five types of water separately in the fivefold western array.
Having placed [the vessels] in the central jars while reciting the Durgā-sūkta,
the preceptor [should offer] milk, curd, and ghee, as well as water infused with juices.
This shall be "kuśa-water" when combined with three blades of kuśa grass;
this, however, is "grain-water" when mixed with rice, nīvāra, and mung beans.
Water mixed with mud and blended with the fragrances of saffron, saffron-wood, and camphor is known as *kardamodaka*; it bestows beauty and auspiciousness.

Tamāla leaves, the tips of dūrvā grass, and the tips of kuśa grass— these combined with water for the fingers is called *aṅgurodaka*, [to be offered] during the five-fold observance beginning with the wind-eating (*mārutāśa*).
Then, one should place and offer [the offerings] into the jars situated in the midst of the array (vyūha), together with the three ripe fruits: grapes, dates, and plantains.
O innocent one, when the jar has gone into the midst of the array,
this is the boiled water combined with rice, mung beans, and wheat, each filled separately.
Known as *cūrṇodaka*, it destroys the instability of the world;
it is prepared with sesame seeds, barley, unbroken grains, rice, and *atīka* flowers.

It is said that "unbroken water" refers to the water in the jar situated in the center of the formation; the water for the *vally* (garland) rite should consist of women, the *śakravallī*, the *sahā*, and *alakṣmī*.
Combined with the buds of the *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *nāśā* flowers,
this is declared to be "bud-water" (*kudmalodaka*), which bestows prosperity upon people.
In this manner, one should install Soma and the others, as well as the counter-array (prativyūha), within the fivefold [group];
while reciting the Āryā-sūkta and other hymns, one should place them in the central jars.
Tintriṇī, ripe fruit, sugar, mango-sugar, and molasses— one part each of these combined with water is called *rajodaka*.
O Goddess, this "dust-water" (rajodaka), joined with the dust of the finest musk-powders, [is to be used] in the center of the previously mentioned pair of arrays.
One should place that [mudrā] upon the two jars and install the three seed-syllables of Bālā.
The substances for the jars situated in the midst of the thirty-two-fold array have thus been described.
Now, the contents for their eight jars, starting from the east and proceeding around, are described:
devadāru, peya, tālīśa, and māṃsī.
O Dear One, having placed these eight substances— rāsnā, that which is called rūttha, kurundra, and nāgakesara— into the eight pitchers;
The Śvetākambakula, Mallikā, Karavīraka,
Padma, Jāti, Kaṅkoṣṭha, and that which is known as Caturaṅgula;
Having placed the eight substances in order within eight separate jars in the eightfold array situated to the south— namely, mādhavī and likewise kurava;
Bandhūka, pāṭala, nandyāvarta, ketakī, water,
and the flower called hema— these are in the eight arrays situated in the west.
One should place the eight substances designated as the "eightfold group" into eight jars:
parched grain, parched grain with molasses, lentils, horse gram, and powdered black gram.
One should place ripe *jambū* fruit, known as "the pair," and likewise lac-powder,
around the eight pitchers situated at the eight outer enclosures.
(p. 76) Now, the arrangement of the ninefold enclosure for the Navadurgā is described within the central pitchers:
the *campaka*, the jasmine (*mallikā*), the *puṣpa*, the *punnāga*, and likewise the *ketakī*.
The *pārijāta*, the flower known as *kadamba*, that which is named *govinda*,
*sevantikā*, *droṇapuṣpa*, as well as the *padma* and the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*).
O Goddess, [one should offer] the maṇi, the kuñca, the goraṇṭa, the mandāra, the karavīraka,
the two types of japā flowers, and the nandyāvarta blossom.
The aśoka, the damana, the pāṭali, and likewise the bakula;
the one called palāśa, the kusumbha, the lodhra, and the cilika flower.
White arka, red arka, bṛhatī, vanamallikā,
then the flower of dhattūra, and the blossom of the coconut.
The two *pūpa* flowers, the *śaṅkhapuṣpa*, the *suma*,
the two *karṇi* flowers, the *kalhāra*, and the lotus known as *rakta*.
And there should be forty flowers of the plant known as *arjuna*;
these one should place in the central jars, along with the offerings for the military arrays (*vyūhas*) up to the enclosure (*āvṛti*).
O Goddess, sandalwood, camphor, kapikacchū, māṃsī, pacoraka, saffron, agallochum, and gorocanā— these are the eight [substances].
And around those central jars, one should place [the offerings] separately upon eight [vessels];
reciting your root mantra, one should install it upon all the jars.
Thus have I described the substances to be placed in the jars situated within all the arrays:
sacrificial grass, sprouts, and coconut fruits.
The Guru should separately offer betel nuts and pairs of garments as the reality;
he should then wrap around the mouth of the jar and place it.
O Daughter of the Mountain, I shall fully declare the deities of the central array and so forth:
Śāmbhavī, Mūladurgā, and Vedamātā, the bestower of happiness.
One should worship Viśvā, who is the form of the syllable Oṃ, the illusion of the universe, and beloved by the people,
in the nine jars beginning with the middle one, ending with Jūṣaṇī.
In the central jars of the Kālikā array, starting from the east, the deities are Kālī,
Karālī, Kalyāṇī, Kāntidā, and Kalāvatī.

She bestows fame, she is a loving woman, she is beautiful, and she possesses the fragrance of lotuses and water-lilies; she is full of virtues, she is a lotus-pond, and her radiance is like that of the blazing fire.
Kṛśāvatī, Kāñcanākṣī, and the rite that increases the lineage—
these sixteen deities one should worship within those jars.
Mādhavī, Māninī, Manyā, Mahāmāyā, Maheśvarī, Mātaṅgī, Mohadā, and Vāṇī— these are the eight deities proclaimed.
And prior to that, the Guru should worship individually within the eight pitchers of the array:
Viśvamātā, Viśveśī, Viśālākṣā, and Vinodinī.
One should worship the eight deities— Brahmaṇī, Vimalā, Brāhmī, Varadā, and the others— individually in the eight pitchers of the southern array.
Jāhnavī, Janmāyā, Japyā, Jaṅghālavīcikā, Jayā, Janārdanaprītā, Hlādinī, and again Mohinī.
One should worship with devotion and full of happiness those jars situated in the middle of the western array, which possess the [sixteen] digits (kalās), and also the eight jars surrounding them.
Gangā, Gandhavatī, Gaurī, Guṇātītā, Guṇāvatī,
Goparāgahinī, Durgā, and Caṇḍikā among the Udvyūhas.
And one should worship the eight auspicious goddesses individually around those situated in the center;
these are proclaimed as the deities of the Kālikā-enclosure array.
I shall now describe, starting from the east, the deities of the central chamber and other areas within the array of the lotus enclosure: first is Ramā, the lotus-eyed one.
Mahālakṣmī bestows sovereignty, removes disease, grants a great treasury,
bestows liberation, confers good fortune, and increases enjoyments.
On another occasion, the goddess is the giver of wealth, the destroyer of sin, and the one who is difficult to overcome;
she is the bestower of fortitude, the giver of riches, the skillful, the giver of dharma, and the sovereign of the universe.
Transcending the universe, free from fear, her nature being innate bliss,
she is stainless and born from the eye within the circle of the assembly of Ramās.

One should worship the deities in the central jars with their names in the dative case followed by "namaḥ"; likewise, one should worship the deities in the eight jars individually with their respective names.
Lāvaṇyā, Lalitā, Padmā, Lokeśī, Sarvasākṣigā,
Kāmukī, Kāmyadā, and Tṛṣṇā— these are the eight [Śaktis] in order, beginning with that [first one].
Having fully worshipped Umā— who is peaceful, the remover of grief,
the bestower of auspiciousness, the bearer of the conch, the fierce, the noble, and who is said to be the end of the auspicious— within the internal cavities, [one attains liberation].
O one of excellent vows, one should worship those situated in the center of the southern array-networks by their own names, and likewise worship eight others individually in the surrounding jars.
Bestower of victory, remover of dullness, eldest in the world, the broad-hipped one;
destroyer of the terrifying, the enjoyer, giver of prosperity, and adorned with ashes.
O Dear One, having again worshipped the Guru situated in the central square of the western array, one should worship him individually in each of the eight surrounding squares.
Sukhaṇḍī, Amaraśreṣṭhā, Śauryadā,
Suvāsinī, Śūlinī, Śītalā, Bālā, and Brahmiṣṭhā are the eight deities at the end.
One should worship the deities of the pitchers situated in the middle row in the eight directions surrounding the northern array;
likewise, one should worship the individual deities of the pitchers located in the enclosure of Ramā.
The correct utterances have been fully declared as they appear in the Śāradā-āvaraṇa;
these are the Vāk-pādas belonging to those situated from the east to the center, whose mistress is Vākyanāyakī.
Vāgīśvarī, Vajrahastā, Kumārī, Vindhyavāsinī, Sarasvatī, Sarveśī, and Parā, who is fond of the chanting of the Sāmaveda.
She is Kalā and Kāṣṭhā, the bestower of contentment and the giver of nourishment and growth;
she is the maker of luster, the maker of strength, the powerful one, and the increaser of might.
When she is stable, she is auspicious; she bestows happiness and good fortune upon the three [worlds].
She is the essence of the letters, composed of the letters, yet transcends the letters—she is Manonmanī.
O Ambika, the thirty-two deities have been proclaimed, beginning with Munistuta and ending with Guṇādhāra: Mohahantrī, Daityahṛtsaudarī, and Malā.
One should worship [the goddesses] within the central jars situated in the array of the autumnal ritual manual:
Cinmayī, Citirūpā, Cañcalā, Bodhinī, and Prabhā.
Candrikā, Dhāriṇī, and Sūkṣmā— these eight deities are proclaimed to reside within the previously mentioned networks of arrays and in the eight jars situated around them.
Having worshipped each with their own names, ending with "namaḥ," the Guru [should know that] the power of action is of the nature of knowledge, and the power of will is immovable.
Nityā, Nirañjanā, Nandā, and Maṅgalā are the eight deities at the end;
they reside individually and in sequence within the midst of the protective net-array (rakṣasthavyūhajāla).
Then, one should worship in the eight jars surrounding [the central one] with their respective initial names:
Nandinī, Nādinī, Jāyā, Gāndhārī, and Taraṅgiṇī.
One should worship Mālinī, Dāhinī, and Mānyā— located in the west among those in the middle—
in each of the eight surrounding jars individually with their respective names.
Dhanvī, Dhīrā, Mati, Medhā, Śuddhā, Buddhi, Tapasvinī,
and Ghorāntā— these are the eight deities in the northern array of the Kadamba formation.
And one should worship those situated in the center within the surrounding enclosures;
thus have the deities been correctly described in the Śāradā-āvaraṇa.
(p. 82) In the enclosure of Navadurgā, I shall describe the deities of the arrays starting from the east:
Durgā, Kapālinī, Āryā, Siṃharūḍhā, and Ambikā.
She who stands upon a buffalo, Caṇḍikā, Vāṇī, the bestower of objects,
Cāmuṇḍī, Sarasā, the all-pervading Vaiṣṇavī, and she of fierce valor.
She who performs auspicious deeds, the delightful one, the established one, and she who has conquered her senses;
she whose nature is fire, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, the mother of Skanda, and the remover of impurities.
Kuśmāṇḍā, Śivadūtī, Śaṅkarī, and the beloved of Śaṅkara;
she is free from affliction, beyond appearance, omnipresent, and the range of all perception.
Kātyāyinī, Kāmākṣī, Viṣṇumāyā, Vimāninī,
Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, and she who bestows the path of the Left (Vāmamārga).
The Pavitrā and the Pāvamānī, which brings about supreme sovereignty—
these forty Māyās have been declared to you by me, O sinless one.
And one should worship within the arrangement of the outer enclosure Sanātani,
Sadānandā, Sāvitrī, and Guṇāgraṇī.
She resides in the sky, she resides in heaven, and she is the supreme sovereign residing on Trikūṭa;
she dwells within the array of external enclosures in the eight jars.
The Guru should worship them, surrounded by the directions starting from the east, with their respective names.
Now, I shall describe the beautiful [mantra] that removes disease, which is to be used on the south.
One should worship in sequence around [the goddess] Tripurāntakā: Bhedinī, Daṇḍinī, Drā, Vinidrā, Caṇḍavegā, and the eight goddesses.
She laughs with a great, boisterous laugh; she is sweet and fond of sweetness;
she holds a noose in her hand, a lotus in her hand, and carries a book of knowledge.
In the collection of the arrays of the Great Means (Mahopāya) and the Goddess of the West (Pratīcī),
one should worship those situated in the center and separately those around them in the eight directions.
She is the bestower of knowledge, the embodiment of knowledge, and resides within the cage of knowledge;
she is known as both the immobile and the mobile, transcending all parts (kalās) yet consisting of those very parts.
In the eight directions beyond the sound [of the central deity], within the collection of the northern array,
one should worship in the eight jars situated around the center.
Thus, regarding the ritual jars (*kumbha*) situated within the five enclosures (*pañcāvṛti*) during the *kālika* rite,
I have described the deities for each individual jar in their respective order.

The Guru, having worshipped [the deities] individually with their own names according to his own tradition— beginning with the *Nṛtyeśvarī-trika* and ending with *Namaḥ*— should worship Gaṇeśa and the others in the central pitcher (*madhyakumbha*).
Having displayed the six mudrās beginning with invocation (āvāhana), as well as the Yonimudrā, the Kālinī, the Dhenumudrā, the one called Liṅga, and the one called Prasannā;
The wise one should sacrifice the seven secondary nooses (upapāśas) with each jar during the first watch of the night,
and all the well-formed vessels during the fourth watch of the night.
The water for honor (arghya), fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, and likewise a lamp— these seven services (upacāras) conclude with the offering of food (naivedya).
Having performed the morning bath and other rites, and having completed his daily obligatory duties,
he should conduct the *nāndī* and *puṇyāhavācana* ceremonies at your residence and in the presence of the preceptor.
Having brought the *varaṇa* and the *madhuparka*, he performed the rite together with the twice-born,
standing around the altar at the nine sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) in due order.
One should perform the fire-offering rites with the image-keepers (mūrtipas) who have mastered the scriptures,
using sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, rice, barley, tips of dūrvā grass, and sesame seeds.
With the root mantra of yours and the Vāruṇa weapon-mantra,
the preceptor should offer one hundred and eight oblations at the time of the conjunction of the planets until its conclusion.
Again, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and apply the residual drops (*saṃpāta*) to the vessel;
having performed the purification of the *liṅga* and other rites, one should offer the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
Afterwards, for the sake of propitiation, one should worship the deities residing in the pitcher;
then, at the beginning of the sixteen nāḍīs, the best of those who know the ritual should perform [the rite] with the Brahmins.
A man [should be honored] by people such as kings, adorned with umbrellas, chowries, and ornaments,
accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, the sounds of musical instruments, and the resonance of lutes and flutes.
Having lifted up nine jars, one should place them upon the shoulders of the disciple;
having circumambulated the house clockwise, they should be positioned in the outer enclosure.
One should enter the interior of the sanctum and place [the offerings] upon the sacrificial ground;
having placed the tufts of grass from the nine jars upon the top of your liṅga.
One should rotate garments three times around your liṅga with the garment-mantra;
one should offer fruits with the fruit-mantras and sprouts with the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
One should sprinkle with the waters from the new jars, using golden images and so forth;
in this manner, one should properly [sprinkle] all the jars, beginning with the obscuration of Kālikā.
Then one should extract eight [vessels] starting from the eastern [direction] up to the central pitcher,
beginning from the bathing pavilion and ending with the gateway of the liṅga.
O Brahmins, on both sides, facing him in the form of a row,
those twice-born ones stood purified, reciting those Mantras.
p. 86) All those situated in every row, having lifted up all the jars in due order, should bring them and cause them to be offered to the Guru.
The wise man, reciting the hymns and mantras, should fill the liṅga with those jars;
furthermore, he should offer the overflowing pitchers, as well as their cloths and fruits.
They should lead [the image] along the left row to the altar upon the pavilion;
there, while reciting the Kālīsūkta and other hymns, it should be placed in the form of a collective assembly.
Then those who have mastered the Vedas should recite the *Rāmāsūkta*, the one called the *Śāradā*, the *Ādimantra* over the water,
and the mantras of the *Navadurgāsūkta*.
Having performed the great worship at the conclusion of the sprinkling according to the prescribed method,
one should then conduct your festival and install [the deity] in the primary image.
Having offered the network of ritual acts at the end, one should thereafter give the ten gifts;
at the conclusion of that, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and feed the best of the Brahmins.
All the jars weighing nine niṣkas, as well as the garments, fruits, jewels, images, the pavilion, and all the ornaments;
There, O lord of men, for the sake of his own prosperity and happiness, the ruler should present the beloved consort of the preeminent teacher along with all necessary articles.
p. 87) Six *niṣkas* are prescribed for the patron (*yajamāna*), five for the Brahman priest;
three *niṣkas* for the Sadasya, and two each separately for the Mūrtipa and the others.
One and a half *niṣkas* are prescribed for those who have crossed over; one *niṣka* is said for those who recite [mantras];
one and a half *niṣkas* for those who guard [the retreat], and at its conclusion, a profuse sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The specific fruit for each [act] must be given; listen as I describe it.
O lord of men, regarding the act of bathing at your liṅga, according to one's capacity—
The power of all prosperity, the treasury, the glory of the increase of one's lineage, fame, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, as well as victory over enemy kingdoms and so forth.
By grace, he will then undoubtedly obtain other kingdoms;
now I shall describe a special [instruction], most secret and difficult even for the gods to attain.
O Mother,
for the sake of your favor, Śakra has performed the bathing of your liṅga with devotion, [hoping] that it may be worthy of your side-glance.
Furthermore, O beloved, the host of gods performed this for their own sake here,
and the host of Mothers performed it for the sake of the fortune of the Daitya and Soma.
For the sake of attaining all prosperity, for the increase of the earth, and for victory— therefore,
having observed this, one should perform the consecration of your linga.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual of the Thousand Vases for Durgā," in the section on Occasional Rites within the Dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī in the *Vātulottara*, the illustrious supreme secret.
It has been stated that the rite of bathing consists of the performance of the Navadurgā ritual;
now I shall describe for you its origin and other such rites, including their various distinct divisions.
Primordially arisen, she is Great Bliss, the Root Durgā who bestows happiness;
she is the granter of victory, the destroyer of enemies, the gracious protectress of the world.
O Goddess, consisting of a web of powers and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, she manifests as three forms: Kālī, Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī.
From his feet up to the secret place arises that which is called Kālikā;
from the navel up to the throat is Ramā; and from the throat up to the crown of the head is [Lakṣmī].
She is known by the name Sarasvatī, celebrated as Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi;
she is called Durgā, Āryā, Śūlinī, Kumārī, and Ambikā.
Mahiṣāsuranāśī, Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, and Vāgīśvarī—these [names] end with the latter [syllable] in sequence, and they are each accompanied by a separate gift. (p. 89)
To the nine Durgās and the three Mūrtis, who are the constant bestowers of prosperity:
Durgā and Kālikā reside in the secret place (guhya), while Āryā is born in the navel.
The Goddess Rāmā is at the mouth of Kālī; Kumārikā is at her feet;
Ramā is at the navel; she known as Ambikā is at her face; and Mahiṣāntakī is at her mouth.
Vāṇī is named Caṇḍikā in the throat, Sarasvatī is in the tongue, and Vāgīśī is in the nose; these have arisen as distinct entities.
From them, nine others were separately born, who were named Prasannā.
Śailajā is Caṇḍaghaṇṭī; she is Sundarī and a celibate practitioner.
She is known as Kūśmāṇḍā, Skandamātā, Kārtyāyanī, and Kālarātrikā;
she is called Gaurī, Śivadūtī, Māhendrī, and Agnisaṃjñakā.
Vārāhī holds a sword; Vāruṇī rides upon a deer;
Kauberī has a trident in her hand; and Brahmāṇī and Vaiṣṇavī are supreme.
She is known as Cāmuṇḍā, mounted upon a corpse; as Jayā and Vijayā;
as the one called Jitā and Parājitā; as Rocanā, and she who is naked.
Udyotinī, Ityumā, Saṃjñā, Mālādhārī, Yaśasvinī,
Citranetrā, Śaṅkhinī, Yamaghaṇṭā, and Manasvinī.
Daṇḍinī, Vindhyasaṃsthā, Gahinī, Trilottamā,
Śaṅkhinī, Śarabhā, Suvratā, and Sugandhinī.
Toyeśī, Somapā, Devī, Bhrāmarī, Haṃsavāhinī,
Kārmukhā, Maṅgalā, Śoṇā, Hrādinī, Mohinī, and Kṣamā.
Rakṣaṇī, Ramaṇī, Rambhā, Rogahantrī, Surapriyā;
Dhanurdharī, Balā, Bālā, Prabalā, Sthūlanāsikā.
Vajriṇī, Śaktihastā, Daṇḍahastā,
Māninī, Kāpālinī, Kāmanī, Bhīmādevī, and Bhairavī.
Jvālāmukhī, Nādanī, Haṃsagā, Ghoṣiṇī, Śubhā,
Māheśvarī, Mahānandā, and Jagadāhlādakāriṇī.
Thus, these known as the Nine Durgās arise from the eighty-one [syllables];
separate sequences have emerged, and from them, infinite powers are born.
The origin of this [deity] is thus proclaimed; now the divisions of Caṇḍī are described by me:
Ekacaṇḍī, Tricaṇḍī, and likewise Pañcacāṇḍī, Saptacaṇḍī, and Navacaṇḍī.
Thirty, eighty-one, a hundred, and a thousand—
these are the divisions of Caṇḍikā, numbering ten thousand and a hundred thousand.
In the same way, from ten lakhs up to a crore, there is Anantacaṇḍikā;
her various divisions should be known as those which bring about the presence of prosperity.
O Goddess, from ten lakhs up to ten million are proclaimed for the world of the gods;
however, on the surface of the earth, O Mistress, it is correctly stated that the ritual ends at ten thousand.

O Dear One, in the occasional rite (naimittika), the sequence begins with one, three, five, and ending with seven Caṇḍīs for the monthly [observances], while for the excellent occasional rite, it begins with seven Caṇḍīs and ends with thirty.
Those known as the "one hundred and eighty-one" and the "thousand" are bestowers of auspiciousness;
they are prescribed for rites performed for specific desires and grant the increase of one's lineage.

In the ritual of recitation, the numbers are proclaimed as follows: beginning with *ayuta* and ending with *lakṣa*, then *daśalakṣa* (ten lakṣas), *gaja* (eighty-four lakṣas), *caṇḍikā* (one hundred and eight lakṣas), and ending with *koṭi*.
One, three, and five [recitations] ending with Caṇḍī are prescribed by me for occasional rites (naimittika);
and for occasional rites, seven and so forth up to thirty-nine are the maximum.
The one known as the Lord of One Hundred and Eighty-one, and the one known as the Thousand, bestow auspiciousness;
they are prescribed for rites performed for specific desires in order to remove the afflictions caused by demons.
O Ambika, that man who, for the sake of increasing his sons, wife, and so forth, and for the sake of attaining power,
always recites the *Ekacaṇḍī* with devotion during occasional rites (*naimittika-karma*),
does so for the purpose of increasing wealth and kingdom, and for the sake of [establishing] a mandala.
One should constantly perform the Tricaṇḍī rite according to the prescribed method for the sake of terrifying enemy kings.
The rite of reciting the *Pañcacāṇḍī* is for the sake of sovereignty and all enjoyments;
the one called *Saptacāṇḍī* is for the sake of the earth of Caṇḍī, for the destruction of enemies, and for prosperity.
For the attainment of a thornless earth, for the destruction of enemy armies,
for the sake of universal sovereignty, and for the increase of power and treasury.
O beloved, every year during the autumn season, and likewise on other auspicious days,
one should recite the Navacaṇḍī with devotion through the chanting of mantras, complete recitations, and other such rites.
For the increase of one's lineage, for the sake of sovereignty, for a fourfold army,
for the acquisition of wealth, and for prosperity, the practice of thirty *caṇḍī* recitations [is prescribed].
Whenever a strange calamity, such as a perilous situation or the like, has arisen,
a woman who desires her cherished goal should [practice this] for the sake of destroying great sins.
And for the sake of removing untimely death, for the attainment of perfect splendor, for fame, for nourishment, and for the removal of disease— to Caṇḍī, who is numbered as eighty-one.
For the purpose of accomplishing sovereignty and for victory over all enemies;
for one who has lost his kingdom to regain his desired object, and for the recovery of lost wealth; for the sake of abundant food, for subjugation, and for the removal of great death.
For the sake of splendor, for being beloved by all people, the auspicious Śatacaṇḍī is [to be performed] with three [recitations].
For the sake of the desired object called "the thousand," for the destruction of the enemy army,
for the purpose of longing for supreme sovereignty, and for the sake of a multitude of great jewels.
For the increase of strength and so forth, for the sake of a wife, for the attainment of immeasurable wealth,
for the expansion of kingdom, fortresses, and the like, during famine, and for the destruction of enemies.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, [one should perform this] for ten thousand years when there is a great plague, fear, or danger from enemies,
and for the sake of obtaining wealth located on another island.
O Śaṅkarī, for the sake of procuring a multitude of cattle, for elephants, horses, and chariots,
for the attainment of a multitude of excellent jewels, and for the fulfillment of desired objects.
Furthermore, Caṇḍī and the one called Lakṣā are used for the affliction by serpents and for killing;
they are also employed for the sake of attaining wealth buried underground or even that which is situated on an island.
Whether situated by the sea, on a mountain, or in the midst of a river,
one should perform seed-rites for the sake of attaining abundance in all prosperity.
O proud one, when desiring to obtain wealth in order to perform the ritual recitation (*japa*) of Caṇḍī,
O beloved, one should recite [the mantra] from one *caṇḍī* up to five, or up to nine, for as many years as desired.
For the daughter of Menakā, one should perform the rite of recitation for seven years, beginning with seven and ending with thirty;
and from eighty-one up to a thousand.
Having led [the disciple] with devotion according to the procedure to be described,
the best of men should perform the recitation (japa) with devotion, numbering ten thousand (ayuta), ending at two times eight (sixteen).
I shall now describe the ritual of reciting the Caṇḍī-mantra one hundred thousand times over the course of years;
this may be performed for half that duration, or down to three months, or for as long as one is able.
And the various forms of Caṇḍī and others have been described by me, O Daughter of the Mountain,
as being located in front of your abode and within the northeastern corner of the enclosure wall.
At a crossroads, likewise in a garden, in a pavilion situated on a path for recitation,
at the boundary of a village, on a riverbank, in the capital city, and on a mountain.
On the bank of the Sindhu, at Grāmahāra, is this auspicious place for recitation (*japa*).
One should perform the *ekacaṇḍī* rite in the morning and recite the *tricaṇḍī* during the *saṅgava* period.
At midday, the Guru performs the rites of recitation, worship, and oblation known as the "five and seven";
in the third watch, he performs the rites of the "nine and thirty" and the "eighty-one."
One should perform the ritual of one hundred recitations at night; for one who desires a thousand, the *gānarātra* [ritual];
and at midnight, the practice known as the *ayuta*, consisting of recitation, fire-oblation, and worship.
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, a wise person should perform the rite of one hundred thousand recitations with the Vāmā [mudrā] in order to accomplish the ritual for all the Caṇḍīs.
"O Goddess of gods, O Sarvacaṇḍī, your departure is auspicious, supreme, and swiftly bestows desired objects; therefore, knowing this, the Guru [should perform] the ritual."
With a pure mind, one should perform the recitation, worship, fire-oblation, libation, and feeding separately at your liṅga and during your watch.
"I shall speak; listen, O affectionate one, for the sake of your presence.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual of Differentiating Caṇḍī and the Origin of Durgā," in the section on Occasional Rites (*naimittika-karmakāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīvātulottara*, within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
Chapter.
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe the ritual for the constant recitation of Caṇḍī;
one should construct a square pavilion in front of your liṅga and that of Śaṅkara.
One should construct [the mandala] measuring five cubits and provided with four gates.
(In this manuscript, only this much remains; from here onwards, there is no writing.
O Gaja, I have correctly explained the various types of Caṇḍīs and their ritual procedures.
Listen to the ritual for the Nine Durgās for the sake of attaining prosperity, sovereignty, and victory;
it should be performed during the bright fortnight prior to the day the rite begins.
On the Śaṅkara portion of your body, one should construct a pavilion nine cubits in size,
square in shape and adorned with doors on all sides.
O Dear One, it should have walls of five or three stories, be provided with windows,
resemble the surface of a mirror, and be adorned at its front with water-pots.
One should construct a square altar (vedikā) using one-third of that [measurement],
and in its center, one should perform the rite of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) on all sides.

O Goddess of the gods, the wise one should fashion squares and circles in the cardinal and intermediate directions; among these, O Sovereign of the gods, the circular *kuṇḍa* for Śiva and Indra is called the primary.
According to the prescribed rite, nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be prepared, each endowed with a yoni and a navel;
these pit-dwellings should also contain three girdles (mekhalās) within their chambers.

O virtuous lady, the sacrificial pits, the excavations, and the ornaments should be prepared as previously described; likewise, all materials and collections of substances for the sake of the ritual must be gathered.
Having prepared them in many ways with devotion, purified, and washed,
the Guru should place them in an auspicious location while reciting the root mantra of that [deity].
Having adorned the temple of the Goddess,
the best of men should then commence the rite on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.
Having risen early in the morning on the day of the ritual, the guards and others, having bathed in the river together with the twice-born,
purified themselves at the outset with cow-dung and water.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having thoroughly purified your home with the root mantra and the Varuna weapon, they should perform the smearing and the sprinkling, O Hamsage.
Having colored the pavilion and other structures before you with colored powders,
one should fill the lotuses there with the five colors.
O best of the twice-born, O beautiful one, from the beginning with "svanityādi" up to the end of "samālyā," they— the preceptor and the others—
should shave [the disciple] with the root mantra and the razor mantra.
If one strikes [the image] with clods of earth or similar objects in the vicinity of the Suna river, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
then, having sipped water according to the Tantra and performed the recitation of mantras, [one should offer] a vessel made of gold, silver, or other materials.
Having filled it with river water, one should consecrate it with the Gaṅgā-mantra;
then, having placed it upon a chariot or other vehicle, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and the presence of the twice-born.
Having entered your house with the sounds of all musical instruments and dances,
the best of men should then pour river water into the *vardhinī* vessel.
One should worship and pray to the Goddess according to the procedure to be described:
"O Goddess, whose nature is a web of powers, salutations to you, the bestower of enjoyments."
"O Caṇḍikā, grant me permission to perform the rite of the Nine Durgās," thus he prayed with true devotion in your presence within the yoga-maṇḍapa.
First, having worshipped Gaṇanāyaka, the preceptor should draw the mandalas;
he should then cause the recitation of the Nāndī and other rites, the products of the cow (gavya), and the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
First, one should choose a preceptor known as Brahmā who bestows wealth;
for the purpose of the fire-oblation, the lords of the eight forms (of Śiva), and for the purpose of the Vedic recitation, sixteen twice-born Brahmins.
Twenty twice-born men for the purpose of recitation, nine chanters of hymns,
one Brahmin for the purpose of libations, and those equal in number to the Rudras (eleven) as sprinklers.

Having given three Brahmins for the purpose of the enclosure, and having given the Madhuparka and the Kṛcchra penance respectively with that root mantra, one should perform the tying of the auspicious thread (kautuka) with the root mantra.
Having brought earth according to the prescribed rite and having deposited that seed in the pavilion, one should perform the protection of the primary image and other objects with the Śāṅkarī mantra.
Then, having worshipped Ketu with a mantra, one should offer fruits and other such items.
Having reached the sacrificial ground, [one should worship] Brahmā, Dhanada, and the others.

Having uttered the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) with those mantras, the Guru should perform the consecration of the pavilion; and having performed the purification of the site and the oblation for that which is called the "Image" (bimba) within that pavilion.

O Goddess, one should place the door-pitchers (dvārakumbha) and so forth starting from the eastern part of the altar; likewise, the eight pitchers known as the Gaṇḍakas and the Vidyeśas should be placed in the corners.
The three jars beginning with Kālikā, known as the "Sacrifice" (yāga) and designated by the name "Root" (mūla),
[should be placed] at the gateway locations, in the corners, and near the gateway jars.
On the altar, one should draw lotuses in the eight directions and in the central region; within those, one should draw eight-petaled wheels.
Having drawn a conch, a spiral, lotuses, a triangle,
and a circle in their proper sequence, one should fill them with rice grains.
Having filled [the vessel] with one *prastha* measure of grain, half of that in rice,
and half of that again in sesame seeds, one should perform the sacrifice with the root mantra of that [deity].
One should place jars wrapped with threads upon the rice,
[filling them] with scented water, sandalwood water and the like, milk, and cool water.
Having filled the root-pitcher with decoctions and honey, and having filled it with clarified butter,
the best of worshippers should gradually worship the Goddess with the Mātṛkās.
Furthermore, one should place the jeweled disc with its root-mantra, along with betel nuts,
tufts of grass and the like, the nine gems, sprouts, and fruits.
Having deposited [the image] with the root mantra, one should then fashion auspicious images of gold according to the measure of one *niṣka* or half a *niṣka*.

O Dear One, the cloth may be made of *dukūla* or woven thread, distinguished by colors such as white, yellow, and so forth; for the nine cloths or the seven, the cloth for the pitcher should be measured accordingly.
Having covered the jars with that very [cloth], the preceptor should invoke the deities individually;
he should worship Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Godāvarī in the east and other directions.
Then, having invoked Sarasvatī, Nirmadā, Sindhu, Kāverikā,
and Tāmraparṇī in sequence into the jars through the opening, one should worship them.
To Kāntidā, Karuṇā, Bālā, Kalyāṇī, Koṭeśvarī,
Gāndhārī, Gāṇī, Durgā, Gāyatrī, and Gānahāyakī.
These [deities] are to be placed individually in jars called *gaḍḍukas*, together with their respective names:
Viśveśī, Vītarāgā, Vajrahastā, and Vaśaṅkarī.
Then, one should worship Vāgīśī, Vasudhā (Vasudā), Vegā, and Vārāhī;
furthermore, one should worship the eight Vidyeśīs upon the eight jars on the altar.
And in the three jars, one should worship Kālī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī with the root mantra;
in the sacrificial jar, Yāgeśī; and in the jar at the edge, Mūladurgā.
With the consecratory rites beginning with invocation and the five types of offerings,
[one should place] vessels made of gold, silver, or brass in front of the three jars.
One should devoutly construct a yantra within a tube measuring three palms;
there, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus and fill it with husked rice grains.

One should write the nine-syllable mantra in the yantra, joined with the vowels according to their respective forms; having worshipped it with the mantra called Prāṇa, one should place it upon that maṇḍala.
Those who know the tradition of the nine-syllable mantra should sit down separately below the altar, surrounding it, and perform the sacrifice according to the previously mentioned method.
They should recite the Saptashati three times, joined with the nine-syllable mantra from the *argalā* to the *rahasya*, and accompanied by the *sampuṭa*.
The Brahmāstra is in the northeast corner; the Vahnyastra is said to be in the southeast.
The Cakrāstra is in the southwest corner, and likewise the Mārutāstra is in the northwest.
Near the principal sacrificial pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*), the twice-born should mutter the sacrificial mantra;
furthermore, for its protection, he should recite the *Devīsūkta* nine times.
He should satisfy [the deities] in the northern direction with water and milk for one-tenth [of the mantras recited];
at the four gates, eight Brahmins should recite the four Vedas;
likewise, in the four directions within your house, there should be eight proclaimers.
O Goddess, all around the courtyard are the progenitors of the nine Durgās.
One should mutter the mantra of Vināyaka on the right, then the Kālīsūkta which consists of the essence of Ramā,
followed by the Gosūkta, the one called Śāradā, and finally the supreme Durgāsūkta.
One should recite individually one thousand times each the hymn known as the Praty-aṅgirasa and that called the Śānti-durgā, until the conclusion of the fire-oblation.

The sprinklers should perform the sprinkling of your liṅga with the essence of nectar and with water and milk, using those respective mantras; then one should commence the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
One should purify the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) situated in sequence around the eastern direction and its surroundings, by means of the various rites beginning with the inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
Having worshipped the image-bearing gurus and Brahmā, the bestower of wealth,
one should worship all the deities of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and so forth according to the procedure that will be described.
Having worshipped them individually with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, by their respective names:
Vāmadevī, Vajriṇī, Vaṃśadā, and Balavṛddhidā.
Jayapradā, Jaganmātā, Niṣkalā, Nitambinī,
and Mahāmāyā— these are proclaimed as the presiding deities of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Having invoked and worshipped them individually in each pit, one bestows wealth;
[one worships] the Earth-form in the eastern pit and the one named Agni in the southeast.
In the south, one should worship Yajñamūrti, and in the Daityakuṇḍaka, Sūrya;
in the west, Jalamūrti, and in the northwest, Māruta.
Having worshipped the one named Soma in the Saumya region, the one named Vyoman in the Śaṅkara [region],
and the one named Mūla in the principal among the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
O Goddess, one should worship the eight guardians of the forms, beginning with Uṣā, among the eight twice-born;
Vijayā generates fire through the distinctions of flame, wood, and so forth.
Having placed [the fire] in the primary sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) which is the womb (yoni), one should perform the consecratory rites;
one should place the fire in the center of the pit and perform the sixteen rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna).
One should perform the rites according to the rule in the eight forms and fire-pits in sequence;
one should then transfer that fire into all the fire-pits and perform the rites of the mouth.
O Dear One, at the outset, the Guru [should perform the oblation] in his own fire-pit with sacrificial wood (samid), clarified butter (ājya), and caru; then, in sequence,
he should offer mustard seeds, wheat, sesame, tuṭika, nutmeg, the tips of dūrvā grass, and milk-rice (pāyasa)— ten items in order.
One should offer sacrificial fuel sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice with the mantras beginning with "Kālikā."
With the root mantra and with new rice, one should offer the six substances beginning with mustard seeds;
then, with ten verses beginning with "khaliṇyādi," one offers milk-rice (pāyasa).
Those guardians of the images (mūrtipās), being thoroughly conversant with the rites, should again offer all the sacrificial substances in eight separate fire-pits during the night.
One hundred oblations for Kālikā, two hundred oblations for Ramā,
three hundred for Sarasvatī, and then the oblation with the root mantra.
And five hundred repetitions of the nine-syllabled mantra are prescribed;
all these should be performed separately nine times in each sacrificial pit with the Durgā-mantra.
O Daughter of the Mountain, one should offer a thousand oblations for each sacrificial pit;
having offered the final oblation at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice, one should present the bali-offering to the pits.
To the east of the Mekhalā-pit, one should first offer the supreme oblation with clarified butter;
then, one should fashion nine piṇḍas in the Guru-pit and the others according to the sequence.
Having placed [the offerings] upon a very smooth *piṇḍa* and having ignited wooden lamps,
the Guru should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homakarma*) and worship the sacrificial pitchers (*vedikumbha*).
Then, having worshipped the nine-syllable yantra, one should worship it along with its attendants;
and on the ground all around the base of the altar, one should draw lotuses.
Having filled eight jars with grain measured at one *prastha* each, and half that amount of rice and sesame seeds, he should then place them in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Near the principal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should fill a jar known as Vāgīśi with scented water, along with sprouts and fruits.
Having weighed the Ratnamantā with gold according to the scale for images,
and having set them down individually and covered them with cloth, one should worship them.
Taking up the jar of Durgā amidst the auspicious sounds of the Vedas,
[he went] with the Mūrtipās and other twice-born brahmins to your temple on the rampart.
Following the clockwise direction, the mantra-practitioner should cause the jar to enter within;
having worshipped the *liṅga* with the root mantra and with the water from the Durgā-jar.
One should sprinkle her with that hymn according to the prescribed procedure,
preceded by the performance of the Great Worship (mahāpūjā) beginning with the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa).
Immediately after the placement of the *golaka*, the *piṇḍikā*, and the *madhu* [mantras], one should perform all the sixfold placements (*ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*) and so forth at the time of worship. (p. 106)
Having invoked Kālī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Dinadurgā with the three mantras beginning with "Kālikā," the Guru should display the six mudrās.
And having subsequently performed the worship of those [deities] according to the previously mentioned method, duly and individually by their names and thousands [of mantras], the Guru—
One should present the food offering (naivedya) along with incense and lamps while reciting the root mantra;
having offered sacrificial fuel sticks (samit), clarified butter (ājya), and cooked rice (caru), one should perform one hundred and eight oblations (āhuti) with the root mantra.
Then, having formally offered the sacrificial food (naivedya) situated before you according to the rules,
one should offer betel-leaf with the root mantra and again wave the multitude of lamps.
Having worshipped the vehicle and the banner, one should worship the attendants;
then the Guru, having summoned the spirits with the ringing of the bell and other instruments, should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali).
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a festival according to the extent of one's wealth;
having circumambulated the Goddess with lotus-lamps, one should cause her to enter within.
Having offered the water of clear reverence (prasannārghya) and displayed the moon-lamp,
the master, having performed the ritual service (karma) and the offering of food (śāla), should feed the Brahmins.
Then those best of the twice-born, the preceptors and others, being pure in soul, zealously worshipped the Goddess with devotion using the fivefold offerings and other rites. (p. 107)
In the northeastern direction of the linga, on the courtyard within the pavilion for the twice-born,
one should duly purify that spot and draw there a grid of nine squares.
Having filled a prastha or even half a prastha of rice with grains,
and having worshipped them with your seed-syllable upon a tripod and three-legged stands;
O Caṇḍikā, one should place a five-faced [liṅga] in the center and three shallow bowls (śarāva) in the three remaining positions;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as the nine seed-syllables.
Rice, mustard, legumes, black gram, mung bean, barley, sesame, flat beans, and horse gram— all these should be soaked in water.
Then, having sprinkled with milk—the seed-syllable of nectar—one should dwell in the state of liberation;
having invoked the nine goddesses, one should worship Soma, the supreme.
Together with the five musical instruments, one should present incense and lamps;
[one should offer] milk-rice mixed with various foods and combined with ghee and milk-porridge.
The proud woman, knowing the ritual procedure, should offer the moon-pitcher filled with milk using the nectar-mantras and the individual root-mantra.
Having completed the ritual of the seed-syllable (*bījakarman*), one should finally cause [the deity] to enter the inner sanctum of the womb-chamber (*garbhageha*).
One should sprinkle the *liṅga* with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and with water mixed with milk while reciting the *Śrīsūkta*.
With the Devīsūkta, the Durgāsūkta,
the hymn known as the Tvaritā, and the Niśāsūkta, the officiant [should perform the rite] with auspicious waters.

O Goddess, O Beloved, at the conclusion of the sprinkling, the Guru, having first performed the worship of the seat and having duly performed the array of nyāsas and other rites according to the rules, should conduct the great worship.
One should worship Kālī, Ramā, and Śāradā individually with their respective root mantras;
and Mūladurgā and Dineśī as prescribed in the Ḍāmara.
One should perform the rite of worship according to the method described in that tantra;
thereafter, one should worship Kālikā and the other goddesses with their names, using [mantras] consisting of a thousand syllables.
One should worship this supreme Goddess of the Day with the thousand names of Durgā,
offering as food rice mixed with ghee, milk-rice, milk, and curd.
One should place, in sequence from the root to the tip, food mixed with honey and sugar, accompanied by soup and vegetables, and finally flower-food.
The preceptor should offer five types of fruits with the ninefold mantra to the Mistress, and then present incense, lamps, and other offerings to the Mother.
The worship of the stage (raṅgapūjā), which bestows satisfaction upon you,
should be performed according to the rules by one who knows the ritual procedure, extending as far as the flagstaff or the gateway (gopura).
Likewise, having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya) and dismissed it, one should then present betel leaves;
afterwards, one should wave many lamps before the mountain-born goddess until the end of winter.
With the blessing of the mantra, the supreme sage should bestow unbroken grains (akṣatas) that are as white as the night;
either in front of him or all around within the courtyard.
He should satisfy the newly married women, the couples, and hundreds of maidens,
as well as the female attendants and others, with oil massages, dry rubs, and other such services.
One should perform worship ending with incense and lamps, and thereafter cause garments to be given;
O Dear One, this gift of garments consists of either nine or seven new cloths.
White and yellow garments, as well as woolen blankets,
fine silk fabrics such as dukūla, and cloths woven from nine threads;
Having purified them, one should sprinkle them with the *prājāpatya* and other mantras;
then, reciting the root mantra (*tattvamūla*), one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.

Then one should perform the rite of giving (dānakarma) to those stationed in the directions, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna, in due order; likewise, white garments and bodices [should be offered].
Then, reciting the Kālī-mantra with devotion, [he should place her] on the two corners;
subsequently, while uttering the Ramā-mantra, [he should place] the bodice and the yellow garment.
A red garment should be offered separately between those two,
as well as a multicolored garment, a bodice, and so forth, while reciting the root mantra of Śāradā.
Thereafter, for the sake of satisfaction, one should perform the worship of the couples of Mūladurgā,
having offered worship according to one's means and performed the ritual rites.

The preceptor should worship Durgā and the other goddesses individually, starting from the first day up to the ninth, increasing by one each day; having worshipped them in that manner, he should likewise offer a garment.
One should offer bodices, necklaces, anklets, and so forth,
as well as garments and bodices in the colors of the respective deities.
One should feed the couples, the maidens, and the groups of women;
then one should worship the seed-syllable (bīja), the emblem (ketu), the vehicle (vāhana), and the attendants (parivāra).

Accompanied by the sounds of the *jayaghaṇṭā* bell and other instruments, as well as the resonance of the five musical instruments, he should invoke the offering goddesses while endowed with their respective substances.
One should cause the offering to be given starting from the gates up to the sacrificial pedestal for the guardians of the directions and the Mothers,
and from Śāstṛ and the others up to the flagstaff for the goddesses of the offerings.

Having offered [the offerings] separately up to the *pālikā* vessels with the initial syllables of their own names, the most excellent Guru should then perform the festival in various ways with abundant wealth and other resources.
Then, having performed the worship of the assembly hall and the offering to the *baliberam* with devotion,
one should enter the courtyard and subsequently perform circumambulation, O beloved.
One should lead the image into the inner sanctum, having placed the linga to the right;
then, having infused consciousness into the linga, one should display the "snow-lamp."
Salutations to you, O support of the universe; salutations to you, O purifier of the worlds.
O Supreme Goddess, accept the multitude of rites performed on this first lunar day.
Having thus prayed with true devotion, one should offer the performed action;
all people, including the preceptor and others, [should do so] with lutes, flutes, and drums.
With the sounds of conchs such as the *vedaghoṣa*, with the various resonances of musical instruments,
with the recitation of the *Purāṇas*, and with the devoted chanting of bards and panegyrists;
The first [group], along with the dancers and jesters, should keep vigil with devotion;
