they should [attend to] all the vessels at the doors, the water-pots, and so forth, as well as the fire situated in the preceptor’s sacrificial pit.

Having protected the yantra situated in the center of the altar, the sowing of seeds, the river, and everything up to the ninth day— including the recitation of mantras and the complete study of the scriptures— [one should proceed].
The performance of the fire sacrifice (*homakriyā*), the worship of the jar (*ghaṭārcā*) situated upon the altar, the worship of the ritual diagram (*yantra*),
the rite of sprinkling with hymns (*sūktādi secana*), and the worship as prescribed separately in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
The gift of clothing, the festival, the worship in the assembly hall, and the meal—
all these rites of the entire family complex should be performed in this manner sequentially until the ninth day.
O Illusion of the World, the specific procedure is now being described:
having bathed in the morning on the second lunar day, one should perform the rite together with the twice-born.
Then, having entered your abode, one should joyfully proclaim an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) with devotion;
thereafter, having consecrated and sprinkled the *liṅga* and the *yantra* with the hymns (*sūkta*) dedicated to Durgā and others.
Having performed the worship according to the rules with the fivefold offerings and other rites,
he then [worshipped] Durgā, who had been worshipped on the previous day, with that root mantra.
Having superimposed Kālī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī upon one's own body,
one should thereafter [worship] that Goddess upon the *liṅga* and the *yantra* by means of the root mantra of Āryā.

Having performed the sacrifice, one should then moisten the seed with water from the night; thereafter, one should perform the entire range of ritual actions, such as sprinkling, recitation, and the complete study of the scriptures.
The mantra-practitioner should perform the fire offering (homa) as previously described with the root mantra of the Noble One;
thereafter, he should worship up to the end of the ritual jars, and finally, having offered the residual clarified butter (saṃpātājya), [he should proceed].

Having completed the fire-offering ritual (*homakarma*), the noble one should lift up the noble jar (*āryākumbha*). Having circumambulated the house clockwise and having brought the jar inside, he should enter.

Having consecrated [the disciple] with the Āryāsūkta, the remainder should be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure. That night, having purified his own self, he should worship Kālikā and the other deities as prescribed in the Kalpa, and likewise honor the preceptor (ācārya).
One should perform the remainder as previously described, and then perform the offering of the web of ritual actions.
Salutations to you, the eternally blissful one who brings delight to the world; O goddess praised by the gods, accept these second offerings of my web of karma.
Having thus prayed three times, one should offer the performed rite;
then, on the third day, having risen in the morning and bathed together with the best of Brahmins—
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) up to the point of the *garbha* rite, the *liṅga* should be sprinkled according to the prescribed rule;
then, having sprinkled the *yantra* situated in the center of the altar with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
Having first worshipped Āryā within himself with the root mantra,
the Guru should then unite Śūlinī there, invoke her, and perform the sacrifice.
Having performed the entire web of ritual actions beginning with service and ending with the rite of fire-oblation,
and having offered the remnants of the oblation, he then lifts up the jar of the Trident-bearer.
Having sprinkled the *liṅga* according to the previously mentioned method, one should worship it;
O Maheśvarī, having performed the ritual acts, one should perform the prayers and so forth during that night.
Salutations to you, O support of all arts, the auspicious one who bestows auspiciousness;
O Sovereign of the Gods, accept this rite performed on the third lunar day.
Having thus made many requests, one should offer the web of ritual actions;
thereafter, one should awaken [the deity] with the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, conchs, and so forth.
On the fourth day, the preceptor, having bathed in the morning and performed his daily obligatory rites,
should declare the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) in the sacrificial hall with the mantra beginning "etadeva."
Having conversed within the temple of the *liṅga* and having worshipped the mechanical *liṅga*,
one should unite the Goddess Śūlinī with the body and then worship the young maiden (*kumārī*).
Having sprinkled the seeds with fragrant water according to the prescribed rite,
and having completed the concluding rites of the fire-oblation (homa), one should bring forth the maiden’s pitcher.
Having entered the interior of the inner sanctum while reciting the Kumārīsūkta, one should slowly sprinkle the liṅga with devotion; the remainder is as previously stated, O beloved.
Having offered prayers to the Goddess with the root mantra to be recited hereafter, the proud one [should say]:
"O Bhadrakālī, salutations to you, the destroyer of great fear!"
"Accept this rite for desired results performed by me on the fourth day;
on the morning of the fifth day, having arisen, the rite for dispelling sleep must be performed."
Having bathed, one should worship the Liṅga and the Yantra with the five types of offerings;
then, having united the Kumārī within the heart and invoked Ambikā with the root mantra.
Then all the rites up to the end of the *homa*, the sprinkling of the vessel for Ambikā,
the seed [syllable] should be sprinkled with water from the clouds, and at night the performance of the ritual is concluded.
O you who possess fragrant scents, salutations to you, the bestower of a perfect network of blessings;
O Ambikā, O Tilottamā, accept this rite on the fifth lunar day.
Having thus prayed to the Great Goddess, one should thereafter observe the vigil;
rising early on the sixth day, one should perform an auspicious bath together with the Brahmins.
Then, one should sprinkle [the area] all around with the Pavamāna mantra and other mantras;
having sprinkled the yantra-liṅga, one should offer it the five-fold services (pañcopacāraka).
Having worshipped Ambikā with the root mantra, the Guru should unite her within his heart;
having invoked Mahiṣaghnī, he should worship her in the *liṅga* and the *yantra*.
Having sprinkled the seeds with water and performed the subsequent rites,
the noble one, having completed the fire-offering (homa) according to the previously mentioned procedure, [should proceed] on the elephant.
Then, with a water-pot, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the *Mahiṣāgnī* hymn itself;
having performed the flood of rites preceded by true devotion until the end of midnight.
For the sake of satisfaction, one should pray to the Goddess who bestows the increase of one's lineage:
"O Slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations to you, the granter of desired objects."
"O Goddess worshipped by the gods, accept the rite performed by me on the sixth [tithi].
Thus one should worship Kriyājālā, worshipping her with the root mantra.
Then, having warded off sleep, he rose at dawn on the seventh day;
thereafter, he duly completed his daily obligatory rites, beginning with the ritual bath.
First, the preceptor, having sprinkled with water consecrated on an auspicious day the temple of the Liṅga and all other locations, as well as the sacrificial ground,
and having empowered the root-mantra, the Yantra, the Liṅgas, and the jars with the seven types of ritual offerings (upacāras), [proceeds].
Having performed the sacrifice to her and to Mahiṣaghnī, one should unite them within the heart from the root.
Having invoked Caṇḍikā again with the root mantra upon the liṅga and the yantra,
one should perform the entire network of rites up to the fire sacrifice (homa), as well as the sprinkling of the Caṇḍikā-pitcher.
Having performed worship at night, one should then offer prayers for the sake of satisfaction:
"Salutations to you, O goddess born from the mountain, who causes fear to all enemies!"
"On the seventh [day], O bestower of wealth, quickly accept the flood of performed rites!"—
thus, at the conclusion of the ritual actions, the great people should awaken [the deity].
Likewise, on the morning of the eighth day, the preceptor should rise with devotion and,
having bathed together with the Cāraka and other twice-born men, perform his daily rites.
The priest should proclaim "An auspicious day" (puṇyāha) with the *mantra*, and sprinkle the *liṅga* and the *yantra*.
Having thus consecrated it, one should worship it with nine offerings and the seven modes of service (*saptopacāra*).
Having united Caṇḍikā with her heart by means of the root mantra,
the proud one [the practitioner] should invoke Sarasvatī with the mantra into both the liṅga and the yantra.
At the conclusion, one should sprinkle the seeds as previously described in the ritual of *homakarma*;
likewise, [one should sprinkle] the jars situated in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the yantra, and the *śāradā* jar itself.
Having performed the sacrifice and taken that jar, the most excellent of men, together with all the twice-born and their attendants,
re-entered the interior of the womb while reciting that supreme hymn.
O Dear One, having performed the worship with the mantra as previously described,
one should sprinkle [the vessel] until the end of the night of the spirits, completing the entire cycle of rites.
Afterward, one should offer prayers and so forth with the Śāradā mantra:
"Obeisance to you, O Kalāvatī, whose essence consists of the letters beginning with 'A'."
"O leader of the gods, accept the ritual performed during these eight days.
Having thus entreated you with true devotion, one should offer all the rites.
On the ninth day, having risen in the morning, he should dispel his sleep with laughter and other such means;
then, having performed his bath, he should carry out his daily obligatory rites along with the brahmins and others.

Then, having separately sprinkled the *nāndī* (the auspicious rite), the products of the cow, the image in the house, and the pavilion with water from the *puṇyāha* ceremony, the Guru [proceeds] with that same [water].
Having thoroughly worshipped the *liṅga* and the *yantra*, and performed the sprinkling and pouring of water and so forth,
one should then unite Śāradā with the heart and worship Vāgīśī once again.
Having worshipped the seed-syllables and the sprouts, and thereafter with the nectar-seed syllable (*sudhā-bīja*),
the Brahmins should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in each sacrificial pit as previously described;
and for each verse in the principal rite, they should offer milk-rice, ghee, and sesame seeds.
As it is said in the Ḍāmara Tantra, the most excellent among all tantras:
Then, with the three verses beginning with "argalā," the Guru should again offer all the oblations of the Saptashatī; furthermore, [he should offer] fine cloth and a bodice.
Then, O observer of excellent vows, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* in the nine sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*),

and having completed the fire-offerings (*homakarma*), O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the vessel containing the residual oblation (*saṃpātājya*) in the pitcher (*kumbha*), the yantra, and the linga; thereafter, one should perform the sacrifice separately for each.
For the sake of the journey and for the sake of the full sacrifice, one should fill two water-pots.
First, having taken water from a jar, she who possesses the jar should place it in the center of the altar;
then, with the root-mantra of each [deity] individually, she should perform the preliminary consecration of the single pitcher.
Having placed that pitcher in the northeast quarter and worshipped it, O people,
the Guru [should worship] the pitchers of the Vidyeśvaras situated at the door, the *gaḍḍuka*, and the corners.
The twice-born should fill the jar known as Vāgīśa with saffron water using the root mantra of Sudhā, accompanied by the sounds of Vedic chanting and other such resonances.
Having taken the preceptor and others with him, he should enter the inner sanctum;
having devoutly sprinkled the Liṅga with the mantra of the Vāgīśī-sūkta.
One should perform the worship, the offering, the festival, and the feeding as before;
and on that night, having bathed well and performed the purification of the linga.

The Guru should sprinkle [the vessel] with various hymns and perform the supreme worship of the Name and so forth; he should then worship the goddesses, Mahākālī and the others, according to the ritual manual.
Having offered the food oblation to the Goddess as previously described, along with flowers, incense, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
and having worshipped with the root mantra, the gift of clothing follows thereafter.
One should feed the foremost of Brahmins, as well as maidens and married women;
finally, having fed the couple, one should perform the offering of the *bali* and other rites according to the festival.

At the conclusion of the ritual procedure for the worship of the assembly, one should commence the *pūrṇayāga* (the final sacrifice). O Śaṅkarī, having placed a bracelet before you and having worshipped with the root mantra, [one should proceed].
One should stir with auspicious waters the rocana, saffron, fragrance, powder of niśā, ghana, and guggulu that are placed upon the crest of your [image].
The knower of mantras should worship and pray with devotion using the root mantra;
this [rite] bestows the complete fruit for those established in the Navarātra vow.
O Goddess, who consists of the nine Durgās, salutations to you, the bestower of auspiciousness;
O you who are worshipped by the gods, I shall perform the powder festival—please accept it.
Having thus offered prayers and recited the mantra over the powdered water, that supreme knower of mantras [consecrated] the primary liṅga,
the multitude of images, the guardian deity, the vehicle, and the banner.
Then the lords of the directions and the Mothers, followed by Bali and the Goddess; then the Mistress of the Field (Kṣetreśī), O Goddess, the Sprout (Aṅkura), and the attendant deities individually.

The Guru, having separately consecrated with sprinkling all the door-jars and so forth, as well as that machine, the deities of the sacrificial pit, and all those [deities], [should then sprinkle] the assembly hall and the image.
Having sprinkled that image with the *anunā* mantra, one should thereafter sprinkle one's own body,
O Dear One, and then [the seats] for Dhanada, the Sadasya, and Brahmā in due order.
Thereafter, one should separately offer powdered water to the image-bearers, those who have crossed over [to the further shore], and the reciters, as well as to the Brahmins.
For the sake of prosperity, one should offer that water to all, beginning with the king;
or else, one should perform the festival of the *bhūtabali* as far as the boundary of the village.
At the edge of the village and at the end of the chariot-road, one should scatter the offering with the fist;
having completed the great offering, the noble one should cause [the image] to enter the enclosure.
At the end, the Lord, having worshipped that which consists of the net of rays with the mantra at its root, having gratified it, and having struck it with coconuts and other fruits;
Having placed the images inside the inner sanctum to the right of the *liṅga*, one should,
with great devotion, cause that consciousness to be absorbed into the primary *liṅga*.
While wandering with the lamp of snow, one should cause the offering of clear water (arghya) to be presented;
then the mantra-practitioner, with all sounds, having entered the sacrificial hall—

The preceptor, having sprinkled the fire in his own sacrificial pit with the Vahni-mantra, [performs the rites] from the Jāta-homa up to the Pūrṇāhuti, saying: "O Lord, this oblation is offered by me."
"O Fire, having accepted my desired object and given it to me, depart.
Having spoken thus, he dismissed the fire and then prayed with devotion to the yantra.
O Goddess Ramā, salutations to you, the bestower of auspiciousness upon the kingdom;
graciously accept this worship and grant me royal sovereignty.
Having thus petitioned the supreme vessel known as Yāgeśa, [one should say]:
"O Yāgeśvarī, salutations to you, the bestower of the fruits of all sacrifices!"
"Accept this water-pot worship of yours; grant me an abundance of wealth. Having thus prayed with the root mantra, one should worship the jar of Śāradā.
O Sarasvatī, salutations to you, the bestower of the perfection of knowledge;
accept this worship of the jar and grant me all branches of learning.
O Mahālakṣmī, salutations to you, the bestower of wealth and sovereignty;
grant me a treasury, valor, and victory; accept this worship performed.
O Mahākālī, salutations to you! Having accepted this worship performed according to the ritual manual, grant me sons, wife, and the like, as well as the increase of my lineage.
Salutations to you, O Root Illusion, whose nature is innate bliss;
grant me manifold prosperities and accept this worship of yours.
Homage to the one known by the name Vidyeśī, who is ever established within the jars.
O you who are well-pleased, may you accept this worship of the eight jars.
O Kumbheśvarī, salutations to you, who dwell within all ritual jars;
O Goddess, bestower of the increase of the lineage, accept this worship of all the jars.
Having thus prayed to all the vessels at the doors, the jars, and so forth,
one should dismiss them while the twice-born, the attendants, and others perform the ritual with the auspicious sounds of the Vedas.
Together with the sounds of various musical instruments, laughter, songs, and dancers; accompanied by parasols and fly-whisks, and along with the ringing of bells and the people.
Having respectfully removed all the water-jars and so forth, as well as that machine and its sprout, while reciting the *mala-mantra* in sequence at that time.
Having led [the disciple] to the house by way of circumambulation and having caused him to enter the inner sanctum,
one should place the yantra upon the pedestal and worship its mantra a hundred times.
First, one should sprinkle the site of the *pāṭā* with water from the jar located in the east;
then, with devotion, one should sprinkle the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with water from the door-jar while reciting the *pīṭha-mantra*.
O Caṇḍikā, one should fill that corner with water from the corner-pitchers using the corner-mantra,
the interior space with the knot-mantras, and the supreme area with water from the large jars.

One should [consecrate] the *liṅga* with the water from the jar associated with the previously mentioned *sūkta*, with the waters from the jars of Vidyeśī and the others, and further, with the waters from the three jars of those [deities] using the three *sūktas* beginning with Kālikā.

O proud lady, while reciting the Devīsūkta, [the priest] should subsequently use the water from the primary Durgā-pitcher to remove the marriage-thread (kautuka) and other such items from the primary image and so forth.
Having placed the *kautuka* with devotion upon the *liṅga* to the north while reciting the root mantra,
[he should sprinkle it] with water from the sacrificial jar, with the powder-water, and with the water from the procession jars.
One should sprinkle that *balibimba* and its *yantra* with the sacrificial mantra;
it should be sprinkled with the *Ramāsūkta* and the ten types of ritual offerings (*upacāra*).
Having performed the sacrifice with seed-sprouts, one should subsequently worship with the nectar-seed (sudhā-bīja);
then, one should cause many streams of lamps to circulate, and again perform flower-observances with mantras.
Having worshipped with the root mantra up to the ninth [generation], the supreme guru,
having again performed worship for the sake of [attaining] grace, should pray to the Śāmbhavī [goddess].
Salutations to the Goddess Mahāmāyā, whose form is the bliss of all things!
The multitude of rites prescribed for the Navarātra, ending on the ninth day, has been performed by me.
Having properly undertaken all of that, grant me the fruit of fulfilled action,
prosperity, sons, wife, and the like, as well as the increase of my lineage, O Daughter of the Mountain!
Having spoken thus, one should offer all the ritual actions with the root mantra.
O Dear One, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given there to the Guru and the others in due order.
O Goddess, one should give nine niṣkas to the preceptor and to the giver of wealth (Dhanada),
five to the three Brahmins, and one and a half niṣkas and one niṣka [respectively].
After that, one should give half a niṣka to the *hotṛ*s, the *cāraka*s, and the *jāpaka*s,
as well as to those who recite the *sūkta*s and the *secaka*s.
Likewise, for those who worship it, for the purpose of its propitiation,
and similarly for those in prison, O Lord, one should give with devotion half of a half-niṣka (one-quarter of a niṣka).
Having given separate sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them, he, who was a giver of abundant fees,
[gave] ritual implements and so forth according to his ability and in accordance with his wealth.
One should give that entire pavilion to the mantra-adept for the sake of auspiciousness,
and gifts such as cattle and land to the Brahmins for the sake of welfare.

At the conclusion of the gift, for those who desire sons, wives, and so forth, one should cause the water used for washing the feet (pādodaka) and auspicious sprouts (aṅkurāṇi) to be bestowed upon the lords of the earth and others.
Having worshipped the Sahadevī plant along with its garments, bodice, and other ornaments,
and having given them to a married woman, [he should then take] the fire from the preceptor’s sacrificial pit.
Then Dhanada, together with the officiating priests and others, took [the image] amidst the chanting of the Vedas, the sounds of musical instruments, and the ringing of conchs and bells. (p. 126)
Having again led [the deity] along with Prabhūttama and the others into the noble abode,
one should unite [the deity] with the fire of the Preceptor and worship it with ritual offerings.
"O sinless one, I have told you that which was performed up to the ninth day;
it is divine, the remover of all sins, and always bestows auspiciousness."

O beloved, it bestows upon the king sovereignty and secure fortresses, as well as a treasury of wealth and military strength; it grants sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and so forth, ensuring the increase of the lineage.
It bestows long life and health upon men, as well as fortitude, valor, and mastery over the mind;
it grants fame, removes sorrow, and destroys all poverty.
Whoever, born of any of the four castes, should perform this rite prescribed for Navarātra every year with true devotion and a pure mind;
If he is a Brahmin, he attains knowledge in this life, as well as prosperity, many enjoyments,
liberation at the end of the body, sovereignty over a kingdom, victory, and fame.
Wealth, networks of jewels, all powers of prosperity,
substances, knowledges, and dharmas— these constitute the essential nature of the supreme Kṣatriya.
If a Vaiśya obtains wealth and grain, he will certainly attain proximity [to the deity];
a Śūdra shall always obtain happiness, health, prosperity, and the state of residing in the same world (sālokya).
Having understood the flood of karmas in this manner up to the ninth [day],
a person should perform them correctly for the sake of prosperity, the increase of their lineage, and auspiciousness.
"Thus indeed is the sequence of the Nine Durgās; now I shall describe the ritual of the cotton-wool (tūlākarma).

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship during the Nine Nights," in the section on rites for specific desires (*kāmyakāṇḍa*) within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī concerning the divisions of Durgā in the *Śrīvātulottara*.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord Maheśvara, by your grace I have heard everything;
now I wish to know when the weighing on the scales will take place."
O Lord, tell me in detail: what is the cause for its mounting, what is the material substance, what is the fruit, and how is its ritual procedure correctly performed?
Īśvara (p. 128): "Well asked, O Great Goddess, that which you have inquired about.
I shall explain all of that; listen with a one-pointed mind."
Long ago, on the bank of the Ganges river, which is frequented by hosts of sages and gods, he inquired about merit and sin: "Who indeed would be superior in this world?"
"I am one of great merit in this world, while he is a man of sin;
having come into mutual conflict, we both have sought refuge in Viṣṇu."
Janārdana said, "Tell me, for what purpose have you come?
Having heard those words of his, [he replied], "Let there be no mutual hostility."
Then Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, spoke regarding the mounting upon the stake:
"In that regard, would there be merit, or rather, would it be the personification of sin?"
Having seen that and reached a firm conclusion, the two attained peace of mind;
for Hari, pacifying them as they were angry, would have lifted up the scale.
Having placed both of them in the pans of a scale and holding it in the middle, Janārdana weighed them according to the proper method; thus they were weighed by Viṣṇu.

O Gaurī, merit entered the scale with its skin of concentration and occupied the ground; sin, however, rose up due to its lightness and its lack of substance. Seeing it as heavier on the scale, the personification of sin was filled with shame.
Having descended from the scales, he himself stepped onto the ground.
From that time forward, seeing a scale even from afar, he would flee;
therefore, both gods and men ascend the scale.
Because it desires to weigh the burden created by merit and demerit with a balance,
for this reason, the "balance-burden" (tulābhāra) is distinguished in the world.
By the mere remembrance of her, all sins are destroyed;
and at the time of weighing on the scales, the fear of death for all men vanishes.
Epilepsy and other such ailments perish at that very moment;
this is remembered as the expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Having thus granted this boon to Tulā, Viṣṇu, the protector of the world, said:
"O Tulā, by residing in temples of Śiva and other sacred places, you shall be the remover of sins."
"O bestower of welfare upon devoted men, eternally dispel the evil of those who are faithful!"—
by this command of mine, O beloved, Viṣṇu [created] this Tulābhāra.
Listen now to that substance, its distinct varieties, and the corresponding results;
I shall explain the specific signs for each one in their proper order.
If one has the financial means, one should then ascend the balance with gold;
such a person shall become an excellent universal monarch (cakravartin) for seven lifetimes.
At its conclusion, one attains union with Śiva and enjoys happiness even in this world;
one shines forth, free from disease, and endowed with sons, grandsons, and progeny.
Having enjoyed many pleasures for a long time, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
by means of copper, there shall be the destruction of enemies and happiness in this world.
At its conclusion, O fair-faced one, there shall be the secret fruit of the world of Brahmā;
by means of bell-metal, there shall be the destruction of fever and the pacification of all [ills] for men.
With tin for the destruction of disease, for fame, and for the increase of wealth;
with lead for the destruction of sin and the eradication of epilepsy.
If it is made of wood, there will be a terrible total destruction; if made of stone, the ruin of one's own family;
and if made of clay, the loss of one's sons. Therefore, O beloved, one should avoid such materials for that [liṅga].
With milk, there is all-encompassing good fortune and the destruction of heart disease and other ailments;
with curd, there shall be an increase in wealth and victory over all enemies.
In clarified butter (ājya), there is an increase in lifespan; in manohara, one gains good intellect;
in honey (mākṣika), when ascending the scale, peace is attained for those seized by spirits and the like.
Or by means of jaggery and sugar, one shall obtain stable prosperity;
by ascending the *pañcagavya* scale of a hundred *tulās*, there is the destruction of even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
By climbing upon a sesame oil vessel, one destroys untimely death;
by climbing upon a coconut fruit, one quickly attains the prosperity of sons and other blessings.

With plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, and the like, one bestows prosperity upon sons and friends; and being satisfied with grapes, dates, and so forth, one finds contentment both in this world and the next.
O Maheśvarī, by weighing out one *tulā* each of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor,
one quickly attains prosperity and the warding off of all afflictions.
Betel nuts with betel leaves, when weighed on a scale, bestow auspiciousness;
and white cloth, O Śivā, when weighed on a scale, bestows contentment and nourishment.
Having procured these materials according to one's capacity,
[one should offer them] at a sacred site such as Ambaliṅga or others, dedicated to Hari, Īśa, or the Enemy of Śumbha (Śiva).
And having ascended that [vehicle] with devotion upon the six-faced Lord of the Gaṇas,
by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras who are the best among men—
O Goddess, the hosts of sages and gods, having determined an auspicious day favorable to the moon and the stars, addressed me as previously stated.
On the front of the temple, or especially in the presence of the Sun (Śākara),
one should devoutly cause a pavilion to be constructed, whether near a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or even upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Or else, one should construct a flower-pavilion adorned with gate-arches,
featuring a pillar there made of solid wood and firmly established.
Having employed five metals, a balance, a cord, and leaves,
one should fix the balance according to the scripture spoken by Viśvakarman, keeping it steady.
Then, having risen at dawn and completed his daily rites,
the pure-souled one should perform the auspicious bath together with the Brahmins.
O fair-faced one, having adorned her with garments, ornaments, and garlands,
O beloved, one should enter the pavilion after arriving at the temple.
Having propitiated Gaṇeśvara, one should perform the Nāndī and Puṇyāha rites;
thereafter, one should offer the madhuparka and choose the most excellent Brahmins.
The preceptor, the patron, the officiating priest who has mastered the Vedas,
the Brahmin member of the assembly, and the twice-born reciters of the japa and pārāyaṇa.
Having given gold, fruit, and clothing, O beloved, he should choose [the bride];
then, when midnight has arrived, the Guru [should proceed] in the consecrated pavilion.
One should worship the door-arches and the water-pots in the charming [shrine];
one should perform the fire-sacrifice for the destruction of the Vāstu-demons and offer the Vāstu-oblation.
One should perform the recitation of the *pārāyaṇa* and likewise the *caturastra*;
as well as for Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Mṛtyuñjaya, and the nine planets.
The preceptor, the patron, and the others, having observed a fast and kept a vigil,
and having drunk the five products of the cow, should remain firm in their vows with their senses subdued.
Then, having risen at dawn and completed his daily rites,
the preceptor should proceed to the pavilion and worship Gaṇeśa.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) one thousand and eight times with the root mantra;
one should then carry out the Mṛtyuñjaya rite, the directional homa, and the domestic homa.

In the four directions, in due order, the mantra-practitioner, together with the officiating priests, should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds in sequence into the fire.
O charming one, the Guru should place the water-pots in the northeast and the eastern part,
as many as there are years, including the Śiva-kumbha and the Vardhinī.
Having worshipped that same number [of images] well, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should sprinkle the *cāmā* [image];
having anointed it with the eight fragrances, one should adorn it with garments, ornaments, and flowers.
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should satisfy [the deity] with food offerings and rows of lamps;
then the patron, holding a golden flower in his hand, should offer this prayer.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, dispeller of the fear of the ocean of worldly existence!
By your command, I desire to ascend the scale for the sake of your pleasure.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers, the practitioner of mantra should enter the pavilion of the balance (tulā-maṇḍapa) and,
having worshipped the balance, worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other deities.
One should place an image of Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the sustainer of the universe, fashioned from gold,
both at the center and within the balance-beam, and worship me there.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu on the right, one should worship Brahmā on the left;
and having fully honored the guardians of the directions, one should do so all around in due order.
In the scales, the two ropes, the asterisms Aśvinī, the Moon, and the Sun,
[and] Śūlapāṇi, Paraśupāṇi, and the four Vedas, in due order.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship Mṛtyuñjaya with the substances for the scales using their respective names,
honoring him with perfumes and flowers up to the offering of food (naivedya).
The sacrificer, standing with palms joined in reverence, should pray:
"Salutations to you, O support of the universe; salutations to you, the witness of all.
O Goddess Tula, lift me up; protect me, protect me! Salutations be unto you."
Thus one should personally pray with devotion for the sake of the fruit and gold.
Having performed three circumambulations accompanied by the auspicious sounds of the Vedas,
one should place the previously mentioned articles for the weighing scale to one's own right.
O Goddess of the Gods, having placed a scale on the left side and sat down, the supreme guru [should place] some substance, specifically a weight from himself, upon it.
Accompanied by hand-claps and the chanting of the Vedas, one should repeatedly utter "Govinda";
then, having stood still for even a moment, one should meditate upon me with the mind.
Having weighed it by turning it three times, one should lower the scale-pan;
then, having removed the resulting gold, one should offer it to the preceptor.
One should worship with devotion ornaments, clothing, and especially cattle, land, and so forth, as well as various kinds of gifts.
O Goddess of the Gods, having given a cow along with its calf to the Brahmins,
the preceptor should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given with devotion to those who performed the ritual.
One should divide the materials for the scale into portions for the sake of the deities;
one portion should be set aside for the gift of land, and these should be distributed separately.
O fair-faced one, one should subsequently feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity;
having received the words of blessing from the Brahmins, the dedication [of the merit] should take place at the end of that.
"O Goddess of the gods, I have declared this burden of the scales for the sake of the deities;
out of affection for you, what else do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual of the Tulābhāra," in the section on rites for specific desires (*kāmyakāṇḍa*), within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī in the *Durgābheda* of the illustrious *Vātulottara*.
May there be well-being!
I bow to the god Vighneśvara, the presiding deity over all obstacles;
I salute that Lord of the Gaṇas and revere him for the attainment of my desires.
The Goddess said:
O Śiva, whose entire body is smeared with ashes, who wears a mass of matted hair, and who is clothed in the directions;
at the times of the evening twilight, you are praised by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods.
O Śambhu, you are surrounded by all the hosts of gods, along with the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, as well as the Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and throngs of sages.
Together with his retinue of attendants, for the benefit of the entire world,
[he taught] this perfect secret, more secret than the secret, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
I ask, O Lord of Gods, O Master of the World, with a serene mind:
O Śaṅkara, [please explain] the twenty-eight mantras ending with Vātula.
You have correctly explained those various divisions that are to be kept secret;
now tell me how my own characteristics and signs appear within those tantras.
The characteristics of the five types of threads, the simultaneous [measurement] of the liṅga and the pedestal,
the proper construction of the limbs of the liṅga, and the characteristics for the binding of the temple structure.
The measurements for the temple-shrine and so forth,
the pavilion, the forecourt and so forth, the enclosure wall, the gate, the palace, and so forth, constitute the characteristics of the primary sanctuary.
O Lord, there should be a separate place for the gatekeepers, the offering deities, their mounts, and their banners;
likewise for the ponds, wells, and tanks.
What are the characteristics of the images known as the surrounding retinue? And tell me, what are the dimensions—the length and height—of their respective abodes?
The characteristics of materials, garments, and the house of the serpent;
the characteristics of bathing, sacrifice, assembly halls, and sacrificial pits.
Now, tell me the characteristics of weapons and missiles, as well as their application;
and how the sequence for the placement of the *kumbha* is performed on palaces, gate-towers, and their summits.

The characteristics of the dwellings of the twice-born, such as those of preceptors and others; the construction of their houses; and the architectural features of the abodes of all [others], such as kings and so forth.
How could there be a house or similar dwelling for cowsheds and the like, for elephants and horses, for shopkeepers and the like,
for spies, for servants and the like, or for musicians?
O Lord, tell me how Ratisthala is the abode of the Vaiśyas,
and the place for those of the goldsmith and other castes who work with bell-metal and copper.
Tell me of the houses of washermen and others, of those who provide garments, of wheel-bearers, of banner-bearers, of artisans, of those who provide clothing, and of those who act as mediators.
O Lord, where is the site for a flower garden characterized by a staircase of threads? And what are the characteristics of the site for planting flowers, or of Tulasī, O Child?
The construction of chariot parts such as the palanquin, their defining characteristics, the arrangement of guest-offerings,
and the specifications for the lamp-pillar.
Tell me, how are the characteristics of rows of lamps and the like, as well as chariot-paths and the like,
and the characteristics of stairs and side-walks defined?

Who are the worshippers and who are those who do not touch [the deity]? What is the state of one who does not touch the *liṅga*? What are the characteristics of an *ācārya*, or how is the sequence of daily rites (*nityakarman*) performed?
How is the rite of the sacred thread investiture (pavitrāropaṇa) performed as part of the occasional worship?
And what is the sequence of ritual bathing for the daily, occasional, and optional rites?
O Lord, how is your birth, how is the ritual procedure for the nine Durgās, how is the act of weighing on a scale, and what are the characteristics of the Kṛttikā constellation and the lamp?
O Lord, describe the time for the festival of the New Year, the procedure for mounting the chariot,
the offering of the *damanaka* plant, and the characteristics of the spring festival.
Tell me, how can one describe the web of activities for the festival of bondage, the binding and crushing,
as well as the substances and the tradition, once that bondage has decayed?
Remove [the defects] of the Jayaghaṇṭā, Mahāghaṇṭā, Kṣudraghaṇṭā, and so forth,
as well as the characteristics of the implements such as the Karakā vessel and the Jāla net.
The sounds of musical instruments such as the *bherī*, *paṭaha*, and *śaṅkha*, as well as flutes,
lutes, drums, cymbals, and the like, including the resonance of the *tittivīṇā* and other such instruments.
What is the procedure for expiation regarding the omission of daily and other obligatory rites?
And what is it when the *liṅga*, the image, or its constituent parts are broken, destroyed, or stolen?
O Lord, [this applies] to the peak of the main temple, the pavilion, the gate-tower, and so forth; as well as to the pinnacle-pot at its summit, the enclosure wall, the courtyard, and the like.
On a lamp-pillar, a banner, a doorway, a retinue, or a vehicle; on an offering-altar, a host of attendants, or wherever there may be a collection of vessels and so forth.
What if a multitude of people such as guides and others, or prisoners, servants, and so forth,
or a collection of musical instruments, or a musician, should fall ill or die?
When salt is broken, split, powdered, or burnt;
or when some wondrous portent occurs, or there is fear of an enemy king—how [should one act]?

In whichever tantra there is whatever secret characteristic of mantra, mudrā, and so forth, as well as the manifestation of deities and the procedures for all rites, such as those beginning with *netrika*; [that is the tantra].
And in this tantra, O Mahādeva, that entire [teaching] was spoken in detail by Prāṇavallabhā out of love and joy for the sake of my proximity.
"O you whose soul is endowed with the tradition, O bestower of enjoyment, speak to me.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Question," in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva within the *Vātulottara*, the supreme secret.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain to you the characteristics of the *liṅga* and so forth,
as well as the divisions of the *kalās* and the origin of the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen now in due order to the characteristics of the five threads, the characteristics for binding the house, and the arrangement of its parts.
Since all beings go to dissolution during the period of reabsorption,
and as there is creation at the time of emanation, it is therefore called the "liṅga."
O Dear One, the *liṅga* is said to be of two kinds: the partless (*niṣkala*) and the with-parts (*sakala*). The partless is my form, and the with-parts is your form.
Wherein there is a union of both, arising in the form of a *liṅga*,
this indeed arises from Śiva and Śakti, which is higher than the highest.
The Niṣkala is indeed devoid of parts, while the Sakala is endowed with parts;
O Maheśvarī, the Sakala is joined with the Niṣkala and takes the form of a Liṅga.
The Liṅga was worshipped with reverence by sages, gods,
and humans for the protection of yogins and for the emergence of the scriptures.
For the benefit of living beings, for the welfare of the deities,
and for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas, the manifestation of the Liṅga occurred from that [source].
O fair-faced one, the self-manifested Sāmba-linga is difficult to attain;
it is marked with the golden line (Svarṇarekhā), my own division, and your division.
And since it falls to your lot as the most excellent among all excellent *liṅgas*,
this *liṅga* which grants all desires is praised in your world.
Where silver is seen, there are the marks of Viṣṇu and his powers;
where coral is seen, there is Sarasvatī through the power of Brahmā.
"The vertical line is Śakti, and the horizontal line is remembered as Śiva. (p.
143) Such are the signs; listen, O Pārvatī, for they are difficult to find.
O Maheśvarī, when the linga is seen at a height of three finger-breadths,
or between five and nine finger-breadths, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
O Śivā, your liṅga— which bestows sons and grandsons— is shaped like a breadfruit or a rose-apple, or has the form of a coconut, or is circular like a lotus.
O Maheśvarī, when a new liṅga manifests in these places— on a riverbank, at a confluence, in a garden, on a mountain, or on a slope— [it is auspicious].

The characteristics of the *liṅga*, which bestows all desired objects in this world and grants the increase of the kingdom for a king, have been declared; now the characteristics of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) are being described.
O Maheśvarī, the pedestal (pīṭha) should be as wide as the liṅga or slightly higher;
it should be square and equal [in height] to that, and its neck (nāla) should be half of that.
The *unnata* (height) should be half of that, and there should be one, two, or three *paṭṭikās* (bands).
[One should install] Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, Mahākālī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Rudras.
Both your pedestal and your Śakti are situated in dependence [upon one another];
having established them at the base of the Liṅga, they are characterized by all auspicious marks.
First, having set aside the upper portion and joined the *liṅga* to the pedestal,
one should place the *praṇāla* to the north of the *liṅga*, which stands facing east.
One should place the water-channel (praṇāla) on the right side of a linga facing west;
for a linga facing north, one should place it on the western side.
One should place [the pedestal] facing east upon a linga that faces south;
O Maheśvarī, if the pedestal is larger than the linga, death will occur, and if it is smaller, [the same result follows].
If it is devoid of the five threads, it causes the destruction of the family for men.
Thus has the characteristic of the pedestal been declared; now hear concerning that which is fixed within the house.
O beloved, for one who is pleased, the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be threefold [the standard measure], and the space between it and the entrance (antara) half of that;
it is joined with two doorways on the exterior of the Lakṣmī-maṇḍapa.
One should make the door twice the size of the inner sanctum (garbha),
and O Dear One, one should construct a wall three times the size of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) all around it.
O Pārvatī, one should construct the vehicle-pavilion (vāhana-maṇṭapa) and half of that size for the enclosure;
the outer construction of the wall should be three times [the inner measurement].
O Pārvatī, the outer door of the pavilion is superior;
in the first [case], there is a wall for the liṅga, while in the second, there is a wall for the door.
O Goddess, the third [enclosure] consists of the gate-towers, and the fourth is the wall of the pedestal;
O Beloved, the fifth enclosure should be the outer wall of the rampart.
O Dear One, there are four pillars in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), eight outside of that,
twelve pillars in the pavilion (maṇṭapa), and [pillars] everywhere on the enclosures (prākāra) and so forth.
O beloved, [the temple] may have one hundred and eight pillars, two hundred, or three hundred;
it may be provided with images, friezes, and so forth, with the appropriate spacing between them.
One should fashion half of the house as the pinnacle (śikhara) and place half of that upon the pitcher (kalaśa);
having had the artisan construct the pitcher from gold, silver, copper, or other such materials.
O Dear One, there should be one, three, five, or seven jars;
the Guru should place those jars everywhere in temples and other such structures.
Having constructed a house according to the rules prescribed in the treatises on architecture,
if the house is built deficiently with respect to the characteristics previously described, [it brings misfortune].
That linga does not deserve worship by piśācas or brahmarākṣasas;
it becomes a great pestilence, and that village is constantly afflicted by it.
Therefore, with every effort, having observed the characteristics as described by the liberated one,
the artisan should construct your temple according to the instructions of the guru.
A house constructed of stone shall deliver ten million members of one's lineage;
at the end, having reached my city, one enjoys happiness right here.
Whether it be made of brick or wood, one obtains sons, grandsons, and other riches, as well as all enjoyments; there shall be victory everywhere.
At the end of the body, he certainly attains my world; of this there is no doubt.
The characteristics of the *cālaya* have been stated; now its limbs (*aṅga*) are being described.
The water-pot, the pedestal, the site-plan, along with the vehicle and the banner—this is said to be the fivefold set; regarding these, the defects shall now be stated by me.
If the water-pot is destroyed, there is loss of fame; if the pedestal is destroyed, there is loss of wealth;
and if the site, the vehicle, or the banner is destroyed, the same result shall occur.

O Pārvatī, all rituals such as the daily obligatory rites, as well as worship performed in that abode, do not lead to the attainment of dharma, wealth, desire, or liberation; indeed, they are not praised.
For the purpose of bringing the deities into presence and for the destruction of the asuras,
one should therefore construct a temple endowed with five components.
"The Ālaya is said to be a constituent part; now hear concerning the gatekeepers and so forth.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of the House Construction and the Characteristics of the Liṅga," in the Nityakāṇḍa of the Śrīvātulottara.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the door-keepers and others;
listen to the description of their vehicles, banners, pedestals, and the abodes of their retinues.
O beloved, for your linga, stone or copper, or even bell-metal, brass, or bronze may be used; however, those made of silver or gold are especially excellent.
O Maheśvarī, the height of the liṅga should be five times [its width], or it may measure fifteen cubits; the Guru [should fashion] its form according to your image.
Then, holding staffs in their hands and bearing conchs, discs, and other emblems,
they stood at the inner gate and the main gate, on both sides of the entrance.
O Maheśvarī, [place] Caṇḍikā and Ambikā as gatekeepers;
and on both sides of the main gate, [place those named] Ślādinī and Mohinī.
O Goddess, one should firmly install Kātyāyanī and Jayantī, both endowed with the proper characteristics, according to the path prescribed by the rules.
O beloved, the characteristics of the door-keepers at your liṅga have been described;
now I shall explain their vehicles according to the different materials, such as stone and others.
One should make the height above the liṅga one and a half cubits,
or three times the width of the liṅga, according to the characteristics described for the fivefold [liṅgas].
The mantra-practitioner should install [the deity] according to the ritual rule upon the banner of the pedestal and the pavilion;
thus, O Goddess, is the characteristic of the vehicle in the context of the division.
O Maheśvarī, I shall describe the characteristics of the banner for your linga:
[it may be made of] stone, a wooden staff, sandalwood, deodar, or substances produced from fragrant sources.
Having observed the essence of the lotus and the essence of the womb, one should grasp the staff;
this staff extends as far as the tip of the jar situated on the summit, O Dear One.
Having made it more than five cubits long and having dug it into the ground as a pillar,
one should fashion a square base at the foot of the staff with one, two, or three tiers.
Above that are eight streams, and above those is a circular form;
having placed the vehicle upon the top, one should fashion the pedestal for the banner.
Having bound it with stone and brick to a measurement of one and a half cubits,
the Guru should create an interval of fifteen [units] and install it according to the prescribed rite.
O beloved, a staff made of stone brings stability and increases one's lineage;
one made of wood brings all prosperity; and when a protective armor is fashioned from copper and other metals, it likewise bestows blessings.
O Śivā, gold brings victory over all enemies for men and bestows sovereignty;
thus has the characteristic of the banner been described. Now hear about the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
A pedestal made of stone or other materials, five fingers wide, should be fashioned;
above that, one should make it either square or circular.
O Maheśvarī, the Guru should fashion and install a pedestal or a lotus marked with the respective forms [of the deities], as well as the goddesses beginning with Caṇḍikā.
Next, O Goddess, I shall describe the deities in their proper order; listen:
one should worship Caṇḍikā, Ambikā, and Siṃha at both sides and in front of the door.
O Maheśvarī, one should place Gaṇanātha and Śaṅkara to the south,
the guardians of the directions (Dikpālas) in their respective directions, and Brahmā in the direction of Śaṅkara (the northeast).
Ananta is situated in the south-western direction in the first enclosure, O Śivā;
in the second [enclosure] are the seven Mothers, and the characteristics of the sacred seats (pīṭha) are now described.
O beloved, one cubit in width and seven finger-breadths in height,
Vīrabhadra and Gaṇeśa [should be placed] upon that pedestal at the location of the doorway.
And upon that seat is a row of seven lotus-shaped forms;
outside of that, O Śivā, in the four directions and above and below, on the ground.
To the Mothers, the Mothers of the Worlds, and even among all the hosts of Mothers—
to the presiding mistress of all the hosts of Mothers, Lakṣmī, who moves upon the earth and through the sky.
Having reached the region of Yama and being in the presence of the Teacher (the Buddha),
one should place Durgā in front of Vāyu, and Guha in the vicinity of Durgā.
O Maheśvarī, the Guru should install Dhanada near Soma,
and he should install Muṇḍinī in the middle, between Soma and Īśa.
One should fashion the form of the Liṅga-pīṭha with a width of seven aṅgulas;
above that, it should be seven aṅgulas high, provided with five lines and the proper characteristics.
One should install [the deities] on both sides of the gateway (gopura), both outside and inside;
Mahākālī at the front of the gateway and Karālī in the southeast.
And in the region of Yama is Virajā; in the region of the Daityas, Mandarā;
in the region of Varuṇa, the one named Vindhya; and in the domain of Vāyu, Suprabhā.
One should install Siṃhavaktrā in the northeast, Daityamardinī in the northeast, the pedestal (pīṭha) starting from the east, and Kṣetrapāla in the northeast.
It should be one cubit in width, square, and beautifully adorned with lotuses;
it is provided with three tiers, and above that, it measures one cubit.
Having established the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), then hear about the great seat (mahāpīṭha):
one should construct it as a square, measuring one and a half cubits in extent.
p. 151) And above that, one should have a level *liṅga* with eight petals at the top;
O Dear One, one should fashion it as a three-tiered pedestal (*tripīṭha*) joined with a fillet (*paṭṭikā*).
Below, on the pedestal, one should fashion lotuses in the eight directions as previously described;
[one should also place them] at the tip of the liṅga, near the banner, and outside the gateway of the gopura.
One should establish the great pedestal and visualize the deities:
Brahmaghoṣī, Sughoṣī, and Sukharāgiṇī as desired.
O Maheśvarī, one should again visualize Sumukhī, Subhujā, and Pramodinī upon the seat, starting from the east and proceeding all around.
O Dear Śivā, having worshipped the one named Piṅgalā below and Sukeśī above,
the Guru should thus install them upon that pedestal in your house.
The characteristics of the pedestal have been declared; now hear concerning the abode of the retinue.
Outside, surrounding the enclosure wall, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding in due order:
O beloved, one should construct the inner sanctum and the pavilion as five or seven cubits in size;
it should be square or oblong, and its height should be one cubit.
One should construct two internal walls and provide a door there;
in the space between them, O beloved, one should place four pillars, and outside of that, eight.
One should construct a gabled roof according to the methods prescribed in the treatises on architecture;
having placed a pinnacle (kalaśa) at its front, one should also set down a single water-pot (kumbha) made of gold.
One should also install the retinue in their proper order, beginning with Vīreśa:
namely, Ṣaṇmukha, Gaṇeśa, Gopāla, and the Son of the Wind (Hanumān).
One should fashion that particular form from various materials such as stone;
it may be one cubit, three cubits, five cubits, or nine cubits in height, O Dear One.
Endowed with their respective characteristics, adorned with their respective weapons and ornaments,
and joined with their respective vehicles, exactly as described in the treatises on craftsmanship.
The mantra-practitioner should establish the excellent abode of the retinue according to the prescribed rite and the path previously described, O Śivā, along with many other [deities].

The mantra-practitioner, with great devotion, should have various forms and their respective temples constructed; then, according to the prescribed rite, he should install them outside, in the area of the enclosure wall.
The residence of the retinue has been described; now hear, O beloved, about the location of the well.
It is in the northeast quarter of your residence, within the enclosure wall, O Maheśvarī.
Having dug the ground down to the water-level, making it either square or circular,
and having bound its width with three or five layers of desired stones and so forth;
O Dear One, the water within should reach up to the height of a man, or measure two or three men's heights;
and there should be a fish, a tortoise, and a lotus, made either of gold or silver, O Dear One.
O Dear One, one should cast it into the midst of water and cover the wooden board;
one should not look at it, but should purify it year after year.
The characteristics of a well have been described; now hear the characteristics of a tank.
One should construct it in front of your residence, or to the west, or to the north.
Then, having dug a square pit measuring eighty cubits on all sides,
one should construct stairs in the four directions using stones and bricks, O beloved.
And having tied a cord separately at the third, fifth, and ninth [units],
and having firmly fastened it down to the water's edge, the water should reach up to the height of a man.
Having dug a water reservoir measuring five by three [units],
one should fashion therein a fish, a tortoise, and a lotus, endowed with their characteristic marks.
Then the mantra-practitioner should install the characteristic pavilion in the center,
and he should have a beautiful pond constructed in front of that liṅga.
O Goddess of the gods, whether it be a king, an excellent Brahmin, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra who should perform this, O Goddess, he shall attain all his desires.
"And others [shall attain] my proximity, truly, truly, O fair-faced one.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of the Gatekeepers and the Embankment," in the Nityakāṇḍa of the venerable Vātulottara.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the characteristics of the storehouse for materials and so forth;
the treasury, the wardrobe, and the dwelling, as well as the bathhouse and the sacrificial hall, each separately.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who are worshipped by all the deities;
and to those who worship the Liṅga during the rites of the chariot festival and other celebrations.

And among those who act as preceptors, who is the most excellent? Tell me, O Lord, which people are untouchable, and likewise, who are untouchable due to distinctions such as entering the inner sanctum of a temple?
"In this regard, O Guru, I desire to hear about the fault, the fruit, and the pacification.
Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess; I shall explain everything for the welfare of the world."
O beautiful one, for the purpose of increasing the royal treasury, which is a secret difficult even for the gods to attain,
and for the sake of the fourfold army and abundant harvests;

One who has received initiation, is of noble birth, is endowed with the Vedas, scriptures, and Āgamas, possesses a [pure] lineage, and knows the ultimate reality— that twice-born man is a worshiper of the Liṅga.
He is a householder, truthful, devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, pure,
a knower of the presence of the Liṅga, moderate in speech, and one who has conquered his senses.
One who is a performer of sacrifices, a believer, righteous, having undergone the preliminary purificatory rites,
and devoted to the conduct of his caste and stage of life, is worthy of worshipping your linga.
Free from pride and envy, having received initiation and being further consecrated,
he is compassionate, heroic in generosity, always contented, and patient.
According to the people, the wise one is the best at worshipping the Sāmba-linga;
these are the worshippers and touchers of fixed lingas and other types of lingas.
I shall describe the characteristics of the teacher; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance! He should be born in Āryāvarta, illustrious, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
Where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct, ascetics whose wealth is their austerity,
as well as the Vedas and sacrifices, that region is known as Āryāvarta.
From sixteen years of age upwards until seventy is said to be the period [for practice];
this is well-established in the *Ekatantro* from the stage of ritual action (*kriyā*) up to the stage of knowledge (*jñāna*).
And one must perform the teaching of the twenty-eight *saṃhitās*,
which have been mentioned, prohibited, and then [once again] authorized.
My words are indeed manifold, both dependent and independent;
a wise man should perform the rites of installation and other festivals, as well as the dance rituals.
One who constantly worships the gods and the fire, who is devoted to his guru,
whose soul is purified by the tradition— such a one may bestow initiation upon a disciple.
One who knows the reality of the pervasion of the deities, is proficient in the sixfold path, and is a believer—such a person should perform the rites; he is called the most excellent teacher.
But if it is performed otherwise, as well as in the case of malevolent rites (ābhicāra),
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the fruit thereof is the destruction of the performer's lineage.
The Goddess said:
"O Teacher, O Lord of the lineage, O Lord of Gods! If there should be many people [present], then tell me, O Śambhu, my beloved, what must be done by the performer of that rite?"
Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips; out of affection for you, I shall now speak in brief, O beloved, of that which bestows auspiciousness and prosperity.
One who is senior in age within that lineage should perform the tantric rite;
if it is performed by anyone other than him, one should predict danger from enemies.
Disease and affliction will arise immediately, especially in that kingdom;
therefore, O Girijā, one who is devoid of vigor should not perform it with effort.
One should perform it with one who is senior to them for the sake of attaining fame, prosperity, and royal sovereignty;
likewise, O Goddess, in a royal lineage as well as in a noble family.
A householder who performs sacrifices should have [the rites] performed by various noble members of his lineage;
otherwise, he incurs fault, and therefore he should avoid [such negligence] with great effort.
Thus, O beloved, I have correctly explained the answers to the questions. O Goddess,
if by chance we two are present at a superior act of worship during a festival rite—

If it was not performed by the Lord of Teachers, O Maheśvara, tell me how it could have been accomplished by anyone else without a cause? If it were not done by him, how could it have been done at all? Speak!
"By whom, O Lord, should rites such as festivals be performed?
Śiva said: 'O beloved, if [the initiation] has not been performed, the Guru [is the one who performs] the rites such as festivals.'"
O Maheśvarī, [the disciple] may be a natural-born son or a younger brother of the Lord of Teachers (deśikendra),
or his son, or his grandson, or a kinsman, by his command.

One should appoint those who have been initiated, who act according to his instructions, who are proficient in the meaning of the Āgamas, and who belong to the same lineage; in doing so, there is no fault whatsoever.
If one who is worthy of honor is insulted by fools, he shall experience hell for as many thousands of years as there are syllables in the Gāyatrī mantra.
"O Goddess, that ritual action is fruitless; there is no doubt that [the deity's] presence is absent.
The Goddess said: "O wearer of matted locks, I wish to hear now about the Ācārya."
"If a sin such as the killing of a Brahmin should occur, tell me, what then?
Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain [the rule] regarding the teacher and the twice-born."
O fair-faced one, whether it be the sin of killing a Brahmin or any other minor offense (upapātaka), even if committed intentionally or unintentionally, should such a thing have occurred;
In that regard, the teacher should not perform any ritual action among all rites;
however, there is never an occasion when expiation is not required in the event of such acts as the killing of a Brahmin.
If one should suddenly perceive a major sin (pātaka) or a minor sin (upapātaka),
purification shall be attained through expiation (prāyaścitta), according to the relative strength or weakness of the fault.
Then, having turned away from that sin with the permission of the king, O Śivā,
one becomes fit for ritual action there, O Goddess, and may perform the rite.

O Maheśvarī, a wise person should not perform ritual acts according to the *tantra* without performing expiation (*prāyaścitta*); nor should he touch the *liṅga* or the image, nor should he worship them.
If one touches the image, the liṅga, or performs worship and festivals [at the former], there will be no presence in the liṅga; Lakṣmī has departed from the village.
The king destroys his fourfold army and shall meet with death;
O Goddess, he is tormented by enemies and by fevers, epilepsy, and other such ailments.
Therefore, having understood [the situation] correctly, the Guru should duly perform the expiation.
The characteristics of the Teacher have been declared; now hear, O Pārvatī, about those who are untouchable.
O Goddess, even for those who have committed faults, if they do not touch the *liṅga*,
there will certainly be an absence of the deity's presence in that *liṅga* when it is worshipped by one who is uninitiated.
One who is uninitiated, even if he knows the four Vedas, should neither touch nor worship [the deity],
whether he be a seeker of worldly enjoyment, a seeker of liberation, a samayin, or even a sādhaka.
The initiated preceptor should worship the deity for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose,
just as an elephant in the forest flees in fear upon seeing the lord of beasts.
O Maheśvarī, [the following types of people] are afraid when a linga has been worshipped by one who is uninitiated:
one devoid of faith, one who is excessively miserly, and one initiated [only] through much talk.
The ungrateful, the one devoid of Vedic knowledge, the man of evil conduct, the wicked person,
those who do not touch the *liṅga*, and those Brahmins who are devoid of truth and other virtues— these are [to be avoided].
Your linga and other marks are of the nature of stable prosperity;
therefore, knowing this, these twice-born ones shall never touch them.
If they should touch [the site] out of negligence, their absence will certainly result;
therefore, having understood this repeatedly, one should perform the rite of pacification.
I shall describe those who enter the house according to the distinctions of their faces, noses, and so forth;
O fair-faced one, those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas) are fit to go as far as the end of the "pleasant nose" (sukhanāsa).
All the twice-born who have been saluted [should be honored] as far as the center of the Ramā-maṇṭapa;
if one has proceeded ahead by mistake, one should mutter the root *prāṇa-mantra*.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times separately for each, one should sprinkle them with jars of water;
those of non-twice-born status [should be sprinkled] up to the boundary of the *khāpālikas*, while Kṣatriyas [are sprinkled] up to the boundary of their mounts.

For Vaiśyas and Śūdras, [the ritual] should extend as far as the edge of the courtyard; during their processions and other such rites, the officiant should perform a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*), a *nāndī* ceremony, and the offering of cow products (*gavya*) and so forth.

Having had the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) proclaimed, he should choose a preceptor (deśika) who bestows gold, as well as four officiating priests (hotṛka) who have mastered the Vedas; such is the duty of the Guru.
One should select ten Brahmins as reciters (jāpaka) and eleven as sprinklers (secaka),
and honor them with the root mantra, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and other offerings for the liṅga.
O Kalādhara, you should perform the fire-oblation with Rudra-mantras, Sūktas, and the like, using water mixed with fragrances, as well as with your own root-mantra and weapon-mantra.

Manu [performed the rite] with the mantras of Śāntidurgā, Ghoradurgā, and others, using sacrificial fuel sticks (samit), clarified butter (ājya), sacrificial porridge (caru), honey (kṣaudra), tuṭika, mustard seeds (sarṣapa), and sesame seeds (tila).
The best of men should offer oblations of cow’s milk and tips of *dūrvā* grass, fifty thousand at a time in sequence,
together with recitations and complete readings of the mantra.
The Guru [should teach] the Tava-mūla, the Tava-astra, the mantras of the five Durgās in sequence, the Gaṇeśa-mantra, the Yoginī-mantras, and the seven-hundred-verse Caṇḍī.
Then one should recite the mantra ten thousand five hundred times separately;
again, one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and offer the remnants (sampāta).
One should sprinkle [the deity] with five hundred jars, and then with half that amount, and again with half of that;
one should worship the Goddess in many ways and offer cooked rice such as *śāli* and other grains.
Having whirled the circle of lamps and again given the tenfold gift,
and having fed the assembly of Brahmins, one should offer the entire array of ritual acts.
At the conclusion, one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given for the removal of the sins of entry;
without this propitiation, the presence [of the deity] perishes along with destruction and famine.
Therefore, peace should be established by the Guru according to the previously mentioned method;
[the deities are] the dyer, the barber, the laborer, the banner-bearer, and the beloved.
Citratāra, Kulāla, and again Ambarasandhikṛt,
Kaivartaka, and Svarṇakārī shall always enter the end of the banner.
If it moves toward the division of the faults (doṣabhāga), there will be the destruction of the kingdom, the depletion of strength,
the king will meet his end, and a drought will occur.
With the root mantra of Ghoradurgā and the mantra of the supreme guru,
the best of teachers should perform the rite of pacification for Śivā using five hundred jars, as previously described.
Having fed the foremost of the Brahmins,
one should offer the bali-oblation to the great elements when a human being is affected by the birth-impurity (sūtaka) arising from a death or a birth, and so forth.

Tell me, O Goddess, if one has entered the body of the *liṅga* at Balidvāra and other such sites, how is it [to be understood] regarding the enclosure wall (*prākāra*), the courtyard (*prāṅkaṇa*), the place called the vehicle (*vāhana*), and the site of Ramā?
Nor [should one build] in the vicinity of a limb of the body, a temple, a residence for attendants, a storehouse for goods or clothing, a treasury, or a guest-house for food.
In the hall for food offerings, on the pinnacle of the temple, and so forth;
in the flag-house, the great pedestal, the city gate, and the pavilion of Dharma.
O proud lady, throughout your entire residence and along the chariot-paths,
there shall be increase and decline among the people, as well as danger from Maghā and misfortune for those who have entered.
O Mountain-born Goddess, I shall describe the individual faults in detail:
there will be famine, affliction by disease, and constant harassment by enemies.
There is fear of an enemy king; the king's army perishes.
That king meets his death, with the destruction of his forces and the depletion of his wealth.
There will be the destruction of the treasury and the loss of wealth; the king himself shall perish.
There will be the destruction of grain and crops, and the ruin of the kingdom—of this there is no doubt.
The destruction of fame, affliction by spirits, great pestilence, and fear for men—
all such things as the conflagration of prosperity and the like— undoubtedly come to an end.
Having thoroughly understood these and other such [rules], one should never allow a person affected by birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) to enter for the sake of increasing wealth and royal power. (p. 164)
Having first performed the worship of Vighneśa, I shall seek peace with compassion;
immediately thereafter, one should cause the recitation of the Nāndī-gavya and the Puṇyāha.
O Goddess, one should select four— the Guru, the Dhanada, the Hotṛkas, and the Ghoṣakas— separately, as well as nine Jāpakas.
Likewise, O Brahmins, one should first sprinkle the consecrators (*secakas*)— numbering eleven Rudras— and the *sūtaka* [materials],
with cow-products (*gavya*) using the *gavya-mantras*, for the purification of the Liṅga.
Furthermore, one should bathe the Liṅga with the Puṇyāha water and the supreme five nectars (pañcāmṛta) using Rudra mantras, and bathe Śivā with pure water and the nine hymns (sūktas).
I shall declare the names of the hymns (sūktas): the Śrīsūkta known by your name, the hymns beginning with the Pañcadurgā, and the hymn called Pratyaṅgirā.

The Guru should [offer] milk that has been purified with the *Ramāsūkta* and other hymns; this is called the "Hymn-Name" (*sūktanāma*). Then, he should offer that cow-product with the *Gavyamantra* and the *Prāṇa-mantra*.
The best of men should offer oblations with sacrificial porridge, fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and the like, as well as with cow’s milk,
until the number of offerings reaches one thousand.
Either with five hundred oblations or one hundred and eight oblations,
he should again perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and offer the residual clarified butter (sampātājya).
If a woman is possessed by *sūtaka* (impurity), wherever she may go, the wise practitioner should offer oblations separately with the respective root-mantras for each location.
Then one should sprinkle mustard seeds, salt, and sesame into a golden vessel,
and cause pumpkins and black gram to be given to the Brahmins.
Having fed many Brahmins, one should worship the root deity;
for this is the general procedure, and now the presiding deity is being described.
In the case of a miscarriage, or when she is situated in the *ramā* or *pratiṣṭhā* asterisms,
or when she is afflicted by the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity), the Great Peace rite (*mahāśāntikriyā*) for the twice-born should be performed according to the previously mentioned method.
Then, with the life-force mantra (*prāṇamantra*), the root mantra (*mūla*), and the mantras of its limbs (*aṅga*),
one should offer oblations (*āhuti*) numbering fifty thousand, twenty-five thousand, and twelve thousand respectively.
One should bathe with a thousand, five hundred, or even half of those jars,
and one should give gifts of cows, land, and so forth, for the pacification of that fault.
One should feed many Brahmins and perform the remaining rites as previously described.
[The four great sins are: killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and violating the Guru’s bed.

O Brahmins, O daughter of the mountain, those who have entered into sexual union with women should not, under any circumstances, enter a temple of the Liṅga or a divine shrine out of negligence; of this there is no doubt.
If they should cause entry into one who breaks down walls and such, there is a distinct fault; O Goddess, hear now the pacification of that in due order.
If those two [planets] are afflicted by the sin of killing a Brahmin and enter within the city walls,
there will undoubtedly be the ruin of the king's kingdom and a period of famine.
Having abandoned that person, one should perform the rite of pacification according to the rules;
one should perform that pacification there, for if it is not done, one incurs many faults.
If a slayer of a Brahmin enters the pavilion while it is comfortably situated, there will be fear of an enemy king for the king, and his loss of sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
Because of the loss of wealth, wife, and so forth, as well as the enjoyment [of power] by the king;
therefore, having understood these floods of defects, one should abandon that very moment.
Having performed the rite of pacification according to the rules, one should offer the bali-oblation to the great elements,
O Maheśvarī, if a killer of a Brahmin has entered within the inner sanctum.
Through negligence, if there is contact with the *liṅga*, the presence [of the deity] perishes;
the death of the king occurs immediately, as does that of the queen.
There will be oppression by enemies, loss of sovereignty, and the destruction of the royal lineage;
his ministers, army commanders, and others will perish without a doubt.
There will be a fear of great pestilence among men and the destruction of living beings;
at that time, the Guru will abandon the Śūdras, the slayers of Brahmins, and other such people.
Furthermore, peace must be performed according to the method that will be described;
O Kalādhara, I shall now explain that peace in brief.
Having worshipped Vināyaka, one should thereafter perform the Nāndī-karman.
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited with mantras beginning with *pavamāna*;
then, the deity should be brought into the enclosure with one hundred and eight jars.
One should sprinkle them according to that same procedure once they have been brought into the courtyard;
one should bathe the Śivas with two hundred and eight odd jars.
When the Brahmins had been invited to the pavilion and the couple had entered the hall of happiness,
he sprinkled the God and the Goddess Śāmbhavī with five hundred jars of water.

If, having entered the temple of the Liṅga, you touch the Liṅga according to the prescribed rite with thousands of jars [of water], then the Sāmba-Liṅga, which is identical to your own self, [is attained].
Then the preceptor should perform the fire oblation (homa) with my Gāyatrī mantra,
with the terrible root mantra (mūlamantra), and with the life-force mantra (prāṇamantra).
With half of half of ten thousand oblations—one thousand five hundred oblations—one should perform the fire-sacrifice;
