with ten thousand oblations, one performs it during her entry into the pavilion and the temple of the *liṅga*.
One should offer eleven thousand oblations (sārdhāyutāhuti) with substances such as fuel-sticks (samit) and clarified butter (ājya),
reciting the Gāyatrī, the root mantra, and the nine-syllabled Ghoramantra.

One should recite the Brahma-mantra, as well as the mantras for the guardians of the directions and their retinues, until the conclusion of the fire oblation (homa); thereafter, one should perform the tenfold gift (daśadāna).
To pacify those defects, one should give gifts such as food and so forth,
and feed many Brahmins at the site of the wall and other structures during the period of impurity.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worshippers of the Liṅga and Others," in the section on Daily Rites within the Durgā-bheda of the Śrī-Vātulottara, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
O Mahādeva, salutations to you for the welfare and happiness of the lord of the earth.
Salutations to you, the support of the universe; salutations to you, the one with the eye in his forehead.
O Śaṅkara, the ritual action pertaining to the *malliṅga* occurs through the piercing of the jar; the cessation of that action likewise occurs through the piercing of the jar in detail.

(169) From the time of dawn until the end of night, the Guru is the master of the time and so forth; O proud lady, listen as I shall explain in detail for the sake of the increase of prosperity and sovereignty.
At the time of dawn, having risen, the wise man should contemplate his own guru:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who are saluted by all the deities."
Who are the worshippers of the *liṅga*, and who are those engaged in the rites of chariot festivals and the like?
Who is the most excellent for the office of *ācārya*, and tell me, who are the people permitted to touch [the deity]?
Likewise, O Lord, there are those that are untouchable due to distinctions such as being inner sanctuaries and so forth;
O Guru, I wish to hear about the defects, the results, and the propitiatory rites concerning them.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, for the benefit of all the world, I shall speak.
For the purpose of increasing the royal treasury, a secret difficult even for the gods to obtain;
for the sake of the fourfold army and for the sake of abundant harvests, O beautiful one.
One who is initiated, born of a noble lineage, endowed with the Vedas, scriptures, and Āgamas, belonging to a virtuous family,
and a knower of the principles— he is a twice-born worthy of worshipping the Liṅga.
He was a householder, truthful, devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, and pure;
he knew the presence of the Liṅga, spoke sparingly, and had his senses subdued.
p. 170) A performer of sacrifices, a believer, and a follower of dharma—[in] Kannaḍa script: "Obeisance to you, O Mahādeva, and for the happiness of the lord of the earth."
For the sake of the welfare of the great multitude and for the increase of the royal treasury, homage to you, O support of the world; homage to you, O one with an eye in his forehead!

O Śaṃkara, regarding the ritual action pertaining to the *malla*-liṅga, which is performed according to the division of *ghaṭī*s, O Śiva, how is that ritual action explained? How is the measure of that rite determined?
I wish to hear separately the number of Brahmins, the preceptors and others, their respective sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), their individual mantras, and their specific weights; please speak.
Śaṅkara said: "In your liṅga, the ritual action is detailed according to the division of ghaṭīs;
from the time of dawn until the end of night, O proud one, the Guru is the master of the times."
Listen, I shall explain in detail for the sake of increasing prosperity and the kingdom:
having risen at the time of dawn, the wise man should contemplate his own guru.
Having gone to the river with the Cārakas and other twice-born at the rising of the sun,
and having performed the rites of purification and conduct, he bathed together with the assembly of Brahmins.
And having reached your abode together with the assembly of Brahmins and others, one should complete the fifty-nine *svanityās* within the channel (*nāḍī*). (p. 171)
Having requested the preceptor, the noble one should perform the opening of the lock with the sound of the *jayaghaṇṭā* and other bells,
and the resonance of conchs, drums, and the like.
O Goddess, for the sake of awakening you, let there be hymns, songs, and dances accompanied by the sounds of all musical instruments, along with the resonance of lutes and flutes.
Having properly rekindled the lamps while reciting the lamp-mantra, O Brahmins, the wise one, with the permission of the preceptor, [should worship] the linga, the pedestal, and its temple.
Having purified it, they should wash it; this is the means for accomplishing success, [performed] by those free from malice.
Having swept it with the wind-bīja, one should sprinkle it with the water-bīja.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the cleansing with the Varuṇa-weapon should be performed with your root mantra;
likewise for the pavilion called Sukhanasi, the Maṇṭapa, and the gateway known as Vāhana.
The assembly hall, pavilions, palaces, and the like, as well as the residential quarters for attendants,
and the guards consisting of Brahmins and others according to their respective castes, [are all situated] within sixty nāḍīs.
In each of those places, O beloved, they should perform [the rites] separately, extending as far as the outer gate:
before you, at the gateway, and in the pavilion for hearing the Dharma.
In the place of the jar (ghaṭi), in that which is called the assembly hall, and in the abode of the retinue,
one should most excellently delight [the deities] with colored powders and the like, using the five colors.
One should worship the vessel of water at the beginning of the first *naḍikā*;
having placed it there with the solar mantra, accompanied by the sounds of Vedic recitations and other such noises.
Having brought water from a river and joined it with the water in the vardhanī vessel, one should perform the rite beginning with the root mantra,
preceded by salutations to you, together with twice-born brahmins learned in their own Vedic branches.
Then the Guru, having entered within, should first worship Vināyaka and draw the mandalas on the right side of the linga.
One should perform the *nāndī-śrāddha* at the beginning of the rite for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), starting from the primary *liṅga* and the temple;
one should sow excellent grains and other seeds everywhere and invite the twice-born.
The preceptor, the grandfather, the giver of materials, the one who provides the image and the vehicle,
the assembly member, and four chanters of the Vedas who recite five hymns.
Then he [saw] five worshippers and reciters of the Śrī Rudra,
three who had performed circumambulations, and three men for the purpose of dancing.
For the purpose of circumambulation, he should station ten Brahmins separately with their respective root mantras;
having placed the *pavamāna* jar and having worshipped the water-pot according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Kālī, Ghaṇṭā, Rudra, Kumbha, and the five nectars (sudhārasas). With the substance from the cow-pot placed within the cow-pot, one should recite the mantra of the cow.
One should sprinkle the Liṅga with water from that jar while reciting the Pāvamāna hymn,
and [worship] the supreme [Liṅga] with the thousand names of Gaṅgā.
Having performed worship with the fivefold offerings and others accompanied by your seed-syllable,
one should offer curd-rice for two and a half nāḍīs while reciting your mantra.
One should cause betel leaf to be offered to the Goddess, look upon a cow with its calf,
thereafter perform the ritual of the five limbs (pañcāṅga-śravaṇa), and then cause the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) to be performed.
Having worshipped the flower with mantras, one should again sprinkle the auspicious Liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) using those same mantras,
and thereafter with the Rudra mantra.
One should devoutly sprinkle Rudra, who is surrounded by eleven [Rudras],
within yourself with the Kālī-sūkta, the Durgā-sūkta, and that which is called the Āryā-sūkta.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] separately with the mantra of the Śūlinīsūkta,
the Guru [should do so] finally with the water from the Rudra-pitcher and then with the water from the Kālī-pitcher.
In the four directions around your abode, perform the recitation of the Vedas and so forth, as well as the mantra of Kālī, the solar mantra, prostrations, and the libation (tarpaṇa).
One should recite the mantra of Durgā, the Vahnyastra mantra, and the excellent mantra of Śūlin,
each separately accompanied by fresh leaves, ending with the offerings to you.
O beloved, after performing circumambulation, prostration, and the offering of oblations (bali),
the preceptor [should recite] the Kālīmālā-mantra followed by the one known as the Durgāmālā.
The Noble Blessed Lady [bestows her grace] upon you who, in due order, recites the Mālā-mantra one thousand times, or five hundred, or one hundred and eight times.
To the right of your liṅga, or in the west, or in the north;
or in a corner, or in the intermediate space between corners, or even in the original shrine.
Then, in the pavilion known as Vāhana, the Guru should separately recite the mantras;
having made supplication with the mantra according to the Kālīkalpa, he should perform [the rite].
Having worshipped the Liṅga with those names joined with seed-syllables (bījas) by the thousands,
one should worship Durgā, Āryā, and Śūlinī with their names by the thousands.
Having offered five handfuls of flowers according to the traditional method,
one should recite the root mantra of the deity one hundred times while performing the sixteen types of ritual service (upacāra).
Mudga-rice mixed with ghee, accompanied by soup, vegetables, and broth,
combined with honey and sugar, and served with young mango fruits.
The Guru [should offer] milk-rice (pāyasa) together with various foods such as those to be chewed, drunk, licked, and sucked,
as well as the five nectars (pañcanāḍya), incense, lamps, and so forth, while reciting the root mantra.
Then, having covered the door with cloth, one should announce [the offering] with devotion;
having entered with the mantra *homāhe*, one should then recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having offered the oblation and taken the *sampāta* (the remnants), the wise one should speak at your base;
then, having washed his feet and sipped water (*ācamana*), he should strike the bell.
One should first offer a garment, then present the offerings and dismiss them;
having given the propitiatory *arghya* at the end, one should first offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*).
The wise one should wave the series of lamps until the end of the *nīrājana* rite;
then, having displayed the lamp of the *nīra*, he should perform the worship with mantra-offerings of flowers.
Having worshipped the retinue with the sounding of victory-bells and other instruments,
the preceptor should invoke the spirits with the root mantra and the garland-mantra.
One should perform the offering of the sacrifice (balidāna) and conduct the festival during the six nāḍīs;
O Goddess, having worshipped the lotus-lamp, one should proceed from the washing of the feet and so forth.
Having entered within your image, the best of mantra-knowers, endowed with true devotion, should display the moon-lamp after offering the net of ritual actions at the end.
To express the completion of the ritual action (*karmasaṃpūrti*), the Guru should prescribe the *kṛcchra* penance.
At dawn, I have declared the sixty-five-fold rite (*pañcottara-ṣaṣṭikarma*).
It bestows all enjoyments, is divine, destroys the flood of all sins,
grants abundance, removes sorrow, and bestows victory over all enemies.
"O beloved, this [rite] immediately increases one's lineage and bestows desired objects.

Thus concludes the description of the procedure for the exposition of the daily morning rites according to the different *ghaṭīs* (time-divisions), within the section on daily rituals (*nityakarmakāṇḍa*) of the *Durgā-bheda* in the *Śrī-vātulottara*, during the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "Nāma.
Now, O beautiful one, I shall proclaim the occasional rite for midday:
the supreme mantra [is to be recited] from the seventh nāḍī of the *saṅgavī* period until its end at the twelfth.
Having purified himself and completed his daily obligatory rites along with the Brahmins,
and having proclaimed the place and time, he should worship your supreme son.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made, he should, as previously stated, choose the most excellent Brahmins,
as well as the preceptor (*guru*), the giver of wealth (*dhanada*), and the presiding member (*sadasya*), who is superior in every respect.
O Goddess, [appoint] five excellent brahmins separately: sprinklers numbering eleven (the number of Rudras), a carrier who recites the Vedas, and reciters of hymns who perform the worship.
Twenty-five reciters joined with the sprouts of mantra,
five people for circumambulation, and five Brahmins for the purpose of prostration.

One should choose as a teacher of the Dharmaśāstras and an astrologer someone who is beloved by the people; one should honor him with the Mūla rite and offer a difficult task according to one's own ability.
Having again performed the sacrifice with the Rudra-pitcher together with twice-born ones numbering eleven,
and having placed the pitcher of Amṛta with the nectar-essences, he should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
One should sprinkle the *liṅga* with the nectar-essences; all these [acts] are preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
With the Rudra-mantras held within, there are eleven separate oblations (*āhuti*).
Having caused the liṅga to be sprinkled by people, one should recite the networks of mantras in sequence:
the four Vedas in the cardinal directions of the house, and again the weapon-mantras in the intermediate directions.
The Brahmāstra, the Vāruṇāstra, and your weapon known as the Cakra;
the mantra of Ramā, that called Kumārī, and the one joined with the Ambikā-manu.
O Goddess, the Guru [should impart] the mantra of Navadurgā, the one called Vāhana, Gaṇeśvara, Skanda, Vīrabhadra, and the mantra of the Son of Vāyu (Hanumān).
Then, O best of the twice-born, those experts in the interpretation of the Vedas recited for you the root mantra known as the *parivāra* within the *pālika*, as well as the *Caṇḍī Saptashatī*.
Then those experts in the tradition explained their respective positions to you:
they were stationed all around Ramakumbha, starting from the east and encircling him.
The wise ones should chant [the mantra], touch him, and perform the ritual up to the sprinkling;
they should also perform prostrations and circumambulations, continuing until the end of the lamp offering.
Having caused the Dharmaśāstras and Purāṇas to be recited at its head,
the most excellent of men should finally sprinkle the Liṅga with water from the Rudra-pitcher.
Having placed various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), one should display rows of lamps;
and at the beginning of the thirteenth channel (nāḍī) and so forth, one should again sprinkle [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having worshipped with five flowers,
the knower of mantras should thereafter [worship] with the Ramāsūkta, the Kumārīsūkta, and the Devīsūkta.
With the mantra of the Ambikāsūkta and substances such as camphor water,
and with the Vanākhyā hymn and the water from the Ramā-pitcher;
Then, with the thousand names of Ramā and others, with the thousand names of Kumārī, and with the names of Ambikā and Mahiṣāntakī;
Having worshipped with thousands of flowers and unbroken rice grains while reciting the names of the Gāyatrīs,
and having offered many prayers, one should display the *liṅga-mudrā*.
Having offered the food offering, incense, lamps, and so forth according to the prescribed rite,
and having performed worship with devotion for as many *ghaṭikās* as there are lunar days (*tithis*), one should proceed.
The Guru should perform the great worship (mahāpūjā) as described in the *Ramākalpa*;
then, O people, you should worship him with the root [mantra] and the ritual services (upacāra), and so forth.

O Dear One, [offer] rice cooked with milk, soups, vegetables, and the like, accompanied by ghee and edible foods; as well as milk-rice, and things to be licked and sucked, endowed with the six flavors.
Then, with the mantra "devasya tvā," accompanied by flowers, unbroken rice grains, and water,
he should offer it to the Goddess, preceded by the covering of the door.
Having performed the sacrifice with the Pālīka vehicle, one should offer oblations with their own names,
together with Brahmā, Dhanada, and Ārya, as well as with the Sadasya, along with the sacrificial body.

Then, having gone to the sacrificial ground, [one should perform the rite] in the fire-pit, on the sacrificial mound, or elsewhere, with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, milk, ghee, and sacrificial porridge.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra;
at the conclusion, having completed the rite of homa, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Taking the remainder of that and reciting the root mantra, the Guru,
accompanied by the residual oblation (*sampāta-ājya*), should cast it into the south-east of the *liṅga*.
Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water with devotion,
he should first strike the bell and then remove the covering from the door.
At the end, one should offer the *naivedya* (food offering) and then wash that [vessel];
thereafter, having offered the *prasannārghya* (water of grace) and *tāmbūla* (betel), and having worshipped, the Guru should perform the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water).
Then, having brought forward a tawny cow along with her calf, adorned with ornaments, one should worship her in front with the Mūla mantra while performing circumambulation.
Having gazed upon [the deity], having worshipped, having offered oblations, and having made supplications according to the prescribed rite,
accompanied by the auspicious chanting of the Vedas and the sounds of the five musical instruments;
The Guru, together with true devotees, singers and others, panegyrists, bards, and eminent persons, should cause a multitude of lamps to be waved.
One should offer incense in the shape of a banner and whirl a lamp made of ghee three times; and for the lamps known as "arrows," one should whirl them five times.
O Goddess, likewise perform seven circumambulations known as the "remainder" (śeṣa), as well as the lamp-circumambulations;
then nine times the circumambulation with earthen lamps, and thereafter ten lustrations (nīrājana).
Reciting the respective mantras three times for each called "Candra," the wise practitioner should rotate them individually at the end, accompanied by the worship of mantra-flowers.
Having thoroughly honored the retinue with incense, lamps, and other offerings,
and having summoned the spirits (bhūtas) with the bell and other instruments, one should [perform] the eighteen channels in sequence.
The preceptor should offer the oblation, starting from the doors and ending at the pedestal of the offering (balipīṭha), using their respective names;
then, having offered it to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) with his specific mantra.
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a festival, and at the end of the festival,
in front of it, O lady of excellent vows, one should circumambulate your image with a lotus-lamp.
Then, having entered that courtyard, the knower of mantras, taking water from the night-vessel with the Night-mantra,
should sprinkle your image three times again.
Reciting your mantra, he should circumambulate and release [the offering] in the leftward direction;
having caused your image to enter within, he should perform the washing of the feet and so forth.
Having placed it to the right of the *liṅga*, one should infuse that consciousness;
then, having offered water for honor (*arghya*) for the sake of propitiation, one should display a moon-like lamp.
Having offered the web of karma at the end, one should mutter [the mantra] a hundred times at your feet;
the water from the feet and the floral remains (nirmālya) belong to the Brahmins who perform the rites.
And for all the devotees, the preceptor should give a vehicle as a sacrificial fee;
at Valabhī, the preceptor should fasten the door with twenty channels.
O Daughter of the Mountain, until the end of the twenty-fourth nāḍī, one should honor the foremost of Brahmins— the guests and others— along with the husband and wife and the maidens.
One should satisfy and feed with devotion those who are emaciated, blind, deaf, impoverished householders, and those who have no other means of subsistence.
The seventy verses on karma, known as the *Naittika*, are to be recited until midday;
they are divine, destroy all sins, and bestow an increase in kingdom and treasury.
O Goddess, it removes all diseases, bestows happiness, destroys the three types of suffering,
brings the three worlds under one's control, and grants the sovereign power of kings.
"At the end of the body, O beloved, it bestows your own form and grants *sāyujya* [union].

Thus ends the exposition on the procedure for the midday daily rites within the Nine Durgās, according to the *Ghaṭibheda*, in the section on daily rituals (*nityakarmakāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīvātulottara*, specifically in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī concerning the *Durgābheda*.
The twentieth chapter [named].
(Page number 182 is missing;
page 183 follows: The network of rituals beginning at dawn and ending at night, as well as the daily rites.
I shall now explain in detail; listen, O you who are born from the mountain.
Having bathed together with the most excellent Brahmins, Āraka, and others,
the supreme preceptor then entered your house amidst the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, and other instruments.
One should then release the door-binding (dvārabandha) after twenty-seven breath-cycles;
having swept and sprinkled, one should then wash the interior and all other parts everywhere.
O lady of excellent vows, having caused the Brahmins to pronounce the "Auspicious Day" with mantras such as the *prājāpatya*,
you should choose the preceptor and others by means of your own root mantra.
One should worship the Guide, the Giver of Wealth, Brahmā the Awakener of All,
and those known as Tvaritā— numbering eleven, like Rudra— as the bearers of the images for the sake of the offering.
For the purpose of praising the meaning of the hymns and for the purpose of worshiping the names, one should appoint five Brahmins each separately;
furthermore, for the purpose of circumambulation and prostration, one should appoint six men of great wealth.
O Caṇḍikā, one should subsequently invite two Brahmins for the Dharmaśāstra, the Purāṇas, and the Nyāyaśāstra, and ten Brahmins for the purpose of surveillance.
Having worshipped the jar named Tvaritā and the one named Śāradā with the essence of nectar,
twenty-one brahmins were then honored according to the prescribed ritual.
(184) Reciting "Namo rudrebhyaḥ" and other mantras preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa),
the twice-born should sprinkle the liṅga with nectar-like fluids and then again with pure water.
At the conclusion, the Guru should worship with the water contained in that jar according to the prescribed rite,
using the *ardhāmbikeśa* mantra and the supreme thousand names.
Numerous offerings of various kinds, including edible foods, milk-rice (pāyasa),
soups, vegetables, and the like, combined with milk, honey, and clarified butter.
Having offered [the offering] into the nineteenth channel from its root,
one should display clusters of lamps and perform the supreme worship with flowers accompanied by mantras.
Then, at the time of *godhūlikā*, at the conclusion of thirty *nāḍīs*,
the Guru, having raised the water-clock (*ghaṭīyantra*), [should act] with the root mantra of that [deity].
Having recited the *gosūkta* while sprinkling [the cows] according to the prescribed ritual,
one should bring those whose limbs are adorned with auspicious marks together with their calves.
Having circumambulated the temple and worshipped it, one should offer the oblation as prescribed;
having worshipped the food offering with the root mantra, one should display a multitude of lamps.
Then, having performed the offering of the five flowers up to the oblation and the lighting of the lamps,
the knower of mantras should again sprinkle [the deity] with nectar-like liquids while reciting the Rātrisūkta.
Furthermore, one should consecrate the *liṅga* separately with the hymn (*sūkta*) of Caṇḍikā, then with the hymn of Vāṇī,
and subsequently with the hymn of Bhuvaneśvarī.
Finally, having sprinkled [the deity] with water from the jar of Vāṇī, one should then worship;
the mantra-practitioner should perform the rite of worship according to the procedure stated in the Vāṇī-kalpa.
One should perform the recitation of the *Pārāyaṇa* in the cardinal directions, as well as the reading of the *Purāṇas* and so forth;
and in the intermediate directions, one should worship the mantras of Caṇḍikā and others, as well as those known as Vāṇī and Vāgīśa.
The *Pratyaṅgirā*, the *Pañcadurgā*, the *Sundarī* which is equal to *Mṛtyu*,
the *Vāstu-mantra* for destroying [evil] influences, and the *Bālakā* known as *Dhāraṇā*.
The Indrākṣī mantra, the Śivakavaca, together with the name of the target (sādhya),
followed by the salutation (nati) and the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa), is said to conclude with the invocation of the spirits (bhūtāhvāna).
First with the names of Caṇḍikā and the names of Śāradā,
then with thousands of names of Vākyanāyikā, and finally with the names of Lalitā.
Having performed worship separately with thousands [of repetitions], he should mutter the root mantra until it is completed;
then, on the thirty-third channel, the Guru should offer various kinds of food offerings (naivedya).
Having offered [the oblation] with the root mantra, one should then whirl the multitude of lamps;
then, having offered five flowers with the root mantra and having bowed according to the prescribed rule.
At the conclusion of that, the practitioner of mantras should perform a great worship (*mahāpūjā*), as well as the array of *nyāsa*s,
the *mātṛkā*, the *golaka-nyāsa*, the *madhyanyāsa*, and the *pīṭhaka*.
Having performed all the rites, beginning with the sixteen-fold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), according to the root text,
and having worshipped the *liṅga* with many leaves, flowers, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

Then, having entered with the utterance "Homage to Her," one should offer to the Goddess an oblation accompanied by incense and lamps, according to the number prescribed for the preliminary service (upacāra).

With the root mantra, one should offer into the fire one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and other offerings, as well as rice, milk, sesame seeds, and the tips of dūrvā grass.
One should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the vyāhṛtis and the root mantra;
then, having given the remainder of the oblation to a cow, it should be accompanied by the residual clarified butter (sampātājya).
Having washed his feet and hands, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra,
the noble one should worship the door and then discard that garment.
Having removed the sacrificial oblation, one should cause the remainder of it to be given to the shaven-headed woman (Muṇḍinī);
and at the conclusion, having offered the propitiatory water-offering (arghya), one should respectfully present betel-leaves.
The worship of the stage (raṅgapūjā) should be performed, especially up to the flagstaff;
it may extend as far as the city limits, the gateway, or ending at the door of the house.
On both sides and all around, one should light many lamps;
the wise practitioner should illuminate a network of lamps reaching as far as the moon-lamp.
Having worshipped the flower with mantras at the conclusion, one should then worship the retinue;
having summoned the bhūtas with the root mantra accompanied by musical instruments such as the jaya-ghaṇṭā and others.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the thirty-eight gurus within the channel by means of their own names,
and having completed it at the conclusion of the bali with the sounds of lutes and trumpets.
Having conducted the image outside for a grand festival accompanied by the sounds of the five musical instruments, and at the conclusion of the festival, together with his own devotees;
O beautiful one, having entered the assembly pavilion at the beginning of the forty *vināḍīs*, I shall describe [the ritual] according to the internal divisions and so forth.
And after Deva is the one called Dīpa; at its end is another called Deśika;
then Vipra, followed by the one called Daṇḍa; and the fifth is said to be Ṛdāhṛta.
O Goddess of the gods, having again placed another deity, one should worship it;
and the two lamp-pillars, known as "Lamps," are on your right and left.
One should place her between the two attendants of the deity, accompanied by three lamp-vessels; O Goddess, likewise, one should place the two bearers of the Guru within the space of the Guru.
Dhanada and Pitāmaha should be established to the left of the Guru;
the astrologer, the minister, and other preeminent Brahmins are stationed [there].

O Goddess, on your back were the disciples of the Guru; on the right side of the rider were the spies; and again, O Goddess, within the interval between the Brahmins on the right were those who had mastered the Vedas.
On the back of the image are the reciters and others; to its left are those who chant hymns;
and in front of you, as well as on both sides, are the expounders of the Dharmaśāstras.
Between the two staffs are two golden staff-bearers who recite hymns;
they are stationed to the right of that [central figure], on the back, and in the region of the left.
The people, established there, pure and having brought offerings and lamps,
stood on level ground in front of you, at a distance of one staff's length below.
O Goddess of the Suras, having measured out the ground five cubits across,
O Devi, on both its sides, those who are restrained in speech [should stand] in the form of rows.
Having led [the deities] individually to their respective positions in the rows, situated at intervals of half a cubit in the center,
according to the sequence and distinguished by their roles as servants and so forth.
The two umbrella-bearers, the two fans of the wind-god, those equipped with auspicious weapons,
the two attendants with staffs and fans, and the two singers whose seed-syllables are associated with the wind.
O Goddess, there are two groups of celestial women endowed with beauty and youth,
holding chowries and bearing betel leaves and vessels for the remains of betel.
Bibhraka carried a water-vessel, while Punarādarśa held a mirror; two mortals bore offerings and lamps, and two men showered down flowers.
The most excellent Brahmins were in the row on the right, while the kings and others were in the row on the left;
the musicians and dancers were in the affectionate [row], and the courtesans were at the dancing platform.
Elephants, horses, and other mounts, adorned with banners, were stationed in two rows;
behind them stood the devoted soldiers, onlookers, and others.
Then, having propitiated the Goddess with chickpeas, fruits,
and various kinds of cooked offerings, the Guru presented ten thousand incense sticks and lamps.
Therefore, one should offer the food oblation (naivedya) and then cause the supreme betel leaf to be given;
likewise, the lamps of the discus known as Bhauma and the ceremony called Padmanīrāja.
One should cause the Goddess to revolve through the Himānta [mantra], followed by worship with *manu* flowers;
then one should recite the network of services (*sevājāla*), the Vedas and so forth, as well as prayers and the like.
Salutations to you, O Mahākālī, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas;
for the sake of increasing the kingdom of the king, listen to this Rig Veda verse, O Pārvatī.
O Mahālakṣmī, salutations to you, who are served by the gods beginning with Brahmā;
for the sake of increasing wealth and the treasury, listen to the mantra of the Yajurveda.
O Sarasvatī, salutations to you who are accompanied by all the hosts of gods;
O beloved, for the sake of fame, splendor, and abundance, listen to this Sāman chant.
O Goddess Maheśvarī, obeisance to you who consist of the three forms;
having heard this verse of the Atharvaṇa, grant me my desired object.
Having caused the Vedas and the Mantras to be recited in sequence, one should offer flowers individually for each;
at the conclusion of each Veda, there should be singing by two singers, and between those, the sounding of a conch.

After that, one should play the five types of musical instruments, beginning with the mouth organ and the cymbals; then follow the rhythmic instrumental accompaniments, and thereafter the dance as taught by Bharata.
The dancer, the drummer, the singer, the flute-player, and likewise the player of the *mauraja* drum— these five are proclaimed as the masters (*ācāryas*).
Women endowed with beauty and youth and skilled in the art of dance,
as well as dancers and musicians, are stationed at your right side.
The singer and the one called Vaṃśaka are stationed on the left side;
in front, to the north, the player of the flute shall likewise play the mouth-organ.
(191) Courtesans endowed with all auspicious marks should perform a dance;
at the conclusion of the dance, they should offer lotus-lamps according to the procedure to be described.
One should have lamp-vessels made of gold, silver, or copper;
they should be one palm-span in measure, circular, and provided with eight petals.
In their center,
the wise one should place nine vessels, or seven, five, three, or even just one, all provided with pericarp-like bases.
O Dear One, having awakened those who are long asleep, one should cause them to revolve three times at the end;
by day and by night, during the worship, the courtesans are eager for the dance.
They should cause [the image] to be carried around three times according to the method prescribed in the science of music;
and at the end of the lamp procession, the musicians should play all the musical instruments.
Furthermore, one should divide ripe chickpeas and other fruits into nine portions,
according to the distinctions of the preceptor (deśika) and others, at the conclusion of the offering of the remains of the deity's meal (nirmālya).
One part [is for] the guide, half a part for the carrier,
two parts for the foremost Brahmins, and likewise for the king and others.
The wielder of the rod should bestow three parts upon the servants and others,
having taken half a part for himself and completed the entire web of service.
p. 192) Having performed the web of service all around... O Dear One, reciting the root mantra there while circumambulating, one should then [enter] your own abode slowly and silently through song.
Having caused the image to enter within for forty-five nāḍīs,
one should cause consciousness to descend from that image into the root-liṅga.
Having again worshipped Maheśvarī with the five offerings and other rites,
[one should offer] milk-rice, as well as preparations from astringent decoctions, together with water and betel.
Having worshipped with your root mantra and performed the *nīrājana* rite known as "snow," the noble one should quickly offer a lamp and perform sacrifice for the sake of [attaining] grace.
Having given a *kṛcchra* penance according to one's ability for any deficiency or excess in the ritual for the sake of the excellent Brahmin,
and having satisfied him, one should then offer the entire web of rites.

O Beloved, one should give the water from the rinsing of the feet and the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering) to the devotees, their families, and the servants and other men at the left side of your *liṅga*.
The Guru should fasten forty-seven door-bolts around the house for its protection; at most, there should be a hundred men.
They should remain awake, and then the supreme man should go home;
one hundred and twenty rites have been correctly described for the middle watch of the night.
O Daughter of the Mountain, it is said that this action always bestows happiness resulting from the attainment of sovereignty, as well as prosperity for kings and their lineages,
throughout all three periods of time.
I shall declare the merit of one who performs this with strict regularity:
in this world, he shall obtain many enjoyments, abundance of food, victory, and fame.
He shall undoubtedly attain the status of a universal monarch for seven births;
and at the end of his body, O captivating one, he shall attain your own form and my own state.
I shall explain the secret therein according to the divisions of the channels at the three times;
it must be performed at each respective time by one who is skilled in ritual action.
If [the rite] is performed after the time has passed, it will be fruitless, leading to famine and the destruction of the kingdom;
therefore, O Pārvatī, having understood this through the division of the channels (nāḍī) as spoken by me.
At the proper time, the preceptor, free from sloth, should correctly perform the entire web of rituals;
O best of men, this rite is to be performed for the seven deities.
The Śāmbhavī [initiation] is performed separately through the distinction of its mantras and the distinction of its ritual actions,
for the sake of attaining the full fruit of one's karma and for the increase of the king's welfare.

(194) O Maheśvarī, I shall now describe in order the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), beginning with wealth and ending with a servant, to be given annually for the purpose of the daily rites at your liṅga.
One should cause one hundred and twenty *niṣkas* to be given to the giver of wealth (*dhanada*),
and one hundred *niṣkas*, along with the materials for the ritual, to the preceptor (*deśika*).
O Goddess, one should cause seventy *niṣkas* to be given to the Brahman priest as the highest gift,
and fifty to the Sadasya, who performs all the rites that bring about awakening.
Forty niṣkas for one who knows astrology and can calculate the time;
thirty niṣkas for one who holds the measure of a ghaṭikā.
Twenty-five niṣkas were given to each of the two reciters of the Dharmaśāstras and Purāṇas; twenty niṣkas were given separately to each of those who proclaimed the four Vedas.
The most excellent lord should give nineteen gold coins (niṣkas) to those who recite the Śrī Rudra, and he should give them separately for their maintenance.
O Goddess of the Suras, eighteen niṣkas have been prescribed for those who recite the hymns;
and for those who worship with your name, eighteen niṣkas are to be given separately.
One should give seventeen *niṣkas* in sequence to the Brahmins for [reciting] the *Saptaśatī* and other texts;
thereafter, one should give a *niṣka* equal in number to the *kalās* (sixty-four) to the reciters (*jāpakas*).
The wise one should give [offerings] equal in number to the lunar days to those who perform circumambulations and prostrations,
and separately to those who worship the jars, along with the appropriate materials.
Beyond that, fourteen niṣkas are prescribed for the jailers;
and separately for the two wielders of the staff, twelve niṣkas are declared.
One should cause ten *niṣkas* to be given for umbrellas and likewise for cloth garments;
for those who carry staffs and fans, one should cause nine *niṣkas* to be given.
Twenty niṣkas each for the two singers and the two seed-sowers;
for the courtesans, the fly-whisks and other items are said to be six niṣkas each.
Furthermore, the most excellent lord took five niṣkas from the people of Bali and Dvīpa,
and four niṣkas from those who offered incense smoke.
Then, O beautiful one, having given three *niṣkas* each to the bards who caused the rain of flowers,
and separately to the panegyrists and the reciters;
Ten *niṣkas* should be given, and furthermore one hundred and fifty *niṣkas*;
one should also give separate wages to the musicians and those skilled in dance.
To the Vaijantīs she gave earrings, and to her beloveds, neck-ornaments; to the guards, she gave twelve distinct gifts each, such as elephants, horses, and other riches.
One should give twelve [offerings] to the guardians of the gates and so forth,
and thirteen to the guardians of the treasury, garments, and wealth.
One should cause nine *niṣkas* to be given to those who prepare the food for guests and others,
and fourteen to the attendants and the worshippers on all sides.
Having given one *niṣka* separately at the end, one should satisfy the people in many ways;
O Goddess of the Mountain, one should give seven *niṣkas* to the guardians of your house and others.
O Goddess, I have explained everything regarding the sacrificial fees for those performing the rites,
as well as the wages for all attendants, such as spies and servants, in their proper order.

Having thus given these offerings every year according to the rules and having gratified the great people, one should bow with devotion and cause them to recite: "The rite of prostration must be performed."
The preceptor must never perform the ritual duties deficiently at the proper times;
for if they are performed deficiently when the time has arrived, the royal prosperity will perish.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, the mantra-practitioner, having understood this repeatedly for the welfare of all the world,
[should perform it] for the sake of increasing wealth, grain, and so forth, and for the sake of abundant food.
O Daughter of the Mountain, for the sake of the prosperity of the kingdom or even for the sake of all enjoyments, the entire network of rituals must be performed without omission.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Exposition of the Night-Rite for the Nine Durgās," within the section on daily rites in the *Durgā-bheda* of the *Śrī-Vātulottara*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī concerning the division of the *ghaṭī*.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of grace upon the world!
I have heard the procedure for the daily worship of my linga, beginning from morning.
O Lord, you have spoken correctly for the benefit of all the world;
now I wish to hear concerning the purpose of rites for specific desires and for the practitioner.
"O Supreme Lord, the ritual procedure for occasional worship must be told.
Śiva said: I shall tell you all of that which has been asked by you."
O Goddess, listen with a one-pointed mind to the detailed procedure for worshipping you specifically within your own linga for the sake of fulfilling desires.
It brings about all kinds of prosperity in the world, confers glory, and grants sons and grandsons;
it pacifies untimely death, and victory over enemies shall be attained.
(198) O Goddess, it pacifies all diseases and increases the lifespan of men; for practitioners in the Kali age, success is achieved through you and not by any other means.
By mere remembrance and by sight alone, the three worlds trembled;
when the Liṅga is worshipped with devotion, the three worlds shall come under one's control.
O Śivā, it bestows upon men their contemplated goals and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform your worship for the sake of desired objects.
On which lunar day and in what worship shall I speak? Listen, O Pārvatī! [It may be] in the month of Māgha, or Phālguna, Caitra, or the month of Vaiśākha.
In the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āśvayuja, and Kārttika, on an auspicious day,
the second, fifth, eighth, and ninth lunar days are especially favorable.
The tenth, thirteenth, fourteenth, and full moon days;
and when the Moon, Jupiter, or Venus are in conjunction with Tuesday, it shall be auspicious.
When the moon and stars are favorable, one should gather the materials for worship;
having risen in the morning and performed the daily worship according to the rules.
O beloved, accompanied by Brāhmaṇas, local guides, and others,
one should perform a bath in the river, preceded by the six-cornered [mantra] and its seed-syllable.
Having written [the mantra], one should perform the libation for the sake of bathing in the midst of the sacred ford;
having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for your pleasure, one should immerse oneself three times.
Clad in washed garments and adorned with ashes and other ornaments,
one should recite the root mantra there twenty-eight times.
O Caṇḍikā, having filled a golden vessel or similar container with that holy water while reciting your root mantra, and taking it along with the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra;
Having adorned the temple with auspicious recitations from the Vedas, with dances, songs, and instrumental music, and with arches made of fruits and sprouts;
Having performed the purification of the ground by sprinkling it with fragrant waters,
and having adorned the house and entered it, one should worship the supreme Śivā.
Salutations to you, O auspicious Goddess Śivā, bestower of desired objects;
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, grant me permission for the purpose of performing this occasional worship.
Having thus prayed with true devotion, one should place a fruit before him;
and having worshipped Gaṇeśa for the sake of removing obstacles, one should begin.
Having recited the *nāndī* and the *puṇyāha*, one should perform the purification of the ritual materials;
for the sake of the rite, the wise man should select the preceptor (*deśika*) and other excellent brahmins.
p. 200) One should perform the *karmajāla* [ritual], the *Śrīrudra*, and the *Pāvamāna*;
the *Lakṣmīsūkta* should also be performed according to the procedure prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
One should sprinkle the *liṅga* according to the ritual procedure for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
The quantity of the substance is said to range from one *prastha* up to one *droṇa*.
The practitioner of mantras should sprinkle [the linga] according to the prescribed rite; this constitutes the purification of the linga.
One should fashion an excellent lotus in front of the deity and in the northeast direction.
O Goddess, one should establish one hundred and eight, or half of that (fifty-four),
or twenty-five, or nine, twelve, or five excellent jars.
Thereafter, one should fill the Ratnāṅgī according to the prescribed rite with fragrant waters,
milk, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), decoctions, and excellent oil.
With various fruits and waters, together with garments and images,
one should invoke the deity at the end of the fourth [syllable] of the mantra and worship Him.
Having touched [the disciple] with the *kalā-mantras* and the root-mantras (*mūla-mantra*), the most excellent Guru should perform the recitation (*japya*) for Gaṇeśa,
Kṣetrapāla, Mṛtyuñjaya, and the nine planets.
O Śivā, the Guru should recite the Adhōrāstra-mantra seven hundred times, the Navadurgā-mantra seven hundred times,
and the Mūla-mantra one thousand times.
O Dear One, one should perform one hundred and eight circumambulations and prostrations;
furthermore, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila), especially in the northeastern quarter.
Having established the fire of generation (jananāgni), one should perform oblations with the root mantra;
thereafter, the Guru should offer half of that amount using the Śāntidurgā mantra.
O Goddess, one hundred and eight [offerings] is the minimum, while one thousand is the best;
one should perform the fire-oblation with seven substances, such as sacrificial wood, clarified butter, or milk-rice.
One should perform the offering with the root mantra using fragrant water mixed with milk;
then one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
The supreme sage should bathe your linga with water from a jar,
performing the ritual bath with various fragrant and captivating oils.
O Maheśvarī, having rubbed [the body] with powders of ground flour mixed with turmeric at night,
and having bathed it with warm water, one should apply water scented with musk and saffron.
Having anointed [him] with the eight fragrances and beautiful unbroken grains of rice,
he should apply a tilaka-mark made of musk, turmeric powder, and collyrium.
Then one should offer two garments made of fine silk cloth, joined with gold and produced from nine threads, and one should likewise worship a bodice.
One should offer ear-ornaments inlaid with pearls and lapis lazuli, along with other decorations,
fragrant flower garlands, and betel with flowers.
Having performed the invocation and other rites, and having worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings,
one should worship with thousands of names preceded by the syllable Om.
The best among those who know mantras should worship with bilva leaves, lotuses, droṇa flowers, sesame seeds, unbroken rice grains, and flowers such as mallikā.
At the conclusion of that, O Goddess, one should offer a golden [image] according to one's capacity,
as well as incense, a lamp, and an offering of food consisting of the six flavors along with various snacks.
O Goddess, one should offer various kinds of fruits accompanied by soups and vegetables,
as well as water with camphor and betel leaf.
The supreme guru should offer blue collyrium, mantra-flowers, and the recitation of hymns;
thereafter, he should especially offer the bali-oblation during the obligatory rites.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should feed as many Brahmins as there are oblations;
first, one should worship couples and nine married women whose husbands are living.
O Goddess, a thousand is the highest [number], or separately one hundred and eight;
these should be joined with the wife of the guru and women who observe the vow of devotion to their husbands.
Having performed an oil massage and then become pure, [one should place them] individually upon excellent pedestals in the form of rows all around your temple.
Having sat down according to the rule, one should perform the worship of the guru;
and having worshipped my form, as well as your form endowed with [all attributes].
Having invoked Śiva and Śakti, one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and so forth,
as well as garments and ornaments, separately for each of the two.
Having worshipped them in due order according to the extent of one's wealth,
one should then present an offering of supreme rice-milk (paramānna) with sugar.
"O Goddess, may Caṇḍikā be pleased with this cake and fruit";
then, O beloved, one should perform the worship of the married women (suvāsinīs) with devotion.
O Pārvatī, one should perform the invocation, the offering of water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, individually with the Thousand Names,
either one hundred and eight times or nine times.

One should worship the Tava-mantra one hundred and eight times and worship the nine Durgās; having worshipped each individually with their names in the dative case, one should cause [the offerings] to be given.
O Goddess, [one should offer] a coconut fruit together with betel leaves,
areca nut, flowers, turmeric root, rice, and garments and so forth.
The Guru, reciting the root mantra, should devoutly give a fine garment;
and having given it out of affection for you, he should then receive the blessing.
One should feed [the deities] with various kinds of food, edibles, and the like, and offer betel-leaf individually;
thereafter, one should worship at night and perform the worship of the colored powders (raṅgapūjā).
O beloved, having brought the lamp to the archways and other places where a beautiful light arises,
one should then offer the bali-oblation and present the oblation (āhuti) for the occasional rite (naimittika).
In a chariot, or a palanquin, or in a decorated vehicle,
he should then hold a festival as far as the boundary of the village.
Having entered and worshipped the Goddess, one should offer the *kriyājāla*.
Then, having risen at dawn, [one should perform] bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and the libations (*tarpaṇa*).
O Maheśvarī, having constructed a temple for your liṅga,
the practitioner of mantras should worship it and perform its ablution, O Mother, in order to avoid the omission of ritual duties.
The preceptor should then mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
thereafter, he should give a cow along with its calf, and the preceptor should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
"Thereafter, one should give abundant gifts, and after that, gifts for the sake of relief from distress;
in this manner, O best of kings, the Brāhmaṇa should cause it to be performed with devotion."
(205) It swiftly bestows desired objects; this I have spoken as the truth, the absolute truth.
Whatever task is conceived in the mind is accomplished through worship and its power.
When the beloved is worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one attains all desires;
this complete procedure for the great worship has been taught out of affection for you.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Occasional Worship," in the section on daily rites within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, in the *Durgā-bheda* of the *Śrīvātulottara*.
May there be well-being.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, omniscient one, treasury of compassion;
O Śiva, rich in inconceivable qualities and form, Lord of the entire world!
O Sadāśiva, you have explained the secret procedure for the fire-oblation (vahnihoma) pertaining to the seven crores of mantras, as well as for the consecrations and festivals.
Tell me how there is a separate injunction for the fire and how the oblation is performed;
for what purpose is it, how is the *homa* conducted, what are the materials, and what is the fruit thereof?
p. 206) "I wish to hear from your own mouth; speak in detail, O Lord.
Śiva said: "Well asked by you, O Goddess! This is a great secret, more secret than the secret."
The fire-ritual is the best of rites for the gods, bestowing the fruits of all desires;
my fire, consisting of radiant energy, is your very form—of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, by means of the tongue as our form, each respective substance is indeed consumed;
O Beloved, even when consumed elsewhere, satisfaction arises upon seeing it.
For this reason, O Goddess, one should cause the excellent fire-oblation (vahnihoma) to be performed by a twice-born man; it is a supreme secret that bestows liberation.
If the best of the twice-born should eat food offered by a Śūdra,
he will undoubtedly fall into the state of a Śūdra, become devoid of ritual action, and incur a state of outcasting.
The best of the twice-born should perform the daily fire-oblation every evening and morning;
by doing so, he attains happiness in this world and, in the end, proximity to the Lord, O Goddess.
One should perform rites for specific desires (kāmyakarman) ranging from one hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma) up to ten million;
O Maheśvarī, the number of recitations (japa) of that mantra shall be ten times the number of oblations.
One should perform a libation (tarpaṇa) one hundred times, worship a thousand water-pots (kumbha),
feed ten thousand Brahmins, and perform circumambulations and prostrations.
One should give various gifts, especially cows, land, and so forth;
thus should one who knows the ritual procedure perform everything for the warding off of death.
It brings about all-encompassing peace and is the cause of the destruction of enemies;
it bestows longevity and health upon the body, and increases vitality and strength.
It bestows prosperity especially, increases progeny and the like,
grants satisfaction and nourishment, and augments the kingdom and treasury of kings.
It increases elephants, horses, troops, fortresses, and the like, as well as fame;
it likewise destroys celestial and atmospheric portents, evil dreams, and other such calamities.
It is the supreme destroyer of planets, spirits, piśācas, and the like;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants the fruits of all desires.
By this rite of oblation, great delight shall be mine;
when I am satisfied, the gods beginning with Brahmā are likewise satisfied—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, in the Kali age, the rite of fire-offering (homa) is the most excellent bestower of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
Therefore, a person of means should perform the fire-offering with every possible effort.

I shall now describe its procedure separately according to the methods for the *lakṣahoma* sacrifice, including the appropriate time, the location, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and so forth, along with their defining characteristics.
O beloved, listen in detail to the number of days for that rite, the preceptors and other officiating priests (ṛtvij), the materials for the oblation, and its fruit.
O Maheśvarī, one should perform [the rite] in the month of Kārttika on the full moon day or on a Monday,
and in the month of Māgha on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
One should perform it on the eighth or tenth day of the month of Phālguna,
or on the thirteenth or eleventh day of the month of Caitra.
On the third day of Vaiśākha, on an auspicious day in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
or on another meritorious lunar date, or during an eclipse of the sun or moon, the practitioner [should perform the rite].
When there is no lunar confusion (amāvasyā) or intercalary month, when the moon and stars are favorable,
when the auspicious ascendant is joined by benefic planets and devoid of malefic planets.
And when the asterism is favorable to the performer and is aspected by auspicious planets—
during such a time endowed with these qualities— one should cause the Lakṣahoma to be performed.
In the sacred field of Śiva marked by the Liṅga, in a grove, on a mountain, on a bank, in a garden, in the house of a Vedic scholar, at a confluence, and on the shore of a river;
O Goddess, the best of kings should perform a *homa* at another sacred site (*puṇyasthala*),
having first inspected that location in the east, the southeast, or the northeast.
One should perform the digging and other rites, purifying the site while avoiding what is defective;
having made it square and level, measuring thirty-six cubits.
O Dear One, the pavilion's width should be twenty-one cubits, or ten plus seven (seventeen),
up to the measurement required for the sacrificial pit.
O Maheśvarī, it should be one cubit (ratni) in height, resembling the surface of a mirror, and occupy one-third of the area of the pavilion.
The mantra-practitioner should fashion nine, five, or even just one sacrificial pits;
that in the east should be square, while that in the southeast is shaped like a vulva.
In the south, however, it is a half-moon; in the southwest, a triangle;
in the west, a circular pit; and in the northwest, a hexagon.

To the north, however, there should be a lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa), while in the northeast there is an eight-cornered one; between the directions of Indra and Śaṅkara (the east and northeast), one should cause a circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) to be made.
One should cause four square pits to be made in the four directions, and likewise a circular pit in the northeast; or, O Śiva, there may be five pits.
O Maheśvarī, one should construct a single pit, either circular or square, and arrange it in the northeast or the eastern part.
A single pit shall be four cubits [in extent], five pits three cubits, and nine pits two cubits; such is the measurement for the excavation.
The width [of the altar] should extend upwards along with the upper girdle;
the girdle should be of the same form as that of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
And it should be provided with three girdles measuring eight, six, and four finger-breadths respectively for a handspan of two,
three, and likewise four cubits.
In the middle above the girdle, however, there is a vulva-shaped [receptacle] like a pipal leaf;
it is six finger-breadths in width, and half that width above it.
In this manner, by increasing the fingers of the fist and likewise those of the others,
[the measure] is one finger in height and eight fingers in width.
For this place of the *praṇītā* water is indeed the place of Brahmā; thus it should be made square, and within the *praṇītā* area, there should be a lotus for Brahmā.
Having thus prepared the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed characteristics, O Maheśvarī,
one should not perform it on a mere leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), for that would result in the displeasure of the deities.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed without the proper characteristics will cause the destruction of the lineage;
therefore, a wise person should construct the pit according to the procedure previously described.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar measuring one cubit;
above that, in its center, there should be four pillars, and around them, twelve [pillars] in sequence.
Outside of that, there should be twenty pillars, eight of which are elevated by six cubits;
outside of that, it should be five cubits wide, and one should establish it with cloth-canopies and other such decorations.
O Śivā, one should have a pavilion constructed on either a single or three levels,
provided with four doors and adorned with four archways.
At the eastern gate there is the yellow-colored one, at the southern the black-colored one,
at the western the red-colored one, and at the northern the white-colored one.
O Dear One, one should fashion the gateway in this manner, marked with the signs of the wheel, trident, *ḍamaru* drum, lotus, and *nandi*, according to the sequence starting from the east.

One should place a banner in each of the four directions, and flags should be situated in their respective quarters. The staff of the banner should be ten cubits long, and it may be either square or circular in shape.
The banners should be seven cubits in length according to the measurement of their staffs;
the cloth for the seven-cubit flag should be made of new fabric.
The preceptor should have the artisan engrave the respective emblems of the mounts;
O Maheśvarī, the banners should be twenty finger-breadths in width.

The preceptor should fashion and install the guardians of the world (lokapālas) in the cardinal and intermediate directions according to the prescribed rite, using their respective descriptions, vehicles, weapons, and emblems.
One should cover the high [pillars] with cloths, adorned with canopies and fruits;
and at every door, there should be two jars, with two jars at the base of the archway.
Each was richly adorned with the beauty of mango sprouts and had a sweet-voiced bird dwelling upon its neck;
they were further decorated with arrangements of plantain trunks, garlands, and strings of mango shoots.
Having adorned it on the outside, one should subsequently encircle it with a garland of *darbha* grass;
in this manner, O beloved, one should construct the pavilion and the sacrificial pits according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the Lakṣahoma for nine days, seven nights, five nights, three nights, or even a single day; this may be either the best or the middling [type].
O Śivā, one should not perform the lowest act during the prescribed number of days;
[one should instead practice] shaving, bathing, silence, wearing white garments, and remaining pure.
The preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should constantly subsist on a diet of milk and rice, avoid all forms of bad association, and observe the vow of celibacy.
O Maheśvarī, initiation should be performed in this manner during the Navarātra;
however, one should not perform the rite of initiation during a Trirātra or an Ekarātra.

Having procured the materials for the sacrifice, [the officiant]— initiated, knowing the essence of the ritual, truthful, and having conquered his senses— [should employ] the reciters (jāpaka) and the twice-born priests (hotṛ).
Having invited the best of the twice-born along with their wives, the sacrificer,
accompanied by the preceptor and the officiating priests, performed the oil massage and other preliminary rites.
O Maheśvarī, having carefully determined an auspicious time according to what was previously stated,
one should rise in the morning and perform the ritual washing of the teeth according to the rules.
The best of the twice-born should perform their morning bath and,
having completed their daily obligatory rites, perform the twilight ritual for the sake of the teacher.
Having first performed a bath with clay, one should smear [the body] with water mixed with *kuśa* grass and cow dung,
accompanied by all the sounds and the respective mantra.

Having performed the ritual bath accompanied by various auspicious musical instruments, the sounds of the Vedas, and hymns of praise, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should then [proceed] with the best of the twice-born for the sake of the fire-oblation (homa).
Clad in washed garments and adorned with auspicious unguents and other ornaments,
having performed the libations to the divine sages and paid obeisance to the Sun, he [proceeded].
Then, O Goddess, having constructed a temple, the patron, with great devotion, should place fruits, flowers, and gold before me.
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should pray with palms joined in reverence;
this shall immediately bring satisfaction to all the gods, beginning with Śiva.
One should make a formal request to the master, saying, "I shall perform the Lakṣahoma";
having thus informed the Lord of Devas, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
Having washed his hands and feet either in the east or in the northeast,
he should place a lotus-seat and set it upon a new cloth.
Having placed [the seed-syllables] upon that and sat down on the seats,
one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), preceded by the salutation to the Guru and other preliminary rites.
Having designated the day and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the extent of one's means,
one should worship Vighneśa, perform the Nāndī-śrāddha and other rites, as well as the Puṇyāha-vācana and the offering of Pañcagavya.
Then, having prepared the madhuparka offering, one should invite the preceptor and the others—
the teacher (ācārya), O Goddess, the patron (adhvarku), the priest (brahmā), and the member of the assembly (sadasyaka).

Having ascertained the number of days for the eight guardians of the forms (mūrtipas), beginning with Bhava, along with the Hotṛ priests, according to the prescribed rule, one should choose them individually.
O Śivā, for the purpose of recitation (japa), there should be fifty [verses] for the complete study of the Veda;
sixteen Brahmins should perform [the rite], and ten twice-born men for the purpose of libation (tarpaṇa).
In the worship of the water-pot (*kumbha*), there is likewise one [offering] for the prostration and circumambulation;
you should choose ten Brahmins for the rite, and twelve twice-born ones for the worship.
Having announced the lineage (*pravara*) and clan (*gotra*) of the preceptor and others according to his own *śākhā* and so forth,
the performer should then choose them in due order with these verses beginning with "Śarma."
O best of the twice-born, you are capable of bearing the burden of all rites for the satisfaction of Śiva;
therefore, I choose you as my preceptor and teacher in this rite of fire-offering.

But if there is a substitute for the patron, the preceptor should appoint another twice-born man at his command, using this very verse: śrīsomeśvaradevena yajamānena dhīmatā | yadanyo vṛta ācāryastasmai dattaṃ svakaṃ phalam || "By the wise sacrificer Śrī Someśvaradeva, whatever other preceptor has been chosen, to him is given my own fruit."
O twice-born one, I choose you as a representative of the performer to have the rite performed for the sake of the patron in that sacrificial oblation ceremony.
Just as the four-faced Brahmā, the Grandfather, resides in the heavenly world,
so do I choose Brahmā himself in person for this rite of oblation.
O Brahmin, so that no violations of the mantras, tantras, and other rites may be observed, I appoint you as the presiding member (sadasya) in this fire-offering ceremony.
For the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), I appoint you, O twice-born priests, as the officiants in this rite of oblation for the root-mantras and the specific mantras of Śiva.
O Maheśvarī, for the purpose of libation and worship of the pitcher,
for the sake of reciting the root mantra, and for the purpose of the complete study of the Vedas.
"I choose you, O twice-born ones, for the purpose of circumambulation and prostration.
Having thus performed the formal invitation, he should offer them water for the feet and other honors.
Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and likewise the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
as well as earrings, rings, and various other ornaments.
O Goddess, he was adorned with a crown of rudrākṣa beads and other ornaments, with a golden sacred thread, silken garments, sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and celestial attendants.
O Śivā, one should cause water for sipping, water-vessels, sacrificial implements, fruit, gold, and betel-leaf to be offered with the mantra.
Having thus offered [the vessel] to the preceptor with the root mantra, the Gāyatrī, and the five Brahma-mantras, he should present it along with perfumes and other offerings.
In this manner, he should satisfy the Brahman, the Sadasyas, and other twice-born men in due order,
with garments, ornaments, and other gifts as is appropriate for each.
Then, preceded by the planting of sprouts, one should fetch earth;
or, O Śivā, one may produce sprouts immediately for a duration measured by the number of days.
O Dear One, one should erect the banners as previously described for the installation of the flagstaff;
then one should perform the sacrifice of the bull and [worship] the deities of the banners and the flagstaff.
O Pārvatī, having worshipped according to the rules with their respective mantras,
the practitioner of mantra should finally offer oblations of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as to Gaṇeśa and the nine planets.
Each respective substance should be offered separately with its corresponding root mantra;
O Maheśvarī, the Guru should perform this rite during the daytime.
Then, having performed the evening twilight devotions and become pure, the supreme guru,
having washed his hands and feet with the best of the twice-born who were holding the ritual vessels for water, [proceeded].
O Maheśvarī, having entered the sacrificial hall through the western door,
one should then gaze with the weapon-vision (astradṛṣṭi) upon the guardians of the directions and the protective boundary.
Having approached the south-western direction and sat upon his seat,
O Śivā, the Guru should perform the binding of the directions, beginning with the salutation to the Guru.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the various ritual placements (nyāsajālān), and the formal resolve (saṅkalpa),
one should worship Gaṇeśa upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
O Goddess, one should place the jar and mix it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya):
one part cow urine and half that amount of cow dung.
Cow's milk is prescribed as seven parts, curd as three parts, and clarified butter as one part;
thus [the mixture is prepared] with the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.
Having touched [the object] with the Astra-mantra, one should recite it one hundred and eight times;
thereafter, the Guru, together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij), should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be proclaimed.
O Goddess, the preceptor should sweep the pavilion with the Vāyu mantra using Palāśa sprouts and Darbha grass, starting from the southeast and ending at the northeast.
The preceptor should smear the lines with cow-dung water while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra,
and then [sprinkle] the lines one hundred times with the Astra mantra.
Having scattered [the flowers], the best of men should sweep the pavilion with his fist;
O Goddess of Gods, he should then wash his hands and scatter flowers in the ten directions.
Having placed [it] down, one should display the *cakramudrā* with my *gāyatrī*,
together with a cord, a *darbha* garland, and sprouts from the Bodhi tree.
O Śivā, having recited the weapon-mantra one hundred times,
the preceptor should sprinkle the pavilion with the five products of the cow using the root-mantra and then encircle it.
Having scattered [the offerings], the practitioner should perform the sprinkling again with the previously mentioned mantra;
then the Guru, having sprinkled it with scented water, [recites] "May the Waters Purify."

Thereafter, O Dear One, having sprinkled the doors with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, one should worship them with unbroken rice (*akṣata*), flowers, and so forth, proceeding in order from the east.
One should place Śānti, Bhūti, Bala, and Ārogya at the arches (toraṇas) by means of their respective names;
one should worship the couples above on the tridents as previously described for the sun.
[He saw] Praśānta, Śiśira, and the others, as well as the Vasus beginning with Pratyūṣa;
the worlds beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ; and the planets beginning with Soma and Bhauma.
One should place Śānti and Nidrānivṛtti at the top of the door of Pratiṣṭhā;
and one should install Gaṇeśa, Bhāratī, and Lakṣmī above all the doors.
Beginning from the eastern gate,
one should place Nandin and the other door-keepers, as well as the rivers such as the Gaṅgā, upon the right and left sides of Śiva.
Having honored them with their names in the dative case, he should then proclaim the knowledge of Śiva:
"For the sake of protecting the sacrifice, you must remain here with great devotion."
O Goddess, one should place the vajra and other symbols as banners, and the kumuda and others upon the standards; these should be arranged as previously described, causing fear to all obstructors.
Having worshipped the door and the archway, the Guru should pray with this [mantra];
O Dear One, he should then begin the worship of the pillars of the pavilion.
In all the internal pillars, one should worship the [deities] beginning with Ādhāra and ending with Dharma, in their proper order, using mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
O Dear One, one should install and worship the Vidyeshas and others, the pitchers at these [locations], the door-arches and the water-jars, as well as Yageshvara and the guardians of the directions.
The Guru should place images made of gold weighing one *niṣka* or half a *niṣka*;
having placed fine garments and auspicious fruits, the best of preceptors should offer his prayer.
O Śakra, by the command of Śiva, you must remain vigilant in your own quarter until the end of the sacrifice in order to pacify all obstacles.
Having thus informed all the world-protectors through various ritual sequences, one should then pray to the Lord of the Sacrifice.
Salutations to you, Śaṅkara, who assumes the universal form;
this Lakṣahoma has been performed by me for your sake.
"You must now observe [the rite] until its completion," he said,
having thus entreated the Lord of Sacrifice and scattered unbroken grains of rice over him.
Therefore, O Goddess, having worshipped the site (vāstu) and performed the Vāstu-homa which destroys Rākṣasas,
the most excellent Guru should scatter the sacrificial offerings (bali) with their respective mantras.
Then, having tied on the protective amulet (pratisara) for the sake of the sacrifice as previously described,
[one should honor] the preceptor (ācārya), the patron (yajamāna), the officiant (brahmā), and the member of the assembly (sadasyaka).
O Goddess, the image-worshippers should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) upon the statues of Yāgeśa and others;
they should bind them with woolen threads while reciting that mantra as previously described.
Thereafter, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should perform the fire-ritual;
one who knows the best kind of wood should use that produced from sun-crystal (sūryakānta), while one who is mediocre may use other [kinds].
Fire originating from the house of a Vedic scholar is proclaimed to be the lowest;
or [fire] from a sun-crystal stone, O Śivā, or from a Bodhi tree and the like.
Having taken the essential parts and prepared two mortars,
one should perform the union in sequence according to the method prescribed in the treatises of the artisans.
One should wrap it very firmly with a cord three cubits long, tripled [in thickness],
and smear the ground with cow dung, making it a hundred-petaled lotus with a beautiful pericarp.
One should draw and fill the powder in five distinct colors;
O Maheśvarī, one should fill the pedestal with a *droṇa* measure of *śāli* rice.
The preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should place the fire-drill (araṇi) upon the pedestal, encircle it with a cord of *darbha* grass,
and worship it thoroughly with perfumes and flowers.
O Maheśvarī, having invoked both of us and performed the rites up to the offering of food (naivedya),
one should perform the recitation of the root mantra along with the hymns beginning with the Pañcabrahma.
Having churned [the fire] with the *praṇava* using husks, cotton seeds, and so forth,
and having combined it with cow dung and the sparks produced from the fire, etc., [one should proceed].
Then the mantra-practitioner should ignite [the fire] in a copper vessel or a shallow bowl;
he should awaken the consciousness with the fire-seed syllable (raṃ) and the heart-mantra using the saṃhāra-mudrā.

Having taken [it], one should join it with the *bindu* by means of inhalation (*pūraka*); then, O Goddess, one should establish it in the heart with the mantra, and [establish] fire with the *citimanttra*.
Having thus meditated upon the fire as being of the nature of radiance, manifestly the very essence of Brahman, the practitioner of mantra should then worship that consumer of oblations.
Thereafter, the preceptor should cause [the vessel] to be given to the patron with devotion;
then, having lifted it up with the mantra "devasya tvā," he should give it to the officiating priests.
"O best of the twice-born, O Maheśvarī, [this] must be protected for the sake of the fire-oblation.
Having said this, he stood with his palms joined in reverence toward the patron of the sacrifice.
One should honor the preceptor by giving him a bed, a vehicle, and ornaments;
one should also give a cow to the officiating priests, or otherwise, one should give garments.
O Goddess of the gods, by giving in this manner, the Fire-god becomes well-pleased;
thereafter, one should perform a vigil followed by the recitation of the Vedas by the best of the twice-born.
Having performed it thus, O Goddess of Gods, [one should act] again near sunrise.
