Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Pavilion for the Lakṣahoma and Other Rites," in the section on Optional Rites (Kāmyakāṇḍa) within the Śrī-Vātulottara, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the ritual instruments,
preceded by the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the rite of generating the fire.
O Pārvatī, listen now to the sequential procedure for the consecration of the vessels.
The preceptor, having become pure and performed his daily rites, [should proceed].
O Goddess of the Gods, having entered the sacrificial hall together with the officiating priests,
one should first worship Gaṇeśa and then satisfy him with offerings of fruit and other such things.

The officiant, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) together with the image-protectors (mūrtipas), who are the best of the twice-born, should perform the Puṇyāhavācana while seated upon a grass mat (viṣṭara) facing the east.
Having sat down and gathered the necessary ritual implements,
one should perform the purification of oneself, beginning with the salutation to the Guru.
Then, having performed the network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*) upon the limbs using the *juhvāṅga* mantra,
the most excellent teacher should thereafter worship his own gurus upon the crown of his head.
One should worship the Lord in the heart-lotus and then honor Gaṇeśa;
one should perform the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the method that will be described.
Reciting the root mantra, the practitioner should gaze upon that sacrificial pit;
then, having struck it with the weapon mantra, he should perform the binding of the ten directions.
O Śivā, having sprinkled the armor with the *tāra* (OM) mantra, the practitioner should then dig up the earth with the mantra:
"O Earth, destroy [impurities]! and thereafter extract the soil.
The practitioner of mantra should worship with the heart-mantra and with the seed-syllable of equalizing vision;
he should sprinkle [the site] with this [mantra], and perform the pounding with the weapon-mantra.
Then one should perform the cleansing with the Kavaca mantra and the smearing with the Heti mantra;
O Śivā, the formation of the triple thread is performed by means of the Kalās, which consist of the Kalās.
The practitioner of mantra should worship with the Kavaca mantra and the Hṛdaya mantra, O Pārvatī;
then, with the Astra mantra, he performs the vajrīkaraṇa (the rite of making [the site] adamantine), and subsequently with the Hṛdaya mantra using kuśa grass.
One should protect the crossroads with the armor-mantra and the grinding of the dice.
Thus, O Maheśvarī, these are the eighteen purifications of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having first made the sacrificial pit square in the center with sand,
one should [draw the lines] with a moistened stick while reciting the mantra "devasya tvā."
Having taken [the cord], one should draw a line with its tip toward the east and another with its tip toward the north;
likewise, there should be three lines facing east and similarly three facing north.
Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Soma are in the middle, on the right and left [sides];
Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Śakra are in the middle, on the west and east [sides].
O Goddess, for the purpose of purifying the ground here, the practitioner of mantra should draw six lines in due order upon the *nāka* using the *brahmajajñāna* mantra.
Then one should worship it by name alone with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
thereafter, having extracted the yantra, [one places it] with its lines pointing eastward and northward.
O Maheśvarī, when there are forty-nine squares and so forth, that yantra is then indistinct;
[it begins] from the outer northeast square and extends to its center.
Having inscribed the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) with its phonemes, the preceptor, moving clockwise,
[draws] in the center of that an eight-petaled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments.
Then, for the purpose of a seat, one should prepare a fine *kūrca* made of twenty blades of *darbha* grass;
having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*) right there, one should invoke the Supreme Puruṣa.
Then, O beloved, one should meditate on the Guru at the side of the Great Goddess—
two-eyed, two-armed, beautiful, with full and sloping breasts.
Adorned with pearl ornaments, holding a lotus in her hand, and possessing beautiful eyes;
resembling pure crystal and embellished by a red lower garment.
[He should place] the woman who has bathed after her menses, seated upon a fine grass mat to the left of Vāgīśa,
[before] the God who is the cause of the worlds, the omniscient witness of all.
Having thus meditated upon Him who is without beginning or end, pure, and manifest in the form of Brahman itself, and having worshipped Him, O Maheśvarī, the practitioner of mantra [should proceed].
O Pārvatī, having worshipped the two gods of gods with the root mantra,
one should offer water for the feet, the arghya offering, and so forth, as well as saffron and red sandalwood.
O Dear One, having worshipped the red lotuses with incense, lamps, and so forth,
one should then [proceed] with the seed-syllable of Śiva, preceded by *Tāra* (Om) and ending with *Namaḥ*.
One should meditate upon that which has attained oneness with the earth;
one should display the *dyotini* mudrā and likewise the *liṅga* mudrā with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
In this manner, one should contemplate [the deity] with the mind and display it for the sake of play;
then, as long as there is delight for the two, so long should the Guru [offer] fire.
With his hand wet with water, he should wipe the generative organ [of the deity] while reciting the weapon-mantra;
thereafter, he should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) to both the God and the Goddess.
For the protection of the fetus, one should tie *darbha* grass upon the hand like a bracelet;
having combined it with three *darbha* blades, one should bind it while reciting the root mantra.
Then, O Maheśvarī, having taken from the preceptor’s wife and the officiating priests the consecrated fire, which is free from ash, smoke, and the like;
Having placed [the fire] in the womb of the sacrificial pit with the mantra "devasya tvā," the practitioner of mantra,
while reciting the seed-syllable of fire, should abandon the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda).
Having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra and gazed upon the right foot and other parts with the Vīkṣaṇa-mantras, one should perform the drying,
burning, and fanning [of impurities] with that same mantra, O Pārvatī.
Then the Guru [performs] the contraction, blazing outwardly with the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī];
it is the second letter of the *va*-group, adorned with the *bindu*.
This is declared to be the seed-syllable of fire; reciting it three times and visualizing it as having emerged there, one should join it with the internal *nam*.
Having touched [the water] with two blades of *darbha* grass and having recited the *Tāra* mantra eight times,
one should then display the *dhenu-mudrā* and protect it with the *astra-mantra*.
Having enveloped [it] with the armor [mantra] and the root mantra, O Pārvatī,
having worshipped with the five offerings, [one should place] both knees...
Having circled three times above the fire-pit while recollecting the root mantra,
the Guru should place the fire within it facing himself.
Having sprinkled it with water, O Maheśvarī, one should place it at the head of the wood;
then, one should slowly kindle the fire with the *citpiṅgala* mantra.
Or else, the best among those who know the mantras should bring forth a fan or a bellows;
with palms joined in reverence, he should worship the blazing fire with this mantra: "I bow to Agni, the kindled one."
Having made the request and performed the ritual attendance, he should approach the Guru;
this is preceded by the salutation to the Guru, followed by the binding of the ten directions.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the placement upon the fire with the seed-syllables (manus);
likewise, one should place Hiraṇyā and the others in due order with the seed-syllables of the tongue, the limbs, and the forms.
The supreme guru should likewise place [the mantras] on the generative organ, the anus, the head, the mouth,
the pair of nostrils and eyes, and on all the limbs.
The Guru should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs beginning with the Ṛṣi, and the placement of the heart and other parts.
[He should assign: Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and the one named Havyavāhana.
The wise one should place these [mantras], beginning with *dhruva agnaye* and ending with *candreṇa namaḥ*,
respectively upon the head, shoulders, sides, and hips, following the direction of circumambulation.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma);
O Maheśvarī, one should accomplish this five times with the [mantras] ending in *sambhava*.
Then, having uttered the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should offer oblations individually with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) in the proper sequence.
And having tied the cords for binding the sacrificial fuel into a single unit, O beloved,
place them on the south, and likewise a handful of *darbha* grass on the north.
The sacrificial ladles (sruk) are made from the wood of the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, and Jāmbū;
furthermore, there are eighteen [types], and the three [measures] for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) are equal in height.
Or [he may perform it] one thousand and eight times with the darbha-grass used for strewing;
the preceptor [should use] a hundred fistfuls of darbha, each measuring six finger-breadths in width.
With two ropes, a collection of essential materials, and seventeen *darbha* blades for the *prokṣaṇī*;
with *darbha* blades for the *praṇītā* vessel, and twelve [blades] for the *brahmakūrca*.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be measured with seven blades of *mānusa* grass; the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is performed with six blades of *kuśa*;
and for the purpose of purifying the vessels used for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), it should be done with two blades of *darbha*.
Fifty, or half of that, or even twenty-five, kuśa-blades are prescribed;
likewise, a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is used.
One should not have [the vessel] made with less than one full prastha;
the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be one cubit (*hasta*) in length, and they should be filled to the measure of a *śukti*.
Having prepared these vessels, one should avoid those that are mismatched in time;
then, having swept around the fire, one should offer the oblation with the consecrated mantra.
Then, having sprinkled [the area] with water using the Astra-mantra,
the preceptors should perform the strewing around the directions with the mantra "devasya tvā".
O Goddess, the Guru should place [the syllables] from south to north, and from north to south,
in the middle above the girdle, according to the proper sequence.
Thereafter, one should prepare the vessels on the ground to the north of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
having spread kuśa grass upon the earth, as well as the praṇītā and prokṣaṇī vessels.

O Goddess, the most excellent of teachers should prepare the vessel for clarified butter, the pot for the sacrificial rice (caru), the large and small ladles (sruk and sruva), a handful of kuśa grass, and the fuel-sticks for the fire.

Having sprinkled this [vessel], which is turned face-down, with the water for the *arghya* offering using both hands joined in the form of a *dvandva* and accompanied by the mantra, one should display the *astramudrā*.
Having performed the *prokṣaṇī* rite, one should then place a vessel with a *darbha* grass ring facing toward oneself;
it should be filled with water while reciting "āpaḥ punantu" and using the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having purified that [fuel] three times with both hands and sprinkled it with water while reciting the Astra mantra,
one should untie the knot of the fuel-bundle with the Varma mantra, O Maheśvarī.
Having purified these vessels and turned them upward, one should sprinkle them with water;
then, one should place a lotus-seat and a bundle of *darbha* grass to the south.
Then, O King, having invoked the best of the twice-born with the mantra,
and having invoked Arvāvasu, one should worship him with perfumes and flowers.
Having placed it in front of the *praṇītā* waters,
one should fill it with water using the *brahmabīja* mantra or the perfected (*siddha*) mantra, O Pārvatī.
Having invoked Varuṇa, one should subsequently worship Brahmā;
and with the permission of Brahmā, one should raise [the water] up to the tip of the nose with both arms.
Having placed the eastern seat upon kusa grass between Dhaneśa and Īśvara and having covered it with darbha grass, the Guru [recites] eight times.
Having taken up a vessel of clarified butter, one should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra.
Having filled it with cow's ghee, one should gaze upon it with the Netra-mantra.
Having established it in the northwestern direction near Mekhala,
the Guru should perform the lustration with the armor-mantra (tanutra) and cast it into the fire.
Furthermore, O Pārvatī, the practitioner of mantra, having displayed the two blades of darbha grass three times with the Astra-mantra, should cast them into the fire while reciting the mantra.
Having taken [the embers] and placed them in the womb,
one should join them together with two *darbha* blades, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length and tied with a knot in the middle.
One should cast [the offering] into the middle of the fire with the mantra "śukram asi," and afterwards cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the mantra "nirvapāmi."
Having recited three times, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni; I offer you, acceptable to Agni," he should show two *darbha* blades to the deity and the principal [victim] and cause them to gaze.
Having sprinkled [the oblation] over it and placed it in the northern [fire], there is neither the fire of birth nor the ritual action.
Thereafter, one should purify the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the pair of right and left hands;
then, one should purify the tips, middles, and bases of a pair of *kuśa* blades.
Having heated [the implements] in the fire and wiped them three times with the root mantra,
one should likewise purify the *sruk* and place those [implements] back in that very same spot.
Then, O Maheśvarī, having taken up the enclosing sticks (paridhis) with the mantras of Varma, Netra, and Asu, one should place them in the west, the south, and the north.
Above that, the Guru should place two [samidhs] with the Kavaca mantra;
there, the Guru should place the *anuyāja* samidh above the *praṇītā* vessel.
One should worship the Fire-god with incense, flowers, and other offerings, as well as his tongues and other attributes;
then, having worshipped the world-protectors and the deities of the sacrificial pit and its girdles.
Brāhmī, Vajrī, as well as Aindrī, Dhanvirākṣī, Maheśvarī,
Śabalā, and Vegā— these are the deities of the fire-pits in their respective order.
O Goddess, having invoked the enclosing sticks (paridhi), the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa), and Brahmā in their proper order,
one should worship Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī in succession.
Then, having offered a fuel-stick (samidh), one should begin the sprinkling (pariṣecana) around [the fire] with the mantra beginning with "Aditi," proceeding in due order.
One should worship Agni Jātavedas according to the prescribed method;
one should take fifteen pieces of fuel-wood and worship them with fragrant flowers.
Once the [oblation] has been offered, the preceptor should then place this rope in the form of a ring;
having thoroughly saturated the heap of fuel sticks with clarified butter, the preceptor [proceeds].
He has two heads and one heart, four ears and two nostrils;
he has two mouths, six eyes, is tawny-colored, and possesses seven hands.
Having three girdles and three feet, surrounded by seven tongues of flame,
possessing four horns and mounted upon a bull, he has a splendor equal to that of Balarāma and the Sun.
Adorned with the sacred thread and graced by a crown of matted locks,
he has four hands on the left side and three hands on the right.
In his right hands, he holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a rosary, and a spear; in his left hands, he holds a javelin, a fan, and a vessel of clarified butter.
Having meditated thus, the mantra-practitioner, having previously obtained the permission of Brahmā,
should thereafter perform the oblation of fuel-wood and then offer clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
At the junction of the channels, however, one should carefully perform the opening of the mouth;
the Guru should offer oblations into the stomach with the mantra "To Agni, Svāhā" while focusing on the right eye.
O Dear One, having taken clarified butter from the left side for the purpose of removing obstacles on the left of the fire,
the Guru should offer oblations with the heart-mantra, saying "Svāhā to Soma."
Then, having taken clarified butter from the center of the fire with the middle finger, one should offer it from the eye while reciting the mantra: "To Agni and Soma, svāhā! (agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā).
O Goddess of the gods, taking clarified butter from the right side with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer it into the mouth of the fire with the mantra: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"
Then, having offered oblations three times with the fire-mantra accompanied by the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis,
one should likewise offer oblations in due order with the mantras of the tongues, the limbs, and the forms.
O beloved of the Guru, having first performed the recitation with the *ṛṣi*, *triṣṭubh* meter, and *mantra* seeds,
the preceptor should worship [the deity] with the root mantra and the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).
Thereafter, one who knows the root-mantra should offer fuel-sticks;
having offered eight oblations of clarified butter for each [mantra], he should do so separately and in due order.
One should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) and ending with *vivāha* (marriage) in their proper sequence:
namely, *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, and *nāmakaraṇa*.
First there may be the naming ceremony, then the first outing;
then the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and then the initiation by the teacher.
The four vows proclaimed in the Vedas and the rite of ceremonial bathing—
these are declared to be the concluding rites for the ceremonies beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception), ending with marriage.
Thinking, "I shall perform the subsequent rite," one should offer each fuel-stick individually;
at the end, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and then offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire.
Then, for the sake of purification from birth-impurity, once the rite of birth (jātakarma) has been performed,
one should discard the ritual implements such as the surrounding grass mats (paristaraṇa) and so forth.
O Maheśvarī, having sprinkled that sacrificial pit with cow-dung water,
the preceptor should perform the ritual practice as previously described, according to the rules.
One should perform the oblation with the tongue-mantras and the form-mantras, which are divided into ten varieties,
and with the mantras of Mahāgaṇapati as they have been previously imparted.
Then, having worshipped the pīṭha and meditated upon the deity within its fire, the Guru should perform the sacrifice for the sake of the deity’s form, together with the retinue and other attendants.
And for the purpose of bringing [the deity] face-to-face, one should offer twenty-five oblations;
one should meditate on the identity of the deity with one's own self by means of the root mantra.
Then, one should offer eleven oblations of ghee for the purpose of unifying the channels (nāḍī),
and one oblation of ghee to each of the deities of the enclosures (āvṛti).
In this manner, the preceptor should perform the rite of generating the fire;
he must not fail to do so, for if he does not perform it, the oblation would be fruitless.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Generating the Fire," in the section on rites for specific desires (*kāmyakāṇḍa*) within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara in the venerable *Vātulottara*.
Hereafter, I shall explain [the procedure] for the Guru together with the presiding deities (*mūrtipa*).
The oblation of substances and so forth, ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the libation (tarpaṇa), and the worship of the water-pot (kumbha).
O Pārvatī, listen now in due order to the specific recitation and its respective fruit;
and having seated the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) within the jars situated inside the pavilion.
O Maheśvarī, one should perform the purification of the seat and so forth, as well as the ritual placement (nyāsa);
one should effect the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta.
Purification, washing, drying, protection,
and sprinkling— these five should be performed with recollections in other sacrificial pits.
Then, the preceptor should move the fire from the sacrificial pit toward the east and other directions;
having first approached the fire with the mantra "agnim īle," he should attend to it.
Then, with the mantra "iṣe tvorje," one should place [the oblation] in the southeast;
with "tvam agne" in the south; and with "upa tvāgne" in the southwest.

In the western [quarter], one should recite the *jātavedas* hymn; in the northwestern, the *vyāhṛtis*, O beloved; in the northern, the hymn beginning with *agniṃ dūtam*; and in the northeastern, the hymn beginning with *agnim agni*.
One should remain thus until satisfied, and afterwards perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
then, preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the tongue, the limbs, the form, and so forth.
Having offered the substances according to their respective numbers while uttering the names of the deities,
O Queen of Gods, one should perform the *abādhā* and other rites separately for each, assuming the form of the Guru.
In each of their respective fire-pits, he should have everything performed by all of them in the prescribed order;
it must not be done without the *caru* oblation, which is said to be cooked by Brahmins.
O Great Goddess, one should not have the enclosing fence (paridhi) constructed by the presiding deities of the images;
rather, having invoked Bhava and the others into the forms, one should worship them with the seat-mantras (pīṭhamantra).

Each one, including the officiating priests, the preceptor, and others, should likewise offer oblations individually with the mantras beginning with "jihvā," as well as with the mantras for the ṛṣis and meters, starting from the root mantra.
They should offer the cooked oblation and five oblations of clarified butter;
thereafter, the preceptors and others should offer oblations of the ritual substances.
In the heart, there is the destruction of one's lineage; in the belly, the cessation of rain;
at the waist, the loss of one's position; and at the knees, there shall be expulsion.
Death occurs at the base of the arm, whereas [oblations] on the tongue grant all desires;
therefore, one should especially perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon the tongue.
Having performed the oblation, O Goddess of gods, one should form the mudrās— the deer, the goose, the sow,
the peacock, and the hen— within the house of the oblation materials, O beloved.
Any fire offering (homa) performed without the mudrās shall be entirely fruitless.
O Śivā, [the materials are] clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, parched grain, wheat, and mustard seeds.
O Maheśvarī, sesame, truṭika, parched grain, flour, milk, and cow’s ghee— these ten in sequence, along with two thousand [units] and one kuḍupa.
The sacrificial fuel-stick (samit) should be made of palāśa or khadira wood, six finger-breadths in length and well-proportioned in width;
it must be free from moisture, devoid of curvature, and beautifully formed.
A prastha of rice grains produced from paddy, when cooked with turmeric, becomes free from defects such as impurities and reaches a weight of five hundred [palas].
Other substances such as wheat and the like are prescribed to be half that amount;
having washed and purified them, one should fill the vessel with the root mantra.
Having first recited the mantra of the deity beginning with the *praṇava* in due order,
one should offer oblations separately to each of those who bear the form of the Guru, using the root mantra.
O Dear One, one should offer five hundred and eight oblations above the thousand in the principal fire-pit to the Guru, preceded by the formal renunciation of the intended object.
Then those guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should again perform the oblations separately in eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
O Goddess, numbering one thousand, three hundred, seventy, and four.
For the image-worshippers (mūrtipās), a separate oblation is prescribed every single day;
for each, there are one hundred thousand measures of distinct substances, consisting of both the previously mentioned clarified butter and the subsequent clarified butter.
And one should perform the supreme oblation (homa) dedicated until the end of the day;
or, O Goddess, the most excellent Guru should offer the ten substances a hundred thousand times.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer clarified butter at the end of the substances and the middle [portion] as well;
offering all the substances a hundred thousand times is proclaimed as the lowest [grade].
Then, in the middle of the altar, the preceptor should draw a lotus and prepare one hundred and twenty-five squares as previously described.
One should fill [the vessels] separately with powders of five colors;
having filled them with śāli rice, half a droṇa and half of that [measure].
Taking one *prastha* each of all the materials, beginning with the principal substance, in their proper order,
one should collect one hundred and twenty-five vessels made of gold and other precious metals.
One should hold a jar containing one *droṇa* of water, half of that, or half of that again;
others should be filled with one *prastha*, provided they are free from being broken or cracked.
O Goddess, the preceptor, having washed the jars with the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
having wrapped them with thread using the armor-mantra (varmamantra), and having fumigated them with incense, [he should do so] by means of the root-mantra (mūlamantra).
O Maheśvarī, one should subsequently place the pitcher while reciting the Kavaca mantra;
one should worship the downward-facing jar as being composed of the Kalās.
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and lifted up the pitcher facing upward,
[one should place] a bundle of thirty-six darbha-grasses and a bundle of twenty-five [darbhas].
Having arranged twenty-seven bundles of darbha grass and five each in their proper order, one should fill the jar with milk.
One should fill [the vessels] with water mixed with the eight fragrances, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), kuśa-water,
the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), decoctions (kaṣāya), and pure water.
One should place the nine gems or the five gems, as well as the [deities] beginning with Mātṛkā;
and one should place ten niṣkas of gold in the principal pitcher.
In the pitchers of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśas), one should place an image made of five *niṣkas* of gold;
outside, in the enclosure, one should place an image made of a single *niṣka* of gold.
One should place [the image] upon a pedestal made of gold, and in other cases, upon statues and jars;
one should install the vital breath (prāṇa) with the prāṇamantra and cast in the medicinal herbs.
O Maheśvarī, one should place a mango sprout upon these with the Netra-mantra, and having placed a coconut fruit, one should do so with the Kavaca-mantra.
O Pārvatī, having covered [the image] with a dukūla garment while reciting the Astra-mantra,
one should then clothe it with various new garments and white cloths in the proper order.
Having covered all the jars and placed a bundle of kuśa grass on the head with the mantra,
one should perform the placement (vinyāsa) beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma), as well as the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā).
Having invoked the lords of the gods into the jars in due order, beginning with the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas),
and having invoked all the gods, including those of the primary enclosure and so forth.
O Goddess of Gods, having invoked and worshipped the one hundred and twenty-five [deities], the mantra-expert should worship the Kalās with the mantras of the thirty-six Tattvas.
Thereafter, one should worship the five Brahmamanus with ritual offerings;
and ten Brahmins should chant the root mantra around [the deity].
Having first performed the nyāsa of the ṛṣis and other elements one thousand and twenty-five times,
[he should worship] Gaṇeśa and Kṣetrapāla in the four directions of the square.
The Durgā-mantra, Vāṇī, Prāsāda, Tryambaka,
Bhuvaneśī, Vāstu, Rākṣoghna, and the Navagrahas.
Then [he should recite] the Śrī Rudra, the Pāvamāna, the Śrī Sūkta, the Viṣṇu Sūkta, the Bhū Sūkta, the Brahma Sūkta, and thereafter the mantra of the Dhṛta Sūkta.
O Goddess, one should recite the seven hundred [verses] all around in the proper order;
at the four gates, the best of Brahmins should recite the four Vedas.
One should satisfy [the deities] with water mixed with milk in the northern direction, offering a tenth part;
and having seated ten Brahmins within the mandala, one should draw a lotus.
Having filled the vessels with rice grains, one should place them there;
or, having filled them with milk or water, one should deposit fragrant flowers within.
Having invoked the deity, the practitioner of mantra, joined with the root mantra, should worship the god and offer libations with sesame seeds and rice one thousand two hundred and fifty times.
O Maheśvarī, one should perform [the rite] anew up until the conclusion of the oblation;
at the end of the oblation, the Guru should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the mantra beginning with "yad asya."
Having prepared the *anuyāja* fuel-sticks and offered the rope,
and thereafter having offered the *jaya* oblations and so forth, one should then offer the expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) oblation.
Then, O Goddess, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter for each of the great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*),
followed by the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and having dismissed Brahmā.
One should conclude the Homa at the end and perform the offering of the bali-oblation;
then, one should prepare nine piṇḍas with clarified butter and sacrificial oblation.
Having installed the Guru-kuṇḍa and the others, and having approached the wooden lamps,
the preceptor and the patron should subsequently worship the altar-pitchers (vedikumbhas).
O Maheśvarī, having summoned the disciple,
the mantrin should hold that primary pitcher upon his head amidst the auspicious sounds of the Vedas.
Having taken up all the jars along with the image-protectors (mūrtipāḥ) and the best of the twice-born,
the mantra-practitioner should cause the jar to enter within by means of circumambulation.
Having worshipped the *liṅga* with the root mantra in the proper sequence, beginning with the *pradhāna*,
one should sprinkle it with its own *sūkta* and the root mantra, O Pārvatī.
O Maheśvarī, the great worship (mahāpūjā) should be performed according to what was previously stated;
having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) to all, one should dedicate it all [to the deity].
O beloved, one should feed two hundred and fifty Brahmins with rice cooked in milk,
accompanied by ghee, soup, vegetables, and delicious delicacies.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should offer food consisting of milk-rice mixed with fine milk, sugar, and honey; once they have eaten, one should also present betel leaf.
The sacrificer should devoutly accept the words of blessing from the mantra;
in this very manner, day after day, until the end of the designated period.
Having performed the final oblation at the end of that, and having completed the purificatory rite (avabhṛtha),
one should then remove the bracelet and perform a pure ablution.
Then, O Dear One, having entered the sacrificial hall and sat down near the preceptor’s fire-pit,
the preceptor [should sit] while the patron and the Brahmins are seated.
One should cause gifts of cows, land, and so forth, as well as goats, buffaloes, rhinoceroses, sesame oil, and oxen to be given.
O Maheśvarī, flowers, fruits, betel leaf, water, bedding and the like, curd-rice, the sacrificial thread, and the gift of a maiden;

O Maheśvarī, one should give a pair of sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and a golden water-pot in a secluded place; at the conclusion of that, one should perform a secret gift and undergo the Kṛcchra penance.
The wise man should duly give to the preceptors and others among the Brahmins a sacrificial fee of twenty-five niṣkas, as well as a secluded vehicle.
One should cause the parasol, the fly-whisk, along with the ritual implements and the secret gift,
as well as a servant, to be presented to the preceptor.
Then, as prescribed for the mantra-expert, one should give an extensive display of wealth,
including seven or ten *niṣkas* and a couch covered with a bedspread.
O Great Goddess, having taken it herself, she should cause it to be given to the Ācārya;
O Beloved, she should cause ten niṣkas and fine garments to be given to the Brahmā priest.
One should cause seven niṣkas to be given to the member of the assembly for the sandals,
and five niṣkas each should be given separately to those representing the deities, along with earrings.
One should cause to be given one and a half niṣkas individually to the twice-born who perform the libations,
and two and a half niṣkas to those who chant the Vedas.
O Pārvatī, for those who recite the root mantra, the fee is one and a half niṣkas;
for others, such as reciters and attendants, it is said to be one niṣka.
And likewise for those who have performed circumambulations and those who have offered worship,
as well as for the poor, the blind, the deaf, and others, he should give sacrificial fees according to his ability.
Having given [the gift] in this manner, one enjoys the complete fruit in due order;
for half of what was prescribed, there shall be half the fruit, and for a fraction of what was prescribed, there shall be a fraction of the fruit.
O Goddess, having understood the Dharma, the wise man who is the best of kings should perform this Lakṣahoma for the sake of the prosperity of his own lineage.
It destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, wards off all death,
pacifies all suffering, and bestows auspiciousness at all times.
It should be known as the bringer of all peace, bestowing the increase of sons and grandsons;
O Goddess, it grants contentment and nourishment, and bestows fame and the increase of splendor.
There shall be an increase in lifespan, happiness, and victory everywhere;
the merit that comes from the gift of land is equal to the fruit of many sacrifices.
At the end of the body, together with twenty-one generations of my lineage, I shall attain union with me;
the fruit of all desired objects will be swiftly attained—this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Ritual Procedure for the Lakṣahoma," in the section on rites with specific desires within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara in the Śrī Vātulāgama.
May there be well-being.
O Goddess, whenever there is a pair of daily offerings (balis) for a particular deity,
then during an occasional rite (naimittika), the practitioner of mantra should offer the bali at the three times of day.
Or, while the daily ritual of offering (balikarma) is being performed at the three times of day,
one should then perform the occasional rite (naimittika) together with that very daily offering.
Alternatively,
O Maheśvarī, in another manner, when there is an occasional occasion, one should perform the daily offering (bali) early in the morning.
At midday and likewise at evening, one should offer the occasional *bali*;
having first performed the daily offering, the [occasional] *bali* should be offered no later than two *nāḍīs* after that.
Or rather, the performer of the occasional bali-mantra should proceed in this very manner;
O Goddess, in the case of a bali rite performed for a specific desire, some special rule is occasionally prescribed.
One should perform it at midday, or in the evening, or even in both; here, it may be done together with the daily bali offering, or separately, with that bali being performed first.
Thus, O Goddess, the sequence of offerings for the daily rites and so forth has been described;
it brings complete satisfaction to the deities of the retinue through these daily practices.
Since the attainment of the full fruit shall belong to Your Majesty and there shall be happiness for all living beings, one should therefore constantly perform the bali offering.
By means of that through which the gods and others residing in worlds such as the Brahma-world may find satisfaction, may there be all prosperity for the king.
Therefore, one who is very dear to Śiva should perform the occasional *bali* offering;
for the performer, there shall be the attainment of desired fruits and the warding off of all enemies.
Since all peace is attained thereby, one should perform the desired offering (kāmyabali);
the propitiation of Brahmā occurs in the forenoon, and that of Viṣṇu occurs at midday.
O Pārvatī, the offering of the *bali* to Śaṅkara indeed takes place at evening;
according to the distinctions of creation and so forth, the *bali* is conceived as threefold across the three periods of time.
Here, the presiding deities are to be known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
[they are worshipped] two times, three times, and four times respectively.
In the daily, occasional, and optional rites, one should offer the bali-oblation to the deities.
Svasti!
Hereafter, I shall now explain [the matter] according to the divisions of time.
O Pārvatī, listen now in due order to the determination regarding the offering of oblations (balidāna) within the various daily rites and other rituals for Śiva and the other gods. (p. 250)
He also [taught] the deities who partake of the offerings, as well as the substances for the offerings,
the mantras for the offerings, and the three kinds of musical instruments prescribed for the offerings.
I shall here state the names of the *indrāditāla* rhythms for the satisfaction of all the gods and for the happiness of all embodied beings.
For the increase of the victory, sovereignty, prosperity, sons, and longevity of kings,
for the cessation of all misfortunes, and for the welfare of the entire world.
Therefore, O Goddess, the offering of the bali should be performed with great effort in due order at dawn, at midday, and in the evening.

O Maheśvarī, the practitioner of mantra should perform the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna) according to the prescribed rules during rites that are regular, occasional, or performed for specific desires.
One should offer the bali at midday, in the evening, during the performance of daily rites, or during a great portent or the rite of the great ablution.
During rites of expiation, for a guru, and especially during the consecration of an image,
as well as on occasions such as great festivals, one should offer the bali-oblation three times a day.
In this manner, the sequence for the ritual procedure of offering the *bali* should be performed toward the Śaiva Teacher;
likewise, it applies to Durgā, Gaṇanātha, and in rites such as the daily *bali* offerings.
One should perform [the rite] at midday and likewise in the evening during festivals of speech and the like;
however, for Viṣṇu, Ṣaṇmukha, Śaṅkara, and Acyuta, it should be performed at all three times of day.
One should offer the bali at two times or three times during the daily rites and so forth;
likewise for Śiva and the other deities during the daily, occasional, and other rituals.
O beloved, listen to the deities of the bali offering as described according to the divisions of time:
Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and Dakṣiṇeśvara.
The guardians of the quarters, together with the lords of the gods, [worshipped] the wielder of the trident and the wielder of the axe;
after them, Mahānandi, Vīrabhadra, and Vināyaka.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers.
The Mothers, as well as the worlds, the Mothers who are the mothers of all;
the entire host of Mothers, Lakṣmī, Bhūcarī, and likewise Khecarī.
The Teacher, Durgā, Guha, Śrīda, and likewise Caṇḍanātha;
Tīkṣṇa and Dauṣṭra, and Mṛgāsya—the guardians of the gates of the city.
Bhṛṅgī, Mahākāla, Bhūtanātha, Mahīdhara, Parvateśa, Guheśa, Kālapāśa, and Kapālī.
At its end is Kṣetrapāla, and beyond that in the great pīṭha are Bhūtida,
Durnirīkṣa, Bhīmarūpa, and Sulocana.
Sumukha and Subāhu, Kālapāśa and Kapālī, with their tawny hair hanging down; and above them is Harasena.
These are declared to be the eternal deities of the Śaiva [tradition], beginning with the crows:
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Garuḍa, Ananta, Vighneśvara, and Śiva.
The guardians of the directions, Vīrabhadra, Ekadanta, those beginning with Brāhmī,
Śāstṛ, Durgā, Dhanada, and Viṣvaksena are likewise [to be placed] at the gate-towers (gopura).
Cakrapāṇi, Śaṅkhapāṇi, and Śrībhūmi are on the outside all around;
then Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, and Saṃpratiṣṭhita;
Kṣetreśa is at the end, and then on the balipīṭha are those beginning with Kiṣku and Dhanu.
Kiṣkindha, Śaṅkara, Bhauma, Bhīma, Sukumāraka,
then Bāhulaka, Vijaya, and Anantavikrama.
Furthermore, Piṅgalakeśākṣa and Harasena are in the middle;
these are the deities of the offering (bali) from the door to the base of the offering-altar (balipīṭha) in the temple of Hari.
Caṇḍikā and Ambikā, Siṃha, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Gaṇeśa, and Īśvara; the Guardians of the Quarters, Vīreśa, Vighneśa, Mātṛkā, and the others previously mentioned.
Then Śāstṛ, Durgā, and Dhanada; then Muṇḍinī at the gate-tower (gopura);
then Hlādinī and Mohinī at the door; and after that, Vijayantī.
Kātyāyanī, Bahirathā, Kālī, and the others are the deities of the bali offering:
Kālī, Karālī, Virajā, Mandarā, and Vindhyavāsinī.
Suprabhā, Siṃhavaktrā, and Daityamardinī follow thereafter;
then the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa) at the Balipīṭha, and the deities beginning with Brahmaghoṣī.
Brahmaghoṣī, Sughoṣī, Māyatheṣṭī,
Sukharāgiṇī, Saṃmukhī, Subhagā, Dikṣupramodinī, and Atha-ātmanī.
Brāhmī is likewise said to be in the center; the deities of Durgā’s offering are Vajrapāṇi, Śaktipāṇi, and the one named Sukumāra.
Bhadrasena, Śikhī, Bhāsya, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Lokapā, Mātṛ, Śāstra, Ambikā, Skanda, Dhanada, and Dhūrtasena.
Agniketu and Sūryaketu were stationed at the gate of the city-gate (gopura) outside of that; and Devasenāpati, Agninetra, and Dagdha were stationed holding swords.
Pāśahasta, Hayaketu (known as Hastasaṃjña), and Gadādhara;
then Śūlavilāsinī and the others, ending with Īśānī, and likewise above.
Then Viprapriya and Kṣetreśa are located at the Balipīṭha;
furthermore, Bhūtidā and the others mentioned in the Śaiva scriptures are enjoined by the Lord in this very place.
The Bali-devas are said to belong to Skanda, the Supreme Self;
likewise, Kṣurikā and Khaḍgapāṇi are the two gatekeepers outside.
Vīrabāhu, Mahāvīra, Nīla, Aśma, Ibha, Śaṅkara,
the Guardians of the Quarters, the Mothers, Śāstṛ, Dhanada, and likewise Ghoṣavān.
Tīkṣṇa, Tīkṣṇadanta, Goptṛ, Piṅgalākṣa, and Vīrasena, the son of Śambhu, are stationed outside all around the city gate.
Tridik, Śūlī, Dakṣa, Bhīmarūpa, and Kṣetrapa;
likewise Vīrabāhu, Mahāvīra, Vidyut, and Vāsavilāsin.
He is sharp, with sharp teeth and star-like eyes, the source of worldly existence;
his hair and eyes are tawny below, while the army of the scriptures is above.
On the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), however, these are declared in the scripture to be the deities of the offering (balideva):
Vajradanta, Gajāsyaka, Mahāpāśa, and Vināyaka.
Then [the deities] Śiva, the Guardians of the Quarters (Dikpālas), the Mothers (Mātṛs), the Teacher (Śāstṛ), Durgā, and Skanda [are placed];
and at the Gopura is the one named Caṇḍavikrama, along with Kumbhodara.
Then, the obstructors in the directions were Vajradanta with the face of an elephant,
Bhīma with the face of a buffalo, and likewise Meghanāda.
Virūpākṣa, Varada, and Sarvabhakṣaka;
then the final Kṣetrapāla, followed by Gajavaktra and the others.
Then there are he who is called Gajavaktra and Gaṇeśa, as well as Vināyaka,
Caṇḍavikramaka, Vighnakara, Śūrpāyu, and Mekhalā.
Then Śūrpakarṇa and Nāgadantī shall be born from the mouths of Rudra;
these are remembered as being located in the cardinal directions and above and below the pedestal of Bali.
Thus, the deities of the offering to Vighneśa at the gates and other locations have been proclaimed:
Nandin, Caṇḍa, Jayatsena, Viṣvaksena, and likewise Vṛṣa.
Garuḍa, Ananta, Vighneśa, Śiva, the Guardians of the Quarters, the Mothers, Śāstṛ, Durgā, Guha, and Caṇḍasena are at the gate-towers (gopura).
Śūla and Ariṇa are in the outer directions, and Nandin is everywhere; Mahākāla, Haya, Bhūtanātha, and Mahīdhara are behind.
Then Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana,
as well as Kṣetrapāla, [should be worshipped] in the northeast on the bali-pīṭha thereafter.
May all the givers of nooses belonging to Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu come;
may they dwell here upon this sacrificial pedestal, satisfied and at their ease.
Having propitiated with the mantra "Oṃ namo yukpārṣadebhyaḥ," one should offer the bali;
hereafter, O beloved, hear about the bali materials for Śarva and the others.
Ghee with rice, bilva leaves, and jasmine flowers;
sacred sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, water, as well as incense and a lamp.
In the Śaiva tradition, this sacrificial offering (bali-dravya) is said to consist of curd-rice, tulasī, the kalhāra flower,
red sandalwood, and so forth.
Aloe-wood, rose-apple leaves, and jasmine flowers,
as well as milk-rice— these and everything else for Durgā are to be offered as before.
To Skanda, one should offer incense mixed with *gorocana* along with jaggery-rice;
and to the Lord of the Hosts of Apes, *śatapuṣpa*, *nirguṇḍī*, and leaves.
Fine sandalwood, honeyed food, and likewise pure flowers,
or else banyan-sandalwood and mung-bean porridge— this is declared to be for Śaṅkara.
Camphor, agallochum, and fragrant substances, as well as *droṇa* flowers and *apāmārga* leaves, are prescribed; now the worship of the Teacher (*Śāstṛ*) is being described.
Kṛsarā rice, sandalwood mixed with camphor,
the Nandyāvarta flower, bilva leaves, and other items as previously mentioned.
If the aforementioned substances are unavailable among all the gods, or even among these [humans],
one may use *śuddhodana* (pure rice) or whatever other substances are obtained.
Fragrant flowers and leaves should be used for the rite of offering (balikarma); these are declared to be the materials for the bali. O beloved, now hear the mantras for the bali.
Having first meditated upon and worshipped the deity, the mantra-practitioner, having displayed the perfumes and other offerings along with the ritual hand-gestures (mudrās),
should present the bali offering using the specific bali-mantras prescribed for each.
The instructor should offer incense with the little finger, flowers with the tip of the thumb,
incense smoke with the index finger, and likewise a lamp with the middle finger.
Having said "May [this] food be free from disease," one should offer the mudrās, scents, and so forth in sequence;
then, after pronouncing the name of the deity preceded by "Savitr" and ending with "Onnamaḥ," one offers water.
One should utter "arcaya" (worship) for the deity, as well as for the leaf and the flower;
likewise, the mantra-practitioner should say "anna" (food), ending with the wife of fire (svāhā).
These are the bali-mantras for the individual gatekeepers and other deities in their respective order, intended for all the immortals in the daily ritual.
However, in certain rites such as the offering of oblations (*balikarma*) performed by those who interpret omens and the like,
there are always nine introductory verses as well as garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*).
There, indeed, were the attendants (pārṣadas) of Manu and the Mothers (mātṛs) in various places;
some were lords of the hosts of offering-deities (balideva), while others were attendants and the like.
It need not be spoken here, as it has already been explained by me in detail during the festivals; these are called the *balimantras*. Now, listen to the musical instruments.
The best consists of twelve musical instruments, the middling of seven, and the lowest of five; thus, musical instruments are of three kinds.
Kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, cymbals, and likewise maddalas;
lutes, flutes, cymbals, trumpets, and the nāga-instrument.
The *yallarī* is a conch-like wind instrument; thus there are twelve musical instruments:
the conch (*śaṅkha*), the drum (*mṛdaṅga*), the small drum (*paṇava*), the lute (*vīṇā*), and likewise the cymbals (*tāla*).
The kahala and the dundubhi—these are proclaimed as the seven musical instruments;
likewise the maddala, the tāla, and the jayaghaṇṭikā.
The conch and the *kalahaṃ* are proclaimed as the five musical instruments;
now, the names of the *tālas* beginning with Indra are stated in their proper order.
The *samatāla* belongs to the Lord of the Gods (Indra), while that of Agni is called *bandhāpaṇa*.
The *bhṛṅgitāla* belongs to Yama, and the *mallatāla* belongs to Nirṛti.
The Vāruṇa [tāla] consists of nine *tālas*, while the Nāga-tāla belongs to Māruta;
the one called Kauśika belongs to Soma, and the Dakka-īśāna-tāla [belongs to Īśāna].
The *vṛṣatāla* belongs to the great bull, the *śaśitālakam* to the Mothers,
the *utkalatāla* to Skanda, and the *taṭaprahāraka* to Durgā.
The difficult song of Caṇḍanātha is proclaimed;
the Gāndhāra song is in the East, and Kolli is in the south-eastern region.
Kauśikī is in the south, and Naṭabhāṣā is in the southwest;
Kāmara-gāna is in the west, and Karkaśī is in the domain of Vāyu (the northwest).
And in the subsequent [sections], one should employ the respective *rāgas* in the *śālā*, *pāṇi*, and *gocara* [styles];
likewise, the *tālas* and songs are prescribed for the daily rite, the offering festival (*balis*), and the ritual procedure.
Whenever the teacher performs the circumambulation of the eternal image during occasional rites and the like,
he should do so together with that occasional image and the offering image (balimūrti).
"Or else, [one should initiate] one who is joined with an Asura king or by the mark of Anta.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the Parameśvara Tantra.
I salute the syllable Oṃ, the Sovereign of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī), the limit of the earth, enriched with yellow pigment (gorocanā), and the two-syllabled state (pada) which is the city of Virūḍha.
If the images (bera) are fashioned for a perpetual festival, they should be provided with brides.
One should determine half of that for them as the desired height of the image (bera).
One should always worship Śivā once, twice, or three, four, or five times; or six, seven, eight, or nine times.
O Pārvatī, if this [mantra], which bestows all desired fruits as thus instructed, is recited daily at dawn, at midday, or in the evening;
If the *balikarman* (offering to the spirits) is omitted, one should perform an expiation;
having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and performed the *nāndīkarma*, [one should proceed].
One should likewise perform one hundred and eight oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra,
and then carry out the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rule using the five Brahma-mantras and the six limbs.
One should bathe the deity with five or nine jars;
having worshipped the deity along with his retinue, one should offer sweet food as an oblation.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the deities and thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas;
thus the procedure for the morning is declared, while at midday it shall be twofold.
"O Goddess, at evening, that [rite] is equal [to the previous one] through the sequence of the rules for penance.
Thus it is stated in the *Candrajñāna*.
